News.title: William Chapman - latest: Inquest updates after man killed by tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park
News.content:
The AI-generated video depicting Trump fighting a tiger has generated strong reaction, with people saying he is "unfit for office" and "mentally disturbed".

The clip, which was posted on Trump's Truth Social account a few hours ago, shows him wrestling a tiger and taming it, with The Lion Sleeps Tonight playing in the background.

One X user reacting to the video, which was posted at 4.17am UK time, said: "Trump actually posted this AI video of him with a tiger in the middle of the night. This man is demented and mentally unwell."

Another commented: "Trump is very sick and unfit for the office of POTUS. The family of said man have now revealed he suffered significant mental illness and they are distressed by social media posts mocking the tragedy and their loss. For POTUS to post this is DISGRACEFUL!!!"

In a statement released last night, victim William Chapman's family said he suffered from significant mental illness "over a number of years" and was prescribed strong medication.

Another person wrote on X: "That is utterly disgraceful for anyone to do. For the president of the US to do it, while the family is still grieving, is a clear sign that he is totally unfit for the job."

One other said: "Musing on the level of ice-cold narcissism that it must take to watch a man being savaged by a tiger and think, 'But what if it was me, and I was stronger than it, and it liked me?'."

Another user simply said: "Trump is mentally disturbed."

Another challenged the president: "Is Trump saying if he jumped into the tiger enclosure he would have survived? Only one way to find out, Donald. Don't be a chicken."

One person questioned if Trump might have more important matters to focus on: "I had always assumed that national leaders would focus their energy on more important matters."

News.title: Key DWP update as PIP claimants 'could get just one payment'
News.content:
Key DWP update as PIP claimants 'could get just one payment'

The Resolution Foundation has published a new report

View 3 Images PIP is likely to be changed (Image: CHEBOTKEVICH via Getty Images)

Approximately one in six working-age people claiming disability benefits do not incur additional expenses because of their conditions, a new report has revealed while highlighting potential "waste" within the system.

‌



‌



Personal Independence Payment, commonly known as PIP, is intended to support people with the extra costs associated with living with a disability. However, the Resolution Foundation stated that its research indicated 16% of claimants surveyed reported zero costs arising from their condition.

‌



The think tank calculated that £4.4 billion could potentially be saved if payments were withdrawn or reduced, based on the degree of limitations reported by those claiming no additional expenses. Savanta polled 2,611 PIP recipients aged 16-64 across England and Wales during May and June, discovering that 12% of those with no costs experienced low limitations, while 4% had no costs despite higher level limitations.

‌



The foundation noted such a reform would particularly affect younger PIP claimants, having established that a fifth (21%) of current 16 to 24-year-old recipients reported minimal limitation and no extra costs from their disability.

View 3 Images The DWP administers PIP (Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

One-off PIP payments proposed

Additionally, the think tank proposed one-off payments instead of ongoing support for individuals who reported specific costs rather than daily requirements. The research discovered 30% of those with higher costs reported expenses relating to appliances, such as purchasing a mobility aid, and over a fifth (22%) reported requiring one-off adaptations, such as modifications to their home or vehicle.

‌



The report suggested that the assessment process should be overhauled to directly ask claimants about their additional costs and what assistance would enable them to lead more fulfilling lives. It also called for more regular but "lower-stakes check-ins" with recipients to gain a clearer picture of fluctuating conditions "and reduce the stress created by infrequent but high-stakes assessments".

Latest on PIP review

A Government review into PIP, along with proposals for reform, is anticipated to be released this autumn.

Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said: "PIP is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live more independently. But the current system is failing on several fronts – recipients don't trust it, awards don't fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.

‌



"As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed PIP system should focus more on support for people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people's needs would also mean that around one in six people who don't face additional costs because of their disability would either no longer qualify for support, or only receive limited help.

"While there is no perfect system of disability support, one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions could target greater support and engagement where it's needed, and avoid waste where it's not."

View 3 Images Sir Stephen Timms is leading a review into PIP (Image: WPA Pool, Getty Images)

‌



The cost of PIP

PIP expenditure stood at £16.3 billion in 2019-20, adjusted to today's prices for inflation, rising sharply to £27.3 billion by 2024-25, according to Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) figures released in September. Projections suggest this figure will soar further to £41.5 billion by 2030-31.

As of July 31, 2026, a total of 4.09 million people were entitled to claim PIP, the latest data reveals. This marks an increase from 3.83 million the previous year – a jump of 262,045, or 7%.

The number of claimants has approximately doubled since comparable records began in January 2019, when the total was 2.05 million. Learning disability charity Mencap challenged the Resolution Foundation survey, stating it was "inconsistent with our own research and understanding around the importance of PIP and what people with a learning disability and their families spend it on".

Article continues below

Chief executive Jon Sparkes said: "A learning disability is lifelong. The extra costs that come with it don't go away, and neither should adequate support to meet them". He stated PIP "can be a lifeline when it comes to covering energy costs, attending appointments, sensory aids and taking part in community life", emphasising that system reforms should be "shaped by disabled people" during the Government's ongoing review.

A DWP spokesperson said: "PIP is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person's day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, PIP is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform."

News.title: Britain to provide £17m to Chernobyl power plant damaged by Russian drone attack
News.content:
Britain to provide £17m to Chernobyl power plant damaged by Russian drone attack

Andy Burnham said he 'will listen to President Zelensky carefully' and promised that he would not be leaving Britain 'empty-handed' after his trip to Downing Street

View 4 Images (Image: Getty)

Britain has pledged to fund critical repairs to the Chernobyl power plant hit by a Russian drone attack.

‌



‌



It comes as Andy Burnham sought to bolster support for Ukraine amid “dark and difficult days” for the war-torn country during Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to Downing Street.

‌



The UK will provide £17 million to help restore its protective shelter and ventilation, which were damaged by an attack last year.

‌



Chancellor John Healey said the Government’s commitment to the Ukrainian people was “unshakeable”, while Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain will “stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail”.

View 4 Images Mr Burnham said the UK would step up support for Ukraine in the face of a barrage of Russian drone attacks (Image: BETTY LAURA ZAPATA/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

The PM hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, October 14 when he told the Ukrainian president the UK was “behind you and that will not change”.

‌



Mr Zelensky received an honour guard made up of troops from the Irish Guards on his arrival at No 10 on Wednesday.

The meeting came during a period of strained relations between Ukraine and the US after Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel last week as high fuel prices in America threatened to overshadow November’s mid-term elections.

The UK responded to news of the deal by pledging to “maintain pressure on Russia”.

‌



The US president has also suggested in recent days that Ukraine needs a new leader and claimed Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants a peace deal more than the government in Kyiv.

Mr Zelensky has also said use of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system was “blocked” and that as a result “people will die”, admitting that he felt betrayed by Mr Trump.

“It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he told Piers Morgan Uncensored.

‌



View 4 Images US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky (file image) (Image: Getty)

Starlink is used by Ukraine to defend against aerial attacks and for long-range drones targeting Russian sites.

Speaking in the Commons ahead of his meeting with Mr Zelensky, the Prime Minister said he would seek to restore Donald Trump’s support for Ukraine.

‌



During Prime Minister’s Questions, Mr Burnham said he was being “careful” in his language after Mr Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, as he said he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation.

He added: “I will listen to President Zelensky carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”

During his meeting with Mr Zelensky, he confirmed that the UK would accelerate the supply of crucial air defence missiles to Ukraine amid “heavy bombardment” from Russia.

‌



The accelerated support will see faster deliveries of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which have proved effective against Russian jet-powered drones.

Russia continues to pound Ukraine’s power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, after Mr Trump claimed that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”.

View 4 Images Mr Zelensky met the Prime Minister for talks at No 10 (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Announcing new funding for repairs at Chernobyl, Mr Healey said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable.

“We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.”

Mr Miliband said: “Our message to Putin is clear – we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail.

Article continues below

“Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”

News.title: The Vatican issues Pope Leo XIV health update after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
The Vatican issues Pope Leo XIV health update after cancer diagnosis

Tuesday’s surgery confirmed that Pope Leo XIV's has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. His doctors have now issued an update on his recovery

View 3 Images It is understood that the King, who is undergoing treatment for cancer, plans to privately write to the Pope to pass on his best wishes (Image: ANGELO CARCONI/EPA/Shutterstock)

The Vatican has issued an update on Pope Leo XIV's recovery after he had surgery to remove a cancerous mass from his lung. Tuesday’s surgery confirmed that Leo has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

‌



‌



Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Pope was in the operating room for approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications.

‌



But questions remained about whether the cancer had spread. Blood tests and a chest X-ray showed the 71-year-old pope was recovering normally, his two doctors said.

‌



View 3 Images The Pope was in the operating room for approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications. (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The Holy See Press Office released a statement on the afternoon of October 14 from Dr. Luigi Carbone and Professor Stefano Margaritora, the chief of Thoracic Surgery at the Gemelli Hospital, who performed the operation along with the medical team, regarding Pope Leo XIV's postoperative recovery:

"This morning, the Holy Father underwent the blood tests and chest X-ray scheduled after surgery. The results confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing normally: the values are within the expected range for the type of operation performed," said the statement.

‌



"The Holy Father has undergone respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room. He has resumed eating normally and had breakfast and lunch," it added. "His recovery is proceeding as expected."

View 3 Images Pope Leo XIV holds the Sunday Angelus prayer from his studio overlooking St. Peter's Square (Image: Getty Images)

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



Later, Matteo Bruni, Director of the Holy See Press Office, told journalists that the Pope concelebrated Mass on Wednesday afternoon in a room specially prepared for the purpose on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital.

In the coming days, post-operation exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. The preoperative tests had already shown the doctors where and how to operate.

No change has been communicated regarding the previously announced hospitalization time of one week. However, Peru’s president suggested Leo might have to alter his planned visit to Latin America next month.

Article continues below

Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes would also have been removed and tested to determine whether the cancer had spread. Those results have not so far been made public.

It is understood that the King, who is undergoing treatment for cancer, plans to privately write to the Pope to pass on his best wishes following the diagnosis.

News.title: Police issue update on four arrested after woman 'raped' in Swindon GP surgery car park
News.content:
Police issue update on four arrested after woman 'raped' in Swindon GP surgery car park

Wiltshire Police arrested four men, including one teenager, on suspicion of rape after a woman in her 30s came forward to report the incident. Police have now issued an update on their investigation

View 2 Images The alleged assault happened outside Great Western Surgery in Farriers Close, (Image: Google)

Police in Wiltshire have issued an update on the four men arrested earlier this week after a woman alleged she had been raped in a GP surgery car park.

The alleged incident happened in the early hours of Tuesday morning when a woman in her 30s reported being sexually assaulted in the carpark of the Great Western Surgery in Farriers Close. Shortly after police were made aware of the report four men were arrested on suspicion of rape and brought into police custody.

Police confirmed the men were aged 19, 20 and two 21-year-olds, but released no further information.

View 2 Images A crime scene remained in place in the GP surgery car park yesterday while investigations continued. (Image: Google)

On Tuesday Detective Inspector Tom Straker said: “We recognise the concern that this worrying incident will have had in the local community." He added: "We are not currently looking for anyone else in relation to this. You may notice an increased police presence in the area. If you have any concerns, please do approach our officers.”

A crime scene remained in place in the GP surgery car park yesterday while investigations continued.

In an update yesterday evening Wiltshire Police issued a further update on their investigation. A spokesperson said: "Four men who were arrested yesterday (13/10) in connection with an alleged rape in Swindon, have been bailed with conditions.

"The men, ranging in age from 19 to 21 years old, have been interviewed by detectives who are continuing their investigation into the circumstances."

Article continues below

The investigation is ongoing and officers are continuing to appeal for information from anyone who was in the Farriers Close area in the early hours of Tuesday morning, or who may have CCTV or dash cam footage taken from the time. If you can help please call 101 quoting log 54260123495.

News.title: Zelensky says he's been 'betrayed' by Trump as Ukraine hit by Starlink outage
News.content:
Zelensky says he's been 'betrayed' by Trump as Ukraine hit by Starlink outage

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky claims his US counterpart and Elon Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight after the the military faced slowdowns in speed

View 3 Images Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says he has been "betrayed" by US President Donald Trump after a key component of his country's defence measures went down.

‌



‌



Zelensky claims that Trump and ally Elon Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight after the Ukrainian military faced slowdowns in speed. Starlink is a satellite internet service operated by SpaceX, Musk's aerospace company. It provides high-speed broadband globally.

‌



Appearing on the YouTube talk show " Piers Morgan Uncensored", Zelensky was asked if he had been "betrayed" by the Trump administration. Zelensky answered, "Yes".

‌



View 3 Images Zelensky claims that Trump and ally Elon Musk deliberately blocked Ukraine's access to Starlink overnight (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"It's a pity that we are losing a strong partner," Mr Zelensky told Mr Morgan. "I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States.

"This decision will bring a lot of human losses. Of course, people will die."

‌



Zelensky also told Mr Morgan that Ukraine would not be sold. "We're not selling our country. Look, guys, it's not about business for us. It's our lives. It's our country, our home, our children," he said.

Musk, in response, said: "And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go".

His comments come after at least nine people were killed in Russian air attacks on Ukraine, while hundreds of thousands were left without power just days after Mr Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" in the war that started over four years ago.

‌



Ukrainian forces were also forced to cancel missions after losing access to high-speed services.

View 3 Images Ukrainian forces were forced to cancel missions (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Mr Musk, in response, said that any military use of the Starlink network was a matter for the US government and the US president, while others said connectivity was being restored after the outcry.

‌



"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Mr Musk said.

"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX.

"Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."

Article continues below

Zelensky's top advisors spoke to White House officials on Wednesday and asked whether there was a decision to shut down Starlink and what could be done to remedy the situation, according to reports by Axios.

Axios reported that two White House officials said Ukraine had contacted the Pentagon, which has control over Starshield, and that the defence department does not have control over Starlink.

Trump was reportedly reaching out to SpaceX to determine what occurred.

News.title: Britain to launch world first satellite-catching robot to destroy Space junk
News.content:
Britain to launch world first satellite-catching robot to destroy Space junk

Spacecraft launched from Scotland with giant robotic claws to grab old satellites which threaten to smash into infrastructure we rely on for GPS and communications

World-first mission puts UK expertise to work to help clean up space

Britain is launching a world-first mission to clear dangerous space debris orbiting Earth.

‌



‌



A spacecraft will use giant robotic claws to grab old satellites which threaten to smash into vital space infrastructure that we rely on for GPS, weather forecasts and communications.

‌



The spacecraft will launch from Scotland in 2029 and destroy two defunct satellites by 2032 by releasing them lower into our atmosphere where they will naturally burn up. If successful it will be the first time a spacecraft has disposed of more than one satellite in this way. There are hundreds of thousands of tracked space junk orbiting at speeds exceeding 17,000 miles an hour.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror just click on the link here to get them at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Graphic of Britain's new satellite-grabbing spacecraft

Jodrell Bank’s iconic telescopes loses funding and set to be axed in government cuts READ MORE :

NASA sends spacecraft the size of a fridge to catch its falling Swift telescope in daring mission READ MORE :

After its first mission, it is hoped Britain’s £60 million satellite catching robot will sweep Space for years to come. A public competition is being launched today to name the spacecraft.

‌



UK Space Minister Liz Lloyd said: “Space junk and debris pose an immense and growing challenge but with our homegrown expertise, the UK is determined to lead the global effort to clean up space.

“By backing this world-first mission, we will protect the satellites that underpin modern life from keeping us connected with loved ones and delivering accurate weather forecasts to keep our country safe.”

View 3 Images Graphic of Space junk clearing mission

‌



The government says hazardous old satellites and their remnants threaten the thousands of active satellites which underpin national security and everyday services. It says swift action now is needed to tackle the problem.

UK's Active Debris Removal mission (UK ADR) is creating a refuellable spacecraft with future-use in mind. It will launch from Saxavord Spaceport in Scotland, which recently received £30 million government funding to maintain Britain’s launch capability.

The mission is part of UK attempts to be at the forefront of a new in-orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing (ISAM) sector, predicted to grow into a billion-dollar industry within the next decade.

‌



Currently, satellites are single use so when they run out of fuel or suffer a fault, they are discarded. Developing the technology to repair, refuel and protect satellites and spacecraft is now a priority for the UK under the recently published Space Strategy.

View 3 Images Graphic of how spacecraft will catch satellites in orbit

Dr Alice Bunn, co-director UK Space Agency said: "This mission is about much more than removing debris. It is about developing the capabilities that will enable future servicing, assembly and manufacturing in orbit.

‌



“The technologies being developed through ADR will help establish the UK's position at the forefront of a new generation of space services while supporting a sustainable future for activities in space."

Protecting the space environment is critical for the future of the UK's space sector which is worth £18.6 billion and supports 55,000 skilled jobs. The UK Space Agency is working with ClearSpace UK as its industry delivery partner on the mission.

Rob Atchison, managing director of ClearSpace UK, said: "UK ADR will be delivered here in the UK. Our team brings together engineers and specialists from across Great Britain and Northern Ireland, as well as allies and partners.

Article continues below

"Our next step is to design, build and test a spacecraft that can get close, safely, to an object never designed to be caught, and take control of it. We will do that with partners across the UK supply chain, working towards operations in 2029."

UK Space Minister Liz Lloyd added: “This is our Space Strategy in action, giving British firms the support and clear direction they need to turn bold ideas into cutting-edge innovation, strengthen our world-class satellite sector and drive economic growth across the country.”

News.title: Almost half a million workers set for pay rise today as Real Living Wage rises
News.content:
Almost half a million workers set for pay rise today as Real Living Wage rises

The Real Living Wage is a voluntary pay for workers over the age of 18, whose employer is signed up to the Living Wage Foundation

View 2 Images The Real Living Wage is rising today (Image: Getty)

Almost half a million workers are set for a pay rise as the voluntary Real Living Wage rises from today.

‌



‌



The Real Living Wage is increasing from £13.45 to £14.10 an hour across the UK and from £14.80 to £15.45 an hour in London. Full-time workers on the real Living Wage will receive a pay rise worth over £1,250.

‌



The Real Living Wage is different to the statutory minimum wage that is set by the Government. It is a voluntary pay for workers over the age of 18, whose employer is signed up to the Living Wage Foundation.

‌



There are almost 17,000 real Living Wage Employers throughout the country, including Lush, Ikea and Aviva. The idea is that the Real Living Wage is based on the actual cost of affording essentials such as food, clothing and household bills.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images The Real Living Wage is voluntary but thousands of employers have signed up (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Amazon and eBay among online firms included in tax loophole clampdown in Budget READ MORE :

Tesco issues Clubcard update and you can now earn points at more than 500 retailers READ MORE :

Living Wage Foundation analysis shows that a full-time worker earning the new, real Living Wage would earn over £2,700 a year more than a worker earning the current government minimum.

In London, full-time workers on the new London Living Wage will earn over £5,300 a year more than the statutory minimum.

Recent research by the Living Wage Foundation shows that many have struggled to make ends meet. An estimated 61% of low-paid workers have cut back on food or heating, fallen behind on bills or housing payments, or taken out a payday loan to cover essentials over the past year, and 37% have used a foodbank.

Article continues below

But more than 2,000 new employers have signed up to pay the Real Living Wage over the past year, including Uniqlo, the Department for Business and Trade and Coventry Building Society, with one in seven UK employees now working for an accredited Living Wage Employer.

Emily Sawh, Co-Director of the Living Wage Foundation, said: "Despite the Living Wage campaign’s monumental impact on wages in the UK, there are still millions of workers trapped in in-work poverty and struggling every day to make ends meet.

"They're forced to skip meals, fall behind on bills and visit foodbanks. That's why we urge employers to do the right thing by signing up to pay the real Living Wage and providing workers with the decent standard of living they need to thrive."

News.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the east African country's government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders.

From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs.

Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans.

Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boats migrants in the 12 months to June - accounting for 18% of arrivals, external, according to figures from the House of Commons Library.

The Eritrean embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

"Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused," said Mahmood.

She said she would not hesitate "to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate".

The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of "abruptly" withdrawing co-operation earlier this year.

The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission.

The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea's capital Asmara.

Earlier this year, the UK threatened bans against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved.

Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced.

When announcing changes to the UK's asylum system in November, Mahmood said visa penalties would be applied to countries that failed to co-operate with returns policies.

Penalties included an "emergency brake" on visas for countries with high asylum claims until they take back citizens in the UK illegally.

According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year.

There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year - an 8% increase on the same period last year.

Of those who had been returned, less than 6,000 has been convicted of a criminal offence.

News.title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings without public outcome, BBC Verify finds
News.content:
BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.

Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.

Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.

For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.

A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.

News.title: Reform faces criticism after councillors filmed making racist comments
News.content:
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.

Reform UK has said "there is no room for racism" in its party after ITV News broadcast undercover filming, gathered over a year, of some of its councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

In the film, Undercover: A Year in Reform,, external a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull is recorded calling Asian homeowners "parasites".

Labour described the investigation as "truly sickening" adding: "Nigel Farage can't shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples."

A Reform spokesman said: "Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced" and that in some cases there had been suspensions.

The spokesman added that the party had improved its procedures but some individuals who did not share their values would occasionally make it through vetting.

ITV's filming involved eight figures in Reform â the BBC does not know how many it spoke to in total.

Reform says the people filmed by ITV are all under investigation, and have already either resigned or been suspended.

ITV News says it had reporters undercover with Reform UK candidates and councillors across England and Wales running up to the elections in May and four by-election campaigns this year and last.

These reporters joined a Reform councillor, Alan Feeney, in Solihull, in the West Midlands, where he was campaigning to retain his seat on the council, having defected from the Conservative Party in 2025.

He told undercover reporters the area has been "infested" with Asian families, and called them "absolute parasites".

Later in the film, he is recorded saying: "I'd be saying no more than one per cent of British population can be non-white."

The BBC has tried to contact Feeney for a response. ITV has reported that on Monday evening he had "mutually agreed" to resign from Reform UK, citing "personal reasons," and would be continuing as an independent councillor.

Reform Party leader Nigel Farage has repeatedly said he wants to get rid of those he has called "bad apples."

Two years ago he said he didn't want Reform to be "a sectarian or racially based party in any way at all".

"I'm going to be absolutely ruthless about it," he said.

In a statement released after ITV's film was broadcast, Reform said the party "had improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting".

The Conservatives said: "Nigel Farage promised to make Reform ready for government. These sorry individuals are proof he has failed."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "This is chilling. I feel for anyone watching this tonight who is frightened to see such racism and hatred festering in their community."

A Green Party spokesman said: "Vilifying migrants and Muslims is Reform's main focus, and these racist comments reflect party policy."

News.title: Global charity withholds report into its role in Syria's 'disappeared' children
News.content:
A global children's charity has said it will not release a report that it commissioned to investigate its role in separating children from their families during Syria's civil war.

The charity, SOS Children's Villages International, has also yet to give compensation to Syrian families impacted by the government-organised detentions, despite pledging to do so in plans seen by the BBC World Service, which has been working with a group of international journalists.

Under former President Bashar al-Assad, Syrian security forces took hundreds of children from their imprisoned parents and told SOS and other orphanages to hide their identities and whereabouts.

A BBC Eye investigation, Syria's Stolen Children, as part of a joint project with Lighthouse Reports and other media in September 2025, revealed the regime used the children to pressure their families and negotiate prisoner exchanges.

Sisters Layla and Layan Ghbeis were eight and four when they were taken from their mother, Omama, and brought to SOS in 2015. It was three years before they were reunited with their parents in a prisoner exchange.

Layan did not recognise her mother when they met again.

The family later fled to the US as refugees through the UN, but the trauma of those lost years still weighs heavily on them.

"Whether we're together or on our own, we're thinking about what happened to us," Omama told the BBC.

"It had a huge impact on every member of our family."

News.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn thanks prime minister as brain cancer review announced
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else.

"Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

News.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
News.content:
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.

China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.

The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.

Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.

The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.

It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".

Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.

A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.

"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.

"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."

Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.

News.title: What if you could turn off your algorithm? Australia is about to try
News.content:
New legislation is being tabled in Australia's parliament on Thursday to force big tech to allow users to switch off algorithms which send them recommended content - but it's not the first country to try.

The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull in Sydney explains what is being proposed.

News.title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
News.content:
The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively".

She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said.

The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009.

The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion.

The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell.

They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further."

She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough â you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry."

The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009.

He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said.

After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting".

On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence.

Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999.

"He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far.

"Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'."

Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far".

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday.

He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States.

News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death.

The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

News.title: We are behind you and that will not change, PM tells Zelensky
News.content:
"We are behind you and that will not change," Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelensky, as he hosted the Ukrainian leader in Downing Street.

Zelensky was in London as part of efforts to reinforce backing from allies after Donald Trump called for him to go and lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.

The prime minister said Ukraine was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire proposed by the US president but said Russia's response had been "further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine".

Zelensky said: "Our people, we survived and continue to do this because we have strong partners and I'm very proud that we have one of the strongest partners in our history and it's your people, Andy."

The Ukrainian president was greeted with a hug from Burnham, cheers from civil servants and a rare honour guard as he arrived in Downing Street.

Ahead of Zelensky's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.

News.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
News.content:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.

Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from Â£7 to Â£10.

Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from Â£6 to Â£8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from Â£5 to Â£8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.

The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".

The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

News.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
News.content:
On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at Â£300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately Â£699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a Â£150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.

Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.

But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.

Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.

"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."

And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."

With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".

When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.

The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.

In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.

The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than Â£830m into their football operations.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.

Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

News.title: I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats, says Swinney
News.content:
Asked about the MI5 chief's comments, the first minister said he was "very worried" about a "lack of coastal and offshore protection".

He identified waters north of Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News.

"There's an obligation on the United Kingdom government to make sure that the country is safe. And I don't think the defence posture of the United Kingdom enables me to have that confidence."

Scotland is home to the UK's nuclear submarine fleet at Faslane, west of Glasgow. The SNP wants those weapons to be removed, but is in favour of an independent Scotland joining Nato.

Swinney insisted that independence would not hamper Scotland's security, but rather give the country "more choices".

The SNP leader said he had "always been a believer in defence co-operation between Scotland and other countries", citing Canada joining the EU's SAFE defence programme, external.

Responding to the first minister's comments, a Ministry of Defence Spokesperson said:

"The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe, and this government is investing Â£298bn over the next four years to ensure we can tackle rising threats.

"The Navy is helping to patrol Nato's northern flank, with this year's carrier strike group deploying to the Arctic and the high north.

"To tackle these threats, we're also investing in new frigates for the Navy and high-tech uncrewed vessels as part of our Hybrid Navy, backed by Â£1.5bn in funding."

Delivering a speech at the UN General Assembly, external last month, Burnham said his government would invest in defence and build up the UK's "hard power and deterrence".

He added: "But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation."

News.title: Teen shot friend by mistake, inquest told
News.content:
A teenager told an inquest he fatally shot his friend with an air rifle at a house party after mistaking the trigger for the safety catch.

Connor Bell, 17, from Tadley, had been drinking with friends at a house in Chineham, near Basingstoke, on 8 November 2025 when he was hit by a pellet fired by Jack Beechy, the Winchester inquest heard.

The pellet entered through his right eye socket, causing an "unsurvivable" brain injury and cardiac arrest. He died at Southampton General Hospital two days later.

Coroner Jason Pegg recorded a conclusion of accidental death, exacerbated by a lack of weapons-handling skills.

The inquest heard Joshua Brown, now 18, had agreed with his parents that only a couple of friends would come round and the air rifle would stay locked in a cupboard.

But he said more friends came than he had told his parents about, and the group drank vodka, cider and beer.

He took out the .177 calibre rifle and it was used to shoot at bottles in the garden from the conservatory.

Beechy, now 18, said he was "a little bit drunk" when Brown asked him to put the rifle away.

He fired off the remaining pellets from the conservatory because he "thought it would be safer", believing the gun was then empty.

Beechy said that as he walked into the kitchen, with Bell standing nearby, he fired the rifle by mistake.

News.title: 'Dark day for Lewis' as one fisherman dead and two missing
News.content:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat, called the Kilda, was overdue from Lewis.

A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers searched off the Port of Ness in north Lewis. Police have warned the public not to make their own searches due to bad weather.

Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men, and First Minister John Swinney said his heart went out to those involved.

Police Scotland said the man's body was found about 02:45, but the remaining two men and their boat remained unaccounted for.

News.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
News.content:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost Â£350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning Â£350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

The trial continues.

News.title: Chinese artefacts damaged in mystery fall at British Museum as calls for their return grow
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The British Museum is investigating how a 300-year-old Chinese porcelain bowl fell from its display shelf and shattered, damaging another artefact in an unexplained incident that has led to outrage in China and raised fears of a diplomatic row.

The blue-and-white bowl, dating to the Kangxi period of China’s Qing dynasty (1662-1722), fell on 4 October, and struck a small porcelain box on a shelf below, according to Chinese news outlet The Paper.

The bowl, which the British Museum has described as “a very fine copy of a 15th century Ming porcelain bowl”, depicts women in a garden admiring a painting, playing a traditional stringed instrument, and taking part in board games.

The second object was a small blue-and-white porcelain box decorated with a Buddha’s hand citron, peach branches and camellias. Both pieces were made in Jingdezhen, a city in China’s Jiangxi province renowned for its porcelain production, during the reign of the Kangxi emperor, according to the South China Morning Post.

open image in gallery The British Museum is investigating how a 300-year-old Chinese porcelain bowl fell from its display shelf and shattered ( The Trustees of the British Museum )

The bowl was on display in Room 95, the museum’s gallery of Chinese ceramics. An international student told Chinese newspaper New Express that staff suddenly evacuated visitors from the crowded gallery at around noon on 4 October.

“After the hall reopened, I no longer saw exhibit B629 on display, and exhibit 634 was also missing,” she told the newspaper.

She added: “The exhibits are quite valuable, and it’s heartbreaking. I think the museum should strengthen visitor control.”

“Regrettably a bowl and small box from the Qing Kangxi period in the Sir Percival David Collection have been damaged after the bowl fell from its shelf and landed on the bottom shelf. The shelf and mount show no sign of failure but we will continue to investigate how this happened,” a museum spokesperson said in a statement to The Telegraph.

“Both objects are already with our expert conservation team for complete restoration. We take the care of objects incredibly seriously and have stringent measures in place within cases to protect from such incidents occurring,” the statement added.

The Independent has reached out to the British Museum for comment.

Pan Jinyu, a Chinese-speaking guide who reportedly works at the British Museum, said in a post on WeChat that he had been giving a tour in Room 95 when it unexpectedly closed, but had not initially suspected that anything had happened to the ceramics.

He only began to believe the reports after seeing photographs of the broken pieces circulating among his contacts the following evening, according to Chinese media.

open image in gallery The blue-and-white bowl, dating to the Kangxi period of China’s Qing dynasty (1662-1722), fell on 4 October, and struck a small porcelain box on a shelf below ( The Trustees of the British Museum )

Mr Pan said he returned to the gallery on 7 October and asked museum staff about the damage.

“They seemed surprised that we had seen photos of it, but confirmed to me that porcelain had indeed been broken,” he told the Global Times.

At the time, he said the label where the artefacts were kept read “object removed for study”, but were changed to “Destination: Conservation” the following day.

The bowl, Mr Pan explained, was placed upside down on a support, apparently so visitors could see its base. Looking at photographs taken after it fell, he felt the mount did not appear particularly secure and that there was enough space for the bowl to drop.

“I am more concerned with why the accident happened, how the artefacts will be restored and how similar incidents can be prevented in the future,” he wrote in his post.

The bowl and box belonged to the Sir Percival David Foundation of Chinese Art, established in 1952 by British businessman and collector Sir Percival David. The collection was displayed at the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies until 2007, before moving to the British Museum in 2009 on long-term loan.

The foundation’s trustees agreed to donate the collection permanently to the museum in 2024, with the transfer receiving formal approval from the Charity Commission in March 2025.

The collection comprises around 1,700 objects and is estimated to be worth £1bn, making it the most valuable object donation in British museum history, according to the Charity Commission.

The damage and lack of clarity on the artefacts has fuelled anger on Chinese social media, with some calling for Chinese cultural items held overseas to be returned.

According to the Global Times, one person wrote: “Chinese cultural relics that were looted and scattered across the world embody the soul of Chinese culture. They must come home, and one day they will.”

Another wrote: “If you can’t take proper care of them, give them back.”

News.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla to attend ceremonial opening of Senedd for first time in five years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The King and Queen are due to attend the ceremonial opening of the Welsh Parliament on Thursday.

This marks the first time King Charles will attend the event as King.

He and Queen Camilla previously joined the ceremony, which takes place following a Senedd election, in 2021 alongside Queen Elizabeth II.

He is scheduled to speak in the Siambr (Senedd debating chamber) alongside First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth and Huw Irranca-Davies, the Llywydd (presiding officer).

Charles and Camilla will be welcomed to the Senedd by the Royal Navy Guard of Honour, who will give a Royal Salute.

open image in gallery King Charles III and Queen Camilla during a visit to the Senedd in Cardiff to mark its 25th anniversary ( PA )

At the ceremonial opening, a mace-bearer will lead a procession of Members of the Senedd (MSs) through the Senedd building into the Siambr.

Ahead of the opening, Mr Irranca-Davies said: “This ceremony marks the start of a new chapter in the Senedd’s history.

“It is a larger parliament, elected through a new electoral system designed to better reflect the diversity of views and experiences across our country.

“We are honoured that Their Majesties The King and Queen are here to share this moment with us.

“We will use this moment to celebrate the people, communities and culture of Wales and remind ourselves of the aspirations of those who put their trust in us to serve them in this seventh Senedd term.”

open image in gallery Rhun ap Iorwerth will also speak at the event ( Jonathan Brady/PA )

Alongside the speeches, the King’s Harpist, Mared Pugh Evans, will perform, and the Merched Plastaf Choir will sing O Gymru.

During their visit, Charles and Camilla will meet party leaders, members of the Welsh Youth Parliament, the chief executive and clerk of the Senedd, and the deputy presiding officer.

To commemorate the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster, they will also meet Noah Jones, whose great-grandfather, Stephen Andrew, was a caretaker at Pantglas Junior School and helped save the lives of many children.

Charles, Camilla and Prince William are scheduled to visit the Aberfan Memorial Garden and the Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre on 21 October, before William visits a primary school to unveil the Aberfan Memorial Tree.

The trio will join survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community to pay tribute to the victims who lost their lives when a coal tip collapsed onto the village on 21 October 1966.

News.title: Video report: Why are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia?
News.content:
At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured in a strike on Riyadh’s international airport.

The attack last Saturday (10 October) was the third facility hit in a week by Houthi forces.

Footage of the strike was released by Saudi Arabia and has been shared widely across social media.

But why are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia and what does this mean for UK?

The Independent’s chief international correspondent Bel Trew takes a closer look.

Watch Bel’s full analysis in the video above.

News.title: Hidden cameras found in women’s showers on Australian navy ship
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A hidden video recording device has been found in a cabin aboard a Royal Australian Navy ship, the Australian Defence Force said.

The disturbing discovery followed a politician’s allegation that concealed cameras had been found in female shower facilities on the vessel.

The device was found in a cabin aboard the navy ship HMAS Leeuwin on Sunday in Cairns, Queensland, prompting an investigation into the incident.

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie, a prominent advocate for members of the Australian armed forces, told the senate that a former navy member had informed her about a hidden camera in the female shower facilities aboard HMAS Leeuwin.

Ms Lambie said she had received even more disturbing information suggesting that footage from the cameras may have already been uploaded online before the devices were discovered.

Senator Jacqui Lambie says hidden camera found in female shower facilities aboard HMAS Leeuwin ( Getty )

“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she said in the senate.

“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”

Later on Wednesday, the ADF said it took the “incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form”.

It said the incident had been referred to the Joint Military Police Unit, which was working with civilian authorities.

"The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship's crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence's priority, and support is ongoing.

"As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time."

Communications minister Anika Wells called the alleged incident “horrific”, saying it demonstrated why new digital duty of care laws were needed.

“This is horrible and I really feel for all of the people who are on that ship, who are learning this, and the people who may have been victims of this act,” she said.

“I can’t say too much about the investigation, because it’s on foot, but you deserve to be safe in your workplace, and the rise of tech-facilitated abuse, particularly upon women like you’re saying, is horrific.”

Greens leader and defence spokesman David Shoebridge said the developments were “incredibly concerning”.

“We know many women aren’t feeling safe inside Defence spaces, and again we say to Labor: you’ve got to restore faith with Defence personnel, you’ve got to make women and other people feel safe in Defence spaces,” Mr Shoebridge said.

News.title: Eritreans face total UK visa ban in row over return of small boat migrants
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Eritrea could be hit with a complete visa ban unless it agrees to the return of more small boat migrants and convicted criminals, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood says.

The east African country had refused to co-operate with the return of its nationals, she told the Telegraph.

Other nations could face similar visa restrictions if they fail to accept migrant returns, she added.

“Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused,” Ms Mahmood said.

“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.

“I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.”

Shabana Mahmood has threatened to cut off visas for all Eritreans ( Getty )

Eritrean diplomats in the UK have had their fast-track visa access stripped, the Telegraph also reported.

They face restrictions on their movements outside London without the permission of the Foreign Office.

The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2025.

Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to co-operate with demands on migrant returns following the warnings.

The Democratic Republic of Congo caved after VIPs and decision-makers were stripped of preferential visa treatment and DRC nationals had fast-track visas revoked, the Home Office said. The country reached an agreement with the UK in February.

More than 3,000 nationals from those three countries could now be removed from the UK due to the agreements, the government said at the time.

In March, ministers placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the Home Secretary accused them of exploiting Britain's generosity to claim asylum.

Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were halted, while work visas for Afghans were halted too.

According to government figures, 6,952 Eritrean asylum seekers arrived in the UK in the year to June 2026.

That was the second highest number of any nationality, behind Pakistan, and included 5,875 asylum seekers who came by small boat.

Eritrea also had the second-highest asylum approval rating of any country, with 84 per cent of claims being accepted. That was behind only Sudan, with 92 per cent.
