Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: ‘A star is needed here in Naturena’: Moloisane on Kaizer Chiefs’ trophy target
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs defender Thabo Moloisane has set his sights on winning trophies and helping Amakhosi end their long wait for league glory following his arrival at Naturena in July.

The 26-year-old was one of five new signings brought in ahead of the season and has already featured in the majority of the club’s matches.

Speaking ahead of Chiefs’ clash against Stellenbosch FC on Tuesday, Moloisane made it clear that winning silverware is a major priority in his first season with the Soweto giants.



The defender believes Amakhosi have an opportunity to challenge for the league title and is determined to play his part in ending the club’s lengthy wait for another Premiership crown.

“A star, guys, it is needed here at home. We have an opportunity to see if we can do it this season, and the league, of course. It is one thing that has gone past us for a long time and, for me, in my first season, I just want to get as many trophies as I can. That’s where the ambition is, and the rest can follow,” he said.

Kaizer Chiefs last won the league title in the 2014/15 season, and Moloisane is eager to help restore the club’s status as one of South African football’s leading forces.



Beyond his ambitions at club level, the defender is also hoping to work his way back into the Bafana Bafana setup.

Kaizer Chiefs star wants Bafana return

Moloisane acknowledged that returning to the national team will not be easy, given the competition for places, but believes hard work and consistent performances at a high-profile club like Kaizer Chiefs could improve his chances.

“We should give credit to the guys, you know. I was speaking to Mdu (Shabalala) last week, saying the line is long to get back into Bafana, but at the same time, I’m at a big institution watched by everyone. For me, it’s just to continue working hard. The journey is still long,” he told media.



For Moloisane, the immediate focus remains on delivering for Amakhosi and helping the club compete for honours, while keeping his hopes of a Bafana Bafana recall alive.

Will he win a star?

World.title: ANC vs IEC: ConCourt to rule on candidate list dispute
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Constitutional Court is expected to deliver judgment on Thursday in the ANC’s bid to have its candidates included on the ballot for the November local government elections.

The party is challenging an Electoral Court ruling in favour of the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), which excluded its candidates from contesting elections in six municipalities.

The dispute stems from the ANC’s failure to click the “Submit as Final” button on the IEC’s candidate nomination system before the 28 August deadline.

The ruling is expected to determine whether the ANC’s candidates will be allowed to contest the elections in the affected municipalities.

World.title: MK Party asks for privacy as questions continue over Zuma's health
World.content:
DURBAN - The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has called for privacy and respect for its leader, Jacob Zuma, amid concerns about his health following his recent hospitalisation.

Zuma was discharged from hospital after being admitted for what the party described as routine health checks.

MK Party secretary-general Sibonelo Nomvalo urged the public to respect the former president and allow him and his family privacy during this time.

“We know that President Zuma is the father of the nation. He’s a family man also, and I think we must respect that. So, I think at this time around, we must afford his family some privacy, and we must afford him some privacy. We all deserve privacy, so I think we must simply do that,” Nomvalo said.

The Jacob Zuma Foundation has also appealed to the public to respect the former president’s privacy.



READ | Jacob Zuma reportedly discharged from Pietermaritzburg hospital

In a statement posted on X, the foundation said it would not provide minute-by-minute updates on Zuma’s health.

Foundation spokesperson Mzwanele Manyi called on the public to respect Zuma’s privacy and dignity, adding that repeated enquiries were not appreciated.

“We see it as persecution and invasion of privacy,” Manyi wrote.

World.title: Political Killings Task Team investigating Sibiya associate Serge Cabonge
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Political Killings Task Team is investigating socialite Serge Cabonge, eNCA understands.

Cabonge was reportedly brought in for questioning on Monday.

He is a known associate of former police deputy commissioner Shadrack Sibiya.

The Madlanga Commission announced on Tuesday that it would obtain a statement from Cabonge after an audio recording was played during Sibiya’s bail application.

In the recording, Cabonge allegedly claimed to have police connections and to have used them to help secure the withdrawal of criminal charges against the daughter of a man linked to the commission.

The investigation comes amid continued scrutiny of alleged police connections and claims of interference in criminal cases.

World.title: SASSA changes November grant payment dates ahead of elections
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Disability grants will now be paid on Monday, 2 November, after the original payment date clashed with the local government elections.

The grants were initially scheduled to be paid on 4 November.

South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) spokesperson Dr Paseka Letsatsi says the agency approached the National Treasury after identifying the potential clash.



Election day has been declared a public holiday, prompting a change to the payment schedule.

Older persons’ grants were initially scheduled for 3 November, disability grants for 4 November and children’s grants for 5 November.

Under the revised schedule, older persons’ grants will be paid on 30 October, disability grants on 2 November and children’s grants on 3 November.

In a statement, SASSA said the adjustment is intended to support the smooth administration of social grant payments around the elections.

The agency has urged beneficiaries not to visit its offices unnecessarily, saying payments will be processed according to the revised schedule.

Letsatsi said beneficiaries would be able to use their cards at retailers and banks once the payments had been made.

World.title: Katlehong mass shooting suspect to appear in court
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The suspect arrested in connection with the deadly shooting in Katlehong is expected to appear in the Palm Ridge Magistrate’s Court on Thursday.

The shooting took place on Tuesday evening when the suspect allegedly opened fire on a group of ANC Youth League members returning from a memorial service for a fellow league member.

Two people were killed at the scene, while two others later succumbed to their gunshot wounds in hospital. Three other victims remain hospitalised.

The suspect reportedly handed himself over to police.

The case is being investigated by the Gauteng Political Killings Task Team.

The suspect is also reportedly a former ward councillor who has previously been affiliated with at least three political parties.

World.title: Trump's new press secretary faces scrutiny over credentials
World.content:
WASHINGTON - The White House was facing mounting questions over new press secretary Katie Zacharia's legal credentials, after a faltering first day in the job when she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.

A US watchdog group filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, asking it to investigate whether President Donald Trump's spokeswoman -- the public face of the administration -- had broken the law by repeatedly presenting herself as a lawyer without a license.

Campaign for Accountability said Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

"Ms Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," said the group's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith.

"The State Bar should investigate whether Ms Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials," she added.

Trump described Zacharia as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment Friday, but journalists have found no record of her being licensed to practice law in any US state.

"I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," Zacharia said in a statement to AFP, without clarifying whether she held a US law license.

Zacharia has not specified where, if anywhere, she was admitted to the bar. Asked by reporters Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied: "When I moved to China."

California's state bar confirmed to US media that it had no record of Zacharia holding a license under either her married or maiden name.

Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011, but obtaining a law degree does not automatically qualify someone to practice law.

Foreign nationals cannot sit China's bar exam, although they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.

Zacharia previously worked for a law firm in Beijing, according to her professional profile.

The controversy followed a rocky first appearance as White House press secretary on Tuesday, when Zacharia read extensively from prepared notes during a briefing lasting just 14 minutes.

She took questions from only three news organisations, all considered sympathetic to Trump, and stumbled over some answers, at one point accidentally referring to the president as her husband.

Her performance drew criticism from former White House press secretary Jen Psaki, now a TV news host, who compared it to a "Saturday Night Live" comedy sketch.

Trump, however, praised Zacharia's debut, telling reporters: "I thought she was very good."

Zacharia succeeded Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August after becoming one of the most prominent public defenders of Trump's second administration.

World.title: In Chicago, pope's hometown, Catholics express shock and support
World.content:
CHICAGO - Priests and parishioners in Pope Leo XIV's hometown of Chicago expressed shock, support and hope Wednesday after doctors discovered that a nodule removed from his lung was cancerous.

"It was a shock to everyone. I have to say my husband passed away from cancer, so I know that feeling," said Gail Spreen after coming out of a service at Holy Name Cathedral in Chicago.

"He is a strong person, and he has so many people that are behind him and are praying for him," she said. "So we totally believe he'll be okay."

Part of Pope Leo's right lung was removed in Tuesday's operation and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics were awaiting the results of a biopsy to determine if the cancer has spread.

Born Robert Francis Prevost on Chicago's South Side in 1955, the 71-year-old pontiff is the first American-born pope and has been warmly embraced by US Catholics since he was elected last May.

He retains strong ties to Chicago and is a lifelong fan of the Chicago White Sox baseball team, whose stadium is on the South Side of the city.

Father Louis Cameli, a priest at Holy Name Cathedral, said the news was "not just a medical event" but a "spiritual summons" to trust God.

"Of course there's great concern and a certain kind of sadness, but at the same time, this has really, I think, provoked people to pray, reaffirm their trust in God, and put him in God's hands," Cameli said.

Standing outside the cathedral, Thomas Abood called the news "really difficult to take" after Pope Leo had brought a "new breath of hope."

The pope was walking and eating Wednesday after the operation, and post-surgery tests showed his progress was normal, his doctors said.

Father Mark Mannion said he's seen an influx of people coming into St. Mary of the Angels Catholic Church since the news broke.

"Everybody's been coming in. They might light a candle for him, pray for him at Mass," he said.

"We love him and we're praying for him and we're very optimistic," Mannion said.

"You know, like I said in my homily the other day, he's from the South Side, so he's tough... and I think he'll roll forward."

World.title: US stocks fall after hot inflation report as leading AI shares tumble
World.content:
NEW YORK - Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday following a hotter-than-expected US inflation reading, with the Nasdaq particularly hit due to weakness in leading artificial intelligence equities.

The consumer price index was up more than analysts expected in September, rising 3.7 percent on a year-on-year basis, a marked increase from August's 3.4 percent reading.

"Today's CPI report came in hot, with annual headline inflation reaching its highest level since May," said eToro analyst Bret Kenwell.

"The knee-jerk reaction may be for traders to reassess the odds of a Fed rate hike later this month," he said.

While all three major US indices dropped, the Nasdaq suffered the deepest declines, losing nearly two percent.

The inflation report was troubling enough to suggest that the Fed's September interest rate hike was "was not one and done," said Angelo Kourkafas of Edward Jones, who described the weakness in AI names as related to the interest rate outlook.

"As we are navigating this higher-for-longer rate environment, we are seeing the realisation that the cost to borrow is moving higher and we know there's a massive cost of building all the AI Infrastructure," Kourkafas said.

Data centre operator CoreWeave lost more than 15 percent, while chip companies Nvidia and AMD also fell sharply.

In Europe, the day ended higher in London, Paris and Frankfurt after Asian equities struggled to claw back the previous day's steep tech losses.

Tech firms had taken a hammering on Tuesday amid concerns about China's progress in developing AI chips and following comments by Broadcom's chief executive likening the AI buying frenzy to gambling.

Tokyo and Seoul, both with big tech weightings, closed lower again on Wednesday.

Hong Kong and Shanghai also fell, with investors appearing unmoved by data showing China's exports picked up pace in September and soared 36.3 percent, far more than expected.

Investors also assessed largely upbeat earnings from Dutch chipmaking equipment giant ASML, which reported record sales and strong profits on huge demand for AI.

ASML shares rose 1.7 percent on the Amsterdam stock market.

Shares in Lufthansa descended 2.2 percent after Portugal announced the German airline group had been chosen to take a 44.9 percent stake in TAP for 1.03 billion euros as part of the reprivatization of the airline.

Bank of America finished down 4.8 percent after US agencies fined the lender $1.2 billion for violating anti-money laundering laws.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: How the Iran war could make Trump an accidental climate president
World.content:
The Iran war was supposed to be a short, sharp strike that brought down the regime within a few weeks. Instead, the US finds itself enmeshed in a conflict that’s upending the world’s energy system.

As oil and gas prices soar, there have been noticeable shifts toward clean energy, and it’s raised a profoundly weird question: Could this war make President Donald Trump an accidental climate president, at least on the global stage?

It would be a deep irony, if so. Trump is the climate-denier-in-chief. He has called global warming a “hoax,” clean energy a “scam,” pushed fossil fuels, and unraveled a slew of climate and environmental protections.

But as the war grinds into its eighth month, it’s highlighting the immense vulnerability of fossil fuels to geopolitical instability. There are signs of global clean energy moves, even as the picture remains complex, with some countries scrambling for coal instead.

The longer the war continues, some experts say, the bigger the impact it could have on undermining global oil and gas demand.

“With all (Trump’s) efforts to encourage fossil fuel use, he might end up accelerating their phase down instead,” said Samantha Gross, director of the Energy Security and Climate Initiative at the Brookings Institution.

The shoreline of the Strait of Hormuz, where blockaded ships are anchored off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on June 1. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/AP

The launch of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in February led to the biggest oil shock in history. Iran strangled the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that transported roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, sending the cost of a barrel of oil surging over $100.

Many analysts predicted the price spike would be short-term, but it has persisted even as Iran’s chokehold over the strait has loosened. Shipping costs to get oil through the Strait of Hormuz have surged, and new fronts are opening up in the conflict, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi oil facilities and tankers.

It’s all affecting demand. Back in January, the International Energy Agency forecast global oil demand would rise by 930,000 barrels per day in 2026. By September, the picture had changed dramatically. The IEA now forecasts a decline of 2.5 million barrels a day due to the “impasse” in negotiations between the US and Iran.

Less oil means less planet-warming pollution. Global fossil fuel emissions are on track to fall around 0.5% in 2026, according to an analysis from Carbon Brief, a non-profit climate change publication. It would mark the first fall since 2020, when the Covid pandemic ground the world to a halt.

It also means big shifts in transportation, where most of the world’s oil goes. People are driving and flying less, but these are likely temporary changes, said Sverre Alvik, vice president and energy transition outlook director at DNV, a Norway-based consultancy. Much more permanent are the vehicles people are buying.

Global sales of electric vehicles were up 4% in the second quarter of 2026, according to the IEA, which said the Middle East crisis “has clearly reinforced the case for EVs as a way to address energy security and fuel cost concerns.”

New electric cars waiting for shipment to overseas markets in a port in Yantai, Shandong province, China, on September 26. Feature China/Future Publishing/Getty Images

Australia and parts of Asia have seen EV booms, as has Europe, where sales hit record highs in 2026, according to a report from the non-profit advocacy group Transport & Environment. Fuel prices were a key factor, with diesel reaching particularly painful highs, up 38% since the start of the war.

The US bucks the trend, however. EV sales have slumped as the Trump administration has cut support for them and effectively banned cheaper Chinese models. They’re down more than 30% this year so far, according to research firm Motor Intelligence.

Then there’s natural gas. The conflict has dealt “a major supply shock” to the world’s gas markets, according to the IEA, which projects global demand will shrink by around 0.5% in 2026.

Countries are seeking alternatives, with dozens implementing policies to switch from fossil fuels to clean power since the war started. Harnessing the sun and wind doesn’t rely on a few volatile chokepoints in the same way as oil and gas.

“The new geopolitics of energy is driving clean energy solutions and electrification,” said Amy Myers Jaffe, director of the Global Energy, Climate, and Sustainability Lab at New York University.

Investment in solar capacity in Southeast Asian countries, for example, has roughly quadrupled in the first two quarters of this year, according to data from the Rhodium Group, an independent research provider. Most of the region’s liquified natural gas comes from the Gulf, so they had to “make a quicker pivot,” said Tess Carter, an associate director for energy and climate at Rhodium.

It will take time to see real evidence of an accelerating shift away from oil and gas, said Gross. A wholesale move to EVs and widespread changes in grid-scale electricity are lengthy processes. “But I do expect that it is coming,” Gross said.

Workers install solar panels on a roof in Carmona, in the Philippine province of Cavite, on July 9. Jam Sta Rosa/AFP/Getty Images

That said, there is a catch. The transition to alternative energy options has not just meant renewables; some countries have turned to coal, the dirtiest fossil fuel. Global coal demand is now projected to rise by 1.2% in 2026, a reversal of earlier forecasts which had projected a small decline.

There is also the possibility that oil and gas demand could come swinging back — the IEA projects a recovery for oil in 2027. And we’ve been here before on big global disruptions. Some environmentalists hoped the pandemic would lead to a clean energy shift, instead, fossil fuel demand surged in 2021.

How permanent the shifts are may depend on how long the conflict endures. For every month it lasts, the probability of permanent oil “demand destruction” increases, a DNV analysis found. “If the war lasts for four years, for example, then our analysis shows that oil demand will never resume to the level we had in 2025,” DNV’s Alvik said.

Some are hopeful that whatever happens, more permanent changes are already ingrained. Iran has shown drones and missiles are all that’s needed to strangle a waterway — not a powerful navy. “The world cannot unsee what has happened, and oil and natural gas supply seem much more insecure than they did before the war,” said Gross of the Brookings Institution.

Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University, said the conflict “could have a sustained effect because dozens of countries are now promoting EV incentives, charging infrastructure and electrification in general.”

Still, he finds the notion of Trump as an accidental climate president “ridiculous.” He may have hastened clean energy uptake overseas, but he has gutted green energy in the US and “set us back decades,” Jackson said.

“The forces driving green energy around the world — cleaner, cheaper fuels — will ultimately prevail despite him.”

World.title: Trump turns to the politics of fear as GOP hopes darken
World.content:
It’s getting ugly out there.

The worse GOP midterm prospects look, the darker the rhetoric from top Republicans becomes as they single out Democratic candidates as weird, threatening and antithetical to what it means to be and look like an American.

President Donald Trump is mocking the name of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and slandering him as a “jihadist.”

Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday made a joke that implied James Talarico is gay. Trump keeps claiming the Democratic Senate nominee is a vegan who is incompatible with the carnivorous Lone Star State. Talarico is now often seen pictured with a plate of meat.

The president has also revived his searing racially derogatory rhetoric suggesting that Haitians and Africans are invading key election states like Ohio.

And after federal officials searched the home of Somali-born Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday, he underscored concerns he’s using executive power to target a political foe by questioning whether she had constitutional rights as a naturalized citizen “from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

Trump’s rhetoric is hardly a surprise, given the linguistic excesses of his presidential campaigns, yet it’s still jarring to see such overt racial language delivered from behind a presidential podium.

Some insults are delivered with a smile, which may offer Trump and Vance a modicum of political cover and the chance to argue it’s all part of the rough-and-tumble of the campaign trail in a polarized age. But that hardly makes maligning someone’s race, faith, personal appearance and manner more acceptable, nor does it absolve an intellectually low form of politics.

Why do they do it?

Trump has been accused of prejudice for years — especially over inflammatory social media posts and fake and racist conspiracies he pushed over former president Barack Obama’s birthplace. The president, in seeking to appeal to voters, has often implied some minority political rivals are incompatible with traditional American culture and values. His anti-immigrant rhetoric seems at least partially aimed at his most conservative base voters who the GOP needs to turn out in huge numbers to stave off a midterm election disaster.

The most obvious explanation for this ominous turn in the campaign, beyond Trump’s propensity for such dark arts, is that the Republicans lack a better story to tell. Trump’s approval rating is at 33% in the latest CNN poll of polls — a daunting number for an incumbent president three weeks from a midterm election. Polls show majorities of Americans blame the president’s decisions for worsening their struggle to cope with the high costs of food, housing, gasoline and diesel. And the rush by Vance and Trump to red states where Republicans never thought they’d be fighting in the campaign’s final stretch tells its own story.

Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas James Talarico speaks at a campaign rally in Houston in March. Danielle Villasana/Getty Images Texas Attorney General and Republican candidate for Senate Ken Paxton walks onstage during the midterm Republican National Convention in Dallas on September 9. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

Branding Talarico as a “freak,” as Vance did in Texas on Tuesday, seems an attempt to distract from the struggling and scandal-plagued GOP Senate candidate — Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was Trump’s personal pick for the seat.

It’s politics 101 for party leaders to seek to disqualify rivals whom they can’t beat on the issues. Trump’s singling out of Muslim candidates parallels his conceit that Democrats are “socialists” and “communists.” And if he can malign El-Sayed and Talarico, he’ll be doing his party a service. The pair are locked in races expected to go down to the wire on November 3.

Trump is going harshly negative on El-Sayed, the former executive director of the Detroit Health Department. “I call him Mohammed,” Trump said in Tennessee on Saturday. “Somebody said, ‘His name isn’t Mohammed’ I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want.” On Monday night in Ohio, he added: “He’s a jihadist.”

It is of course legitimate for Republicans to highlight and attack El-Sayed’s record. They want to draw attention to his claim that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza shortly after the October 7 attacks. Many American Jews — Democratic voters among them — balk at the term, even while mourning the tens of thousands of Palestinians killed in the Israel-Hamas war following the terror attacks that killed more than 1,200 people, mostly Israelis, in 2023.

Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters in Detroit on August 2. Scott Olson/Getty Images

But calling El-Sayed a “jihadist” — namely a radicalized terrorist who rejects democracy, suggesting he’s aligned with groups like Al-Qaeda or ISIS — crosses a rubicon. It’s obviously intended to frighten voters into thinking that the Democratic candidate is a terrorist and security threat. And calling El-Sayed “Mohammed” demeans him and insults the humanity and individuality of all Muslims.

More broadly, the president seems to be portraying the Michigan-born Democrat and anyone who shares his faith as un-American and unworthy of the political rights of every citizen. His tactics recall his still-incessant use of Obama’s middle name, Hussein.

El-Sayed responded to Trump’s deliberate mangling of his name by arguing the president’s focus insults the intelligence of voters. “He knows my name is Abdul. He says it everyday,” El-Sayed wrote on X. “But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us. He thinks so low of us. He thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor’s office.”

Trump escalates offensive against Ilhan Omar

Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar attends a news conference in Washington, DC, in January. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images

The president’s rhetoric toward Omar, with whom he’s furiously sparred for years, has similar apparent goals. He implies that the Minnesota representative is importing what he depicts as the anarchy of Somalia to Minnesota. “She’s a disaster. She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, without — all they do is shoot each other,” he said in Ohio on Monday. “They come into the United States of America and they tell us how to run our country. We’re not going to stand for it. They drive up taxes. They drive up healthcare costs, insurance costs, childcare costs.”

Minnesota welcomed tens of thousands of Somalis in the early 1990s when their East African country collapsed into violence. The administration claims the community is laced with violent criminals and widespread fraud centered in day care centers. Somali leaders say violent criminals are a tiny minority, and that Trump and Republicans are maligning them without justification.

The Department of Justice said it carried out an enforcement operation at the home of Omar, who is running for reelection. It is not yet possible to independently verify any evidence or accusations against her. Omar responded that Trump had smeared her for years and was now targeting her as a political enemy.

Agents of the Homeland Security Investigations work at the entrance of the Washington, DC, residence of Rep. Omar on Monday. Annabelle Gordon/Reuters

Trump’s aides repeatedly deny that he is racist or guilty of racist rhetoric, pointing out that he holds events to mark milestones like Black History Month and that he increased his support among minority voters in the 2024 election. In February, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt slammed “radical Democrats throughout the years who have accused this president falsely of being a racist.”

Many Republican voters also claim double standards, pointing out that Democrats often speak in demeaning terms about conservatives and Trump’s voters more generally — including those who adopted Hillary Clinton’s phrase that half of them were in a “basket of deplorables” as a perverse badge of honor. Some senior Democrats have openly charged that Trump is a fascist.

But Trump and Vance are also intensifying a trend that animates the newly populist Republican Party: a tendency to make specific judgments about who can be considered an authentic American.

In the 2008 campaign, GOP vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin argued that “real America” was defined by small-town patriots and hard workers who lived in “pro-America areas of this great nation” — implying that those outside the heartland lacked legitimacy and pride in the country.

Those remarks seem tame by comparison to the vitriol that Trump ushered in, and her subsequent apology now looks like a historical curiosity.

World.title: Ukraine says SpaceX restricted Starlink services, disrupting military operations as Russian attacks continue
World.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine —

Ukrainian authorities say SpaceX has restricted Starlink internet services, disrupting military logistics and operations amid an escalating dispute with the Trump administration.

Ukrainian authorities said they were caught off-guard by restrictions on the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink, called Starshield.

“Our defense forces received no warning of this restriction, and this has led to the disruption of a number of missions,” Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said in a social media post. “It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”

The Starlink disruption is compounded by the Ukrainian government’s recent reports of turmoil with intelligence-sharing from allies.

It comes after the Trump administration warned Ukraine last weekend that the US could suspend intelligence sharing and European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt its long-range strikes on Russian energy facilities.

Intelligence provided by the US and other partners helps Ukraine defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks by providing the locations of missile launchers as well as data on where the strikes are heading, and when.

Late on Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his government had received “no early warning from our partners” before a deadly ballistic missile attack hit a major power plant in Kyiv and damaged a residential building.

However, when asked earlier Tuesday, Trump said the US had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end,” he said.

People gather at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Wednesday. Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

A Ukrainian military source with direct knowledge of day-to-day operations impacted by Starlink told CNN that “the complications are substantial.”

“We’re investigating connection issues in detail. What will be affected is the front line and occupied territories,” the military source said. “We were getting ready for this.”

“We’re currently investigating the cause,” a Ukrainian Defense Ministry source told CNN. “This situation significantly complicates logistics, unmanned systems, forces operations, mid-range strikes, etc.”

CNN has reached out to SpaceX for comment.

On Saturday, SpaceX CEO Musk criticized the Ukrainian president in a post on his social media platform X, writing that “Zelensky has gone too far” when it comes to strikes on Russian fuel facilities.

CNN has also reached out to the White House, the Pentagon and the Ukrainian Defense Ministry for comment.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that Russia had no further information about the Starlink disruptions in Ukraine. He also said the Kremlin is “carefully noting” reports of shifts in Washington’s support for Kyiv, adding that it’s “too early to draw any systemic conclusions.”

Attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure

Meanwhile, another massive Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure left more than 600,000 people without power early on Wednesday, according to Zelensky.

Russia launched more than 120 drones and 39 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kharkiv, specifically targeting energy facilities, said Zelensky – causing widespread power outages and “significant damage” to oil and gas facilities.

These are “the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote, referring to the surprise “energy ceasefire” that President Donald Trump announced last weekend.

CNN journalists in the capital reported hearing multiple explosions.

“This is absolutely unjust: when they (Russia) are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches,” Zelensky said.

Intelligence sharing is no guarantee of protection. Russia’s ballistic missiles can reach Kyiv in just minutes, leaving little time to respond; in some recent attacks, air raid sirens sounded at the same time as the first explosions.

For months, Zelensky has urged partners to help bolster Ukraine’s air defenses, especially in providing more ballistic-missile interceptors – one of the few weapons capable of knocking down ballistic missiles that travel faster than the speed of sound.

His presidential adviser Beskrestnov warned that Starlink is also used for the operation of interceptor drones that help protect Ukrainian airspace from Russia’s jet-powered attack drones.

“In effect, through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few opportunities we have to defend the country against jet-powered ‘Shahed’ drones,” he said on Wednesday.

Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strike at an apartment building in Kyiv on Wednesday. Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images

Russia’s latest attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure has raised further questions about the so-called “energy ceasefire” announced by Trump on Sunday, which appeared to take both Kyiv and Moscow by surprise. After the left-field US announcement, Zelensky said he supported the ceasefire even though he did not know about it in advance.

By Monday, Zelensky said Russia had already violated the supposed ceasefire with fresh strikes – but said he was willing to abide by the agreement if Moscow does too.

When asked by reporters on Tuesday whether Russia had violated the ceasefire, Trump said: “I’ll let you know about that later,” according to Reuters.

The Kremlin finally addressed the “energy ceasefire” on Wednesday after days of silence, questioning the specifics of the US proposal and saying that “work in this direction is continuing.”

Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure in recent months, as front lines on the ground stay largely unmoved.

Russia’s defense ministry also said it had downed 902 drones overnight, according to Russian news agency Interfax.

World.title: Character.ai files for bankruptcy following lawsuits alleging ties to teen suicides
World.content:
New York —

Artificial intelligence chat startup Character.ai— which has faced a wave of claims that its app contributed to mental health issues and suicides among teens — has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

Character.ai lets users message with a range of chatbots, often modeled after celebrities and fictional characters, or create their own. Its bots often respond with human-like conversational cues, adding references to facial expressions or gestures into their replies.

The company said it plans to seek a court-supervised sale by the end of the year in hopes of keeping the platform running long-term.

Disney has already set itself up as a bidder for the company’s assets, agreeing to pay $20 million for some of the company’s intellectual property and to provide transition services via former Character.ai employees it has hired. The deal will allow Character.ai to keep its platform operational at least during the bankruptcy process. Karandeep Anand, who was brought on as Character.ai’s CEO last year to help improve its reputation on safety, joined Disney as Chief Technology Officer last month.

Former Google AI staffers Noam Shazeer and Daniel de Freitas launched Character.ai in 2021. Both founders have since returned to Google. Within just over a year, the company said it had reached a $1 billion valuation, following a $150 million funding round.

Character.ai has between $50 million and $100 million in assets, according to its bankruptcy filling.

In 2024, amid growing concerns about human dependance on AI chatbots, Florida mother Megan Garcia sued Character.ai, alleging that the platform was responsible for the suicide death of her 14-year-old son Sewell Setzer III. Other families filed a string of additional lawsuits, accusing the platform of providing sexual content to their children or encouraging suicide, self-harm or violence. Character.ai agreed to settle five cases, including Garcia’s, earlier this year.

Matthew Bergman, founder of the Social Media Victims Law Center, which represents several of the families who sued Character.ai, declined to comment on the bankruptcy filing.

Character.ai made a number of safety changes in the wake of the lawsuits, including adding pop-ups directing users to mental health resources. It also blocked users under 18 from engaging in back-and-forth conversations with bots, instead allowing them only to create one-time stories or videos.

The company also faced a probe into its safety practices by Senate Democrats last year, along with other AI “companion” apps. Character.ai was also in competition with chatbots from much larger players, such as ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

When Anand took over as CEO of the then-70-person company last year, he told CNN he saw a future for the company in interactive, personalized AI entertainment — where users could co-create stories and conversations with AI characters for fun. He told CNN at the time that the company was “doubling down on entertainment, doubling down on trust and safety.”

Character.ai says that if a sale is not completed, the platform will be “wound down.”

“Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” Colin Adams, CEO of Character.AI, said in a statement, adding that the company’s board reviewed its options and “determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders.”

World.title: Al-Azhar condemns Riyadh Airport attack, targeting of civilians, Umrah pilgrims
World.content:
Al-Azhar has strongly condemned the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which left civilians and Umrah pilgrims dead and injured, stressing that attacks on civilian infrastructure and pilgrims visiting Islam’s two holiest mosques constitute a grave provocation to Muslims, a violation of humanitarian values and international norms, and a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and territorial integrity.

In a statement, Al-Azhar reiterated its unequivocal rejection of repeated attacks that have claimed innocent civilian lives and undermined the Kingdom’s security and stability.

It warned of the consequences of continued aggression, emphasizing that safeguarding regional security requires an immediate halt to such attacks and full respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states.

Grand Imam of Al-Azhar Ahmed al-Tayyeb extended his heartfelt condolences to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz, Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques; Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; the Saudi people; and the families of the victims.

He prayed for the victims to be granted Allah’s mercy and forgiveness, wished the injured a speedy recovery, and asked Allah Almighty to protect the Kingdom of the Two Holy Mosques and all Muslim countries from harm and adversity, and to ensure the continued security, peace and stability of their peoples.

World.title: FM calls for further efforts to prevent regional conflict from widening
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty emphasized the importance of intensifying efforts to achieve de-escalation, contain regional tensions and prevent the conflict from widening, in a way that safeguards regional security and stability.

In an interview with Sky News Arabia, Abdelatty also discussed developments in the Iranian file and their implications for regional security.

He addressed key regional issues, including Egypt-Gulf relations and ways to strengthen coordination and consultation on current challenges.

The interview also covered developments in the Gaza Strip, Egyptian water security as an existential issue and the situation in Sudan.

World.title: FM highlights Egypt’s efforts to de-escalate US-Iran tensions
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty outlined Egypt’s efforts to de-escalate regional tensions and create conditions for an agreement between the United States and Iran, as well as the conflict’s economic repercussions for the global economy, supply chains and energy markets.

In an interview with Thailand’s CNA television channel, Abdelatty discussed prospects for Egyptian-Thai relations and ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation across various fields, during his visit to Thailand — the first by an Egyptian foreign minister in 30 years — as Egypt seeks to expand its partnerships with Asian countries.

The minister also outlined Egypt’s assessment of the challenges facing the global economy amid mounting pressures, stressing the importance of stronger international cooperation and a greater role for international financial institutions in providing concessional financing.

Such financing would support developing countries’ efforts to achieve sustainable development and address current economic challenges, he said.

World.title: FM highlights expats’ role in strengthening Egypt’s global standing
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said Egyptians living abroad represent an extension of their homeland and contribute their expertise and skills to enhancing Egypt’s image and standing internationally.

Abdelatty made the remarks during a meeting with members of the Egyptian community in Thailand on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of his visit to Bangkok. The meeting was attended by Egyptian Ambassador to Thailand Hala Youssef.

The minister praised the role of Egyptians residing in Thailand in strengthening ties and communication between the two countries.

He reaffirmed the Foreign Ministry’s commitment to maintaining contact with Egyptian communities abroad, protecting their interests, addressing their needs and facilitating access to consular services.

In this regard, Abdelatty outlined the ministry’s efforts to modernize consular services and expand digital service delivery to simplify procedures and improve efficiency. He also highlighted initiatives for Egyptians abroad, including “Your Home in Egypt” and “Open Your Account in Egypt.”

The minister praised the Egyptian community’s participation in the seventh edition of the Conference of Egyptians Abroad, held in August 2026, and expressed hope that they would continue to participate actively in future editions.

He described the conference as a platform for direct dialogue and the exchange of views between Egyptians abroad and state institutions.

Abdelatty also listened to community members’ views and proposals on issues affecting their interests, stressing the importance of sustaining dialogue and developing communication channels to address their demands and aspirations.

World.title: Liberia: State Jumped the Gun, Judge Finds, in Case That Shut Down Sekou Dukuly’s Three Care Homes in the United States of America
World.content:
An administrative law judge says Minnesota regulators failed to prove Golden Touch Health Care posed an imminent danger to residents, a finding supporters of owner Sekou Dukuly call long overdue.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

ST. PAUL, Minn. – For two months, Sekou Hussein Dukuly has watched the business he built in the Twin Cities suburbs sit empty, its residents relocated and its licenses frozen by order of the state. This week, a judge told Minnesota health officials they got it wrong.



In a ruling dated October 14, 2026, Administrative Law Judge Suzanne Todnem concluded that the Minnesota Department of Health “prematurely” suspended the three assisted living licenses held by Dukuly’s company, Golden Touch Health Care LLC. She found the department failed to show that the company’s problems posed an imminent risk of harm to residents, the legal standard required for an emergency suspension. Her formal recommendation to Health Commissioner Brooke Cunningham is to rescind the suspension.

For Dukuly and the Liberian community members who have followed his case closely, the language was unusually direct. Reading the judge’s findings, one supporter said, was the first time in weeks that anyone in authority had said out loud what the family had argued from the start: that the state moved before it had the evidence.

The ruling is a recommendation, not a final order, and it does not resolve every dispute facing the company. But on the question before the judge, it was a clear win.

The Day Everything Changed

Golden Touch Health Care operates three licensed assisted living facilities in Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center, serving residents with physical and mental health needs. Two of the licenses date to August 2021, and a third was issued in April 2025. The Department of Health renewed all three earlier this year.

On August 19, 2026, investigators visited each facility. By the end of the day, the department had issued orders immediately suspending all three licenses for 90 days. Golden Touch complied, transferring all 11 of its residents to other facilities.

The department’s reasoning rested on two concerns. First, as of August 12, Dukuly was no longer registered with the state’s licensing board as the director of record for the facilities, and no replacement had been registered. Second, the state Department of Human Services (DHS) had signaled it would withhold Medical Assistance payments to the company starting September 21, citing credible allegations of fraud that it was investigating. The health department concluded that unclear leadership combined with a coming loss of revenue would likely disrupt care.

Golden Touch appealed within days. On October 1, its attorneys from the Greene Espel law firm faced off against two assistant attorneys general in an expedited hearing before Judge Todnem.

A Narrow Question, a Clear Answer

The hearing was limited by statute to two questions: whether there was sufficient evidence of violations posing an imminent risk of harm to residents’ health and safety, and whether the suspension should remain in effect.

The judge began with the meaning of the word that decided the case. “Imminent” is not defined in the statute, so she used its ordinary meaning: likely to happen very soon. Then she measured the department’s evidence against it, and the evidence fell short.

Thirty-Three Days

The department’s first argument concerned the coming payment withhold. But the suspension was issued on August 19, and the withhold was not scheduled to begin until September 21, a gap of 33 days.

“By definition,” Judge Todnem wrote, any concerns resulting from a disruption in revenue were not imminent. Golden Touch had experienced no change in its revenue. According to the findings, company staff did not even know the withhold notices were coming until the investigator raised the issue during the on-site visit.

The judge also noted that the DHS notices gave Golden Touch until August 29 to tell the state whether it would keep serving residents without Medical Assistance payments. By suspending the licenses first, she found, the department took that decision away from the company.

She was pointed about the consequences. The company’s nurse supervisor, Ishmael Komara, testified that Dukuly had financial options to keep the facilities running for six months. The testimony was not backed by documents, but the judge found it reasonable that the company had not locked in financing for facilities the state had already shut down. “It is not appropriate to strip a licensee of its options and then use the lack of exercising those options against it,” she wrote.

The department’s second argument concerned leadership. Minnesota law requires every assisted living facility to employ a licensed director who is registered with the state board as the director of record, and it was undisputed that none was registered after August 12.

The judge did not excuse that. She rejected the company’s suggestion that approval of its replacement director’s application was a mere formality, and she found that the facilities were in violation of the statute.

But a violation is not the same as an emergency. A department official conceded at the hearing that when a facility’s only problem is a missing registered director, the department’s standard practice is to issue a correction order telling the facility to fix it. The judge found the department never showed why this case called for something far more drastic than its usual response.

The company’s explanation for the gap was a leadership transition. On August 13, the day after Dukuly’s registration lapsed, Tabitha Vickie Briggs, a registered nurse who holds an assisted living director license, applied for a Shared Director License that would allow her to lead all three facilities. Dukuly’s brother-in-law and company coverage administrator, Sheikh Dukuly, who also holds a director license, was on site, as was Komara, who holds one too. In effect, Golden Touch argued, three licensed directors were working at or available to the facilities even though the paperwork had not caught up.

Piling On

The department’s strongest card was supposed to be the combination: that a leadership gap plus a revenue disruption together created the danger. The judge was unpersuaded.

She called one element of the department’s argument “disingenuous.” The department had pointed out that staff did not present a six-month plan to stay operational after payments stopped. But the company had not yet received any withhold notice, and the investigator never asked for such a plan.

She also observed that the investigator spoke with Sheikh Dukuly, Briggs, one resident and three unlicensed staff members, but did not ask staff how often they were present at the facilities and did not ask to speak with Sekou Dukuly. And she found it unclear when the department first became concerned about the director issue. The record suggested officials did not view it as an imminent threat until the DHS notice arrived, a notice still 33 days from taking effect.

Her conclusion on the combined theory was blunt: even taken together, the record did not establish an imminent risk of harm to residents.

What the Judge Did Not Say

The ruling is favorable, but it is not a clean sweep, and an accurate account must include its limits.

The judge sided with the department on the underlying violation, finding that the facilities lacked a registered director after August 12. She also noted that the company’s explanation for staff confusion about who was in charge did not fully hold up. One staff member told the investigator Sekou Dukuly was the director, another named Sheikh Dukuly, and none named Briggs.

More importantly, the ruling does not touch the DHS fraud investigation. The judge made no findings about the allegations, and nothing in her report lifts the payment withhold, which is a separate action by a separate agency. The department’s notices of revocation, which are also separate, are likewise outside this case.

And the recommendation itself is not binding. Both sides have ten calendar days to file exceptions. The Commissioner then has ten business days after the record closes to issue a final decision, which she may adopt, reject or modify. Any party can then appeal under Minnesota’s administrative procedure act.

The judge also observed that because no residents are currently in Golden Touch’s care, there was insufficient evidence to keep the suspension in place.

Why Supporters Call It Vindication

For Dukuly’s supporters, those caveats do not diminish what the ruling establishes. A state agency exercised one of its most powerful emergency tools, shutting down three licensed homes without a prior hearing, and an independent judge reviewing the evidence found the agency had not justified it.

That matters in a field where a license is the entire business. An immigrant entrepreneur who spends years building a regulated care operation can see it dismantled in a single afternoon, with residents relocated and revenue stopped, long before any hearing takes place. The expedited hearing process exists to check that power, and in this case the check worked in Golden Touch’s favor.

Members of the Liberian community, which has deep roots in the Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center area, have followed the case with intense interest. In social media posts after the ruling, supporters described it as proof of Dukuly’s resilience and credited his faith. One close friend wrote that “God has the final say,” and asked critics who had celebrated the company’s troubles why they had not prayed for his success instead.

That friend’s post also reflects how personal the case became. When the suspensions were first reported, some in the community reacted with gloating or gossip, a response that stung the family and its allies. The judge’s findings have, for now, given them an answer grounded in the record rather than in rumor.

For a man whose supporters say he has endured the storm with his head up, that finding is not the end of the road. But it is the first time the record has spoken, and what it said was that the state moved too soon.

The Minnesota Department of Health and Golden Touch Health Care did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

World.title: Liberia’s Council of Churches warns justice “must not become political revenge” as ex-ministers convicted in Saudi aid case and Chief Justice floats scrapping jury trials
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s most influential Christian body has called on the government, the courts and the country’s political class to keep politics out of the courtroom, days after a jury convicted a former foreign minister and other ex-officials of stealing rice donated by Saudi Arabia for disaster victims.

By Rodney D Sieh

In a statement issued Tuesday titled “Justice Without Political Interference; Reconciliation Without Impunity,” the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC) said it “neither determines guilt nor dictates the outcome” of the case, but insisted that justice be “governed by evidence and law, free from political interference, intimidation, and public pressure.”



“No one should be prosecuted because of personal hatred or political opposition, or escape lawful accountability through political influence,” said the Council, which is led by Rev. Dr. Samuel Broomfield Reeves, Jr., who also serves as vice president of the Inter-Religious Council of Liberia.

A verdict that split the jury, and the country

The statement follows a mixed verdict delivered Friday, October 9, at Criminal Court “C” in Monrovia. According to the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce (AREPT), which prosecuted the case, the jury found eight of the 13 defendants guilty, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf. Three were acquitted, and verdicts on two others were inconclusive.

Kemayah was reported guilty on all five counts: theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy. But the jury was far from united. Four of the 12 jurors reportedly voted to acquit him of theft, and four voted against conviction on both economic sabotage and conspiracy; only the abuse-of-office count was unanimous.

Former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) chief Henry O. Williams was reported not guilty on all charges, a notable outcome given that his agency was responsible for storing and distributing the rice. Charges against Mary Broh, the former head of the General Services Agency and one-time acting mayor of Monrovia, were dropped by the Justice Ministry in August.

Jurors were reportedly seen wearing masks to hide their identities during the trial, an indication of the pressure surrounding a case involving some of the most recognizable figures from Liberia’s previous government.

Rice meant for the vulnerable

The case centers on a humanitarian gift. In 2023, Saudi Arabia donated 29,412 bags of rice, valued at about US$500,000, for disaster victims and vulnerable Liberians. The indictment alleged that 25,054 of those bags were unlawfully diverted or misapplied. Rice is Liberia’s staple food, and the alleged diversion of aid in one of West Africa’s poorest nations has made the case a lightning rod for public anger over corruption.

Kemayah, who helped secure the donation while serving as foreign minister, has consistently denied stealing, receiving or misappropriating the rice. His defense argued that the financial side of the donation was handled directly by Saudi humanitarian authorities and the supplier, not by him.

The prosecution grew out of President Joseph Boakai’s anti-corruption drive after he defeated incumbent George Weah in the 2023 election. Kemayah and Sirleaf both served in Weah’s cabinet, and supporters of the defendants have increasingly cast the trials as politically motivated.

‘Score-settling masquerading as justice’

That charge was sharpened on Monday when one of the convicted officials, former NDMA official and ordained Baptist minister Rev. Rosetta L. Gbassay Bowah, rejected her verdict on Facebook. She alleged that prosecutors had persistently pressed her to become a state witness, a claim her post offered no evidence for and which has not been independently verified. She warned that Liberia risks a cycle of vengeance, political persecution and “score-settling masquerading as justice.”

The government sees it differently. AREPT welcomed the verdicts as a significant milestone in the fight against corruption, and its chairman, Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin, said the taskforce was ready to defend the convictions if defendants appeal to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice questions jury system

The Council’s call for judicial independence also lands amid a fresh controversy over how Liberia’s courts reach verdicts. Opening the Supreme Court’s October Term on Monday, Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. said jury manipulation was eroding justice in civil and criminal cases, declaring that “a corrupt jury is worse than no jury at all.” He cited suspected interference in proceedings at Criminal Court “C,” the same court that heard the rice case.

The Liberia National Bar Association condemned tampering but said its participation in any review should not be read as support for abolition, while Senator Darius Dillon argued that removing jury trials would require a national referendum.

Reconciliation ‘not a shield’

The LCC’s statement reaches beyond the courtroom to a sensitive national theme. Liberia is still grappling with the legacy of civil wars that killed an estimated 250,000 people between 1989 and 2003, and debates over accountability and forgiveness remain raw.

“Reconciliation must not become a shield for wrongdoing,” the Council said. “Forgiveness cannot erase the need for accountability, and accountability must never become an instrument of revenge.”

Recalling the country’s “painful history,” the churches warned that “justice pursued without fairness can deepen division, while peace pursued without accountability can preserve injustice.”

The Council urged public officials, political parties, the media and citizens not to prejudge the case or pressure the courts. “Public scrutiny is legitimate; political interference is not,” it said, and called on congregations to “reject hateful rhetoric” and encourage peaceful dialogue.

“Let the courts follow the evidence, the Government respect the law, and the Church speak the truth,” the statement concluded.
