BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What is happening Brazil’s Senate passed the constitutional amendment ending the 6×1 work week on Wednesday, 14 October, by 75 votes to 1 in both rounds; only Hamilton Mourão voted no.

— Why it matters The change gives workers two paid rest days and cuts the maximum week from 44 to 42 hours two months after promulgation, then to 40 hours a year later, and it lands 11 days before the 25 October runoff.

— The numbers The amendment needed 49 of 81 senators in each round and got 75; the Chamber of Deputies had passed it in May, so it now goes to promulgation without returning to the Chamber.

— Who is who Senate President Davi Alcolumbre scheduled the vote, Omar Aziz of the PSD (Social Democratic Party) was rapporteur, and runoff rivals Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro now both say they support ending 6×1.

— What to watch Congress still has to promulgate the amendment, and Alcolumbre has said that could happen as soon as next week.

— Prediction markets Polymarket 83.0% and Kalshi 84.0% for a Flávio Bolsonaro runoff win, 15 October, 12:51 a.m. ET. Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 83% and Kalshi at 84% (Lula: 17% and 18% ), as of 15 October, 1:00 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US companies with Brazilian payrolls, from retailers to call centres, will have to plan new rosters, while investors in Petrobras, Vale and Itaú Unibanco will watch how labour costs adjust.

Brazil’s Senate voted 75 to 1 on 14 October to end the 6×1 work week, sending a shorter week and two paid rest days to promulgation 11 days before the presidential runoff.

Brazil’s Senate on Wednesday, 14 October, passed the constitutional amendment that ends the 6×1 work week, in which millions of employees work six days and rest one. The vote was 75 to 1 in both rounds, far above the 49 of 81 needed.

For US readers, the vote reshapes labour costs in Latin America’s largest economy and removes one divisive issue from the 25 October runoff. It also affects every American company that employs staff in Brazil.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Senate Approved

The text is PEC 221/2019, known in Brazil as a PEC (proposta de emenda à Constituição), or constitutional amendment. It lowers the maximum working week from 44 hours to 42 hours two months after promulgation and to 40 hours a year later, according to Agência Senado and Gazeta do Povo. It also raises weekly paid rest from one day to two, with one of them preferably on a Sunday.

Agência Senado, the Senate’s own news service, reports that daily work is capped at eight hours, with room to offset hours between days. It also says pay may not fall and that some changes will be phased in.

How the Vote Went

The Chamber of Deputies approved the text in May, and the Senate’s Constitution and Justice Committee (CCJ) cleared it on 2 September. The full Senate held five discussion sessions before the first round, then dispensed with the three sessions normally required before the second.

Hamilton Mourão of the Republicans, a senator for Rio Grande do Sul, cast the only vote against in both rounds. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre told the chamber that millions of Brazilians were following the session with hope.

Why the Timing Matters

The vote came 11 days before the runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the Liberal Party’s Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, 25 October. Lula made ending 6×1 a central promise of his campaign, according to Gazeta do Povo.

Flávio, a Rio de Janeiro senator, said on Tuesday, 13 October, that he would vote for the change after earlier calling it runoff.

01 Getting Around

Mexico’s Pacific coast: Hurricane Simón. Mexico’s weather service (SMN) kept a hurricane watch (hurricane conditions are possible) for the Sinaloa coast from Escuinapa to Bahía Tempehuaya, and a prevention zone for hurricane-force winds around the Marías Islands. Spanish-language reports on Wednesday disagreed on whether Simón was a Category 1 or Category 2 hurricane and on exactly where and when it would come ashore.

Some forecasts pointed to a landfall near Mazatlán on Thursday 15 October, while Uno TV reported on Tuesday that the storm was almost stationary at sea and would stay a threat for days. Heavy rain and high waves are forecast for Jalisco, Nayarit and southern Sinaloa, and the rainfall figures differ between bulletins. We could not read the latest SMN or US National Hurricane Center bulletin this morning, so treat these points as likely to change. Our checklist for foreigners sets out what to prepare, and local civil protection orders come first.

Panama: schools and daily routines. Panama’s education ministry (Meduca) announced that a gradual reopening of public schools would begin on Wednesday 14 October, once safety inspections are done. We have not confirmed how many schools opened. On Tuesday 13 October, Minister Ventura Vega counted 619 damaged schools in 15 education regions, and 35 schools destroyed, according to Telemetro.

Not every building will open on the same day. Ask your child’s school which building is open and when, because the reopening depends on each inspection.

02 Cost of Living & Money

Each measure is labelled, and dates differ by country. Brazil’s PTAX, Colombia’s TRM and Argentina’s rates are official or public-service quotes; Mexico, Peru and Chile are Wednesday market closes from RT, a market-data provider, not official fixings.

Brazil. The PTAX fixing (the central bank’s reference dollar rate) was 5.0441 reais to sell on Wednesday 14 October, after 5.0096 on Tuesday 13 October. At 5.0441, R$1,000 is about US$198.

Mexico. The dollar closed at 18.497 pesos on Wednesday 14 October, up from 18.371 on Tuesday 13 October. It is not the official FIX rate (Banxico’s daily reference rate). At 18.497, MXN 10,000 is about US$541.

Chile. The market close was 985.0 pesos per dollar on Wednesday 14 October, a market-data quote, because we could not read the central bank’s observado (its reference rate) this morning. At 985.0, CLP 1,000,000 is about US$1,015.

Colombia. The TRM (the official representative rate) is 3,197.65 pesos per dollar for Thursday 15 October, up from 3,181.74 for Wednesday 14 October, according to the financial regulator’s open data. At 3,197.65, COP 1,000,000 is about US$313.

Argentina. DolarApi shows the official Banco Nación rate at 1,485 to buy and 1,535 to sell on Wednesday. The blue (informal market rate) was 1,530 and 1,550, and the CCL (contado con liquidación, a rate for dollars bought through securities) was 1,615.8 and 1,617.3. ARS 1,000,000 is about US$651 at the official sell rate and about US$618 at the CCL sell rate, and ArgentinaDatos puts country risk (the extra yield investors demand on Argentine dollar bonds) at 611 points on 14 October.

Peru. We could not obtain SUNAT’s (the tax authority’s) rate. The market close was 3.4304 soles per dollar on Wednesday 14 October, and banks quote their own rates. At 3.4304, PEN 1,000 is about US$292.

The wider picture. The real and Mexico’s peso each weakened about 0.7% on Wednesday, and Colombia’s TRM is about 0.5% higher. One day does not set a trend, and currencies often overshoot after news and then settle.

03 Visas, Residency & Tax

Argentina: what 33.4% inflation means for your budget. Argentina’s statistics institute INDEC reported on Tuesday 13 October that consumer prices rose 1.9% in September and 33.4% over 12 months. Housing, water, electricity and gas rose 3.1% in the month, which matters most for anyone renting or paying utility bills. Our guide to what this means for expats has the detail.

Colombia: 16 days left. Foreigners holding a permanent-resident visa issued under earlier rules must transfer it before 31 October 2026, the Foreign Ministry has reiterated. The process is online; the ministry advises using its official site without intermediaries. Our earlier explainer sets out who is affected.

Peru: regional runoff on 6 December. The electoral court (JNE) moved the second round of the regional elections from Sunday 29 November to Sunday 6 December, according to Gestión. Foreign residents cannot vote for governors, and our expat guide to the runoffs carries the new date.

Panama: the US$300,000 investor visa. Our explainer on the 15 October date, which falls today, sets out the real-estate threshold and what the 2024 decree said. Check the current rules with Panama’s immigration service or a licensed lawyer before you commit money.

Brazil: foreigners and the runoff. Most foreign residents cannot vote. A Datafolha poll released on 8 October (2,520 interviews, 6 to 8 October, margin of error 2 points) put Flávio Bolsonaro at 49% and Lula at 45% in the runoff, a gap at the edge of the poll’s margin of error, and polls are snapshots. Our runoff guide covers the practical side.

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

05 The Calendar Ahead

Thu 15 Oct Hurricane Simón near the coast of Sinaloa, according to Mexico’s weather service. Forecasts may change.

Thu 15 Oct September inflation in the Dominican Republic and Ecuador; Peru’s August economic growth (the RT calendar forecast is 3.4% over 12 months, against 3.56% before) and September unemployment rate (forecast 5.0%, against 4.8% before).

Thu 15 Oct Brazil’s August retail sales, a gauge of how households are spending as prices change.

Fri 16 Oct Brazil’s IBC-Br index for August (a monthly gauge of economic activity), with a forecast of 0.3% against -0.2% before, from the RT calendar.

Thu 22 Oct Mexico’s mid-October inflation (the RT calendar forecast is 0.3% for the fortnight and 3.5% over 12 months).

Fri 23 Oct Brazil’s October mid-month inflation (IPCA-15), with a forecast of 4.6% over 12 months against 4.47% before, from the RT calendar.

Sun 25 Oct Brazil’s presidential runoff, with voting from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time.

Tue 27 Oct Chile’s central bank decides its interest rate (4.5% before), according to the RT calendar.

Sat 31 Oct Colombia’s deadline to transfer older permanent-resident visas.

Tue 3 – Wed 4 Nov Brazil’s central bank sets its Selic rate (Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, now 13.75%).

Dates come from official calendars and the RT economic calendar; forecasts are not ours. The region does not move as one block, and each release can push a currency either way.

Frequently Asked Questions

Mexico’s weather service kept a hurricane watch for the Sinaloa coast from Escuinapa to Bahía Tempehuaya, and some forecasts pointed to a landfall near Mazatlán on Thursday 15 October 2026. Spanish-language reports differed on the storm’s category and track, and one said it was almost stationary at sea, so check the latest official bulletin. When do Panama’s schools reopen after the earthquake? Panama’s education ministry said public schools would begin a gradual reopening on Wednesday 14 October 2026, after safety inspections. It counts 619 damaged schools, 35 of them destroyed, after the magnitude 7.7 quake of Friday 9 October. Which buildings open first is not yet known. What is Colombia’s deadline for older permanent-resident visas? Foreigners holding a permanent-resident visa issued under earlier rules must transfer it before 31 October 2026, according to Colombia’s Foreign Ministry. Today’s Focus Precious metals fell hard on Wednesday 14 October after US inflation came in hotter than forecast. Gold dropped below US$4,100 and silver plunged about 6%, Kitco reported. The GLD gold fund lost 1.49% and the SLV silver fund 6.11%. Gold miners fell more, with the GDX fund down 4.40%. Higher US yields and a stronger dollar make metals that pay no interest less attractive. What matters today. Silver’s fall was four times gold’s, which matters to US holders of silver funds and to Mexico and Peru, two of the world’s main silver producers.

01 The session in one read

Gold fell below US$4,100 and silver plunged about 6%. The SLV fund’s fall of 6.11% to US$50.22 is the biggest one-day loss in the group.

Gold had closed near US$4,155 on Tuesday in our RT data, so the fall is at least 1.3%.

Assessment — A rate shock, not a supply story MEDIUM The fall came after a hot inflation print and rising yields, and silver amplified gold’s move. Miners fell more than the metals. The variable to watch is whether markets keep pricing Fed rate rises, because that decides the direction for gold.

The US consumer price index rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over twelve months, above the 3.6% forecast, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Core prices rose 2.6%, above the 2.5% forecast.

Kitco said the report lifted Treasury yields, strengthened the dollar and raised expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening. The dollar index rose 0.34% to about 102.5.

Mexico is the world’s largest silver producer and Peru is among the top three. Both countries’ mining shares fell, with Buenaventura down 3.11% and Pan American Silver down 4.94%.

Metals will follow US yields and the dollar. US retail sales on Thursday 15 October at 12:30 UTC are the next test.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves 2,700 Corals Deeper to Escape El Niño Heat
World.content:
Scientists in Costa Rica have moved 2,700 corals into deeper water in the Gulf of Nicoya to shield them from ocean heat driven by El Niño. Warming Pacific waters are raising the risk of bleaching on the reefs. The corals belong to the restoration project run by the State Distance University (UNED) at Isla Tortuga, off the southern tip of the Nicoya Peninsula. Researchers relocated them from about 5 meters (16 feet) down to 13 meters (43 feet), where the water stays cooler than near the surface.

UNED researcher Yeison Lizano Rojas, who leads the Isla Tortuga project, said El Niño is already putting Costa Rica’s corals under heat stress. The university warned that if high temperatures persist, that stress can lead to bleaching and, eventually, to the death of the corals. Bleaching happens when heat breaks down the partnership between corals and the microscopic algae that live in their tissue. Those algae, known as zooxanthellae, supply most of the coral’s food and energy.

Under prolonged stress, the coral expels them, loses its color and weakens. A bleached coral is not necessarily a dead one. According to UNED, some corals recover once water temperatures return to normal, which is why the team is trying to buy them time in deeper, cooler water. The team has also paused the routine work of the nursery.

Coral gardening, fragmentation and the installation of new structures are on hold, while monitoring of bleaching, water temperature, salinity and other conditions has been stepped up. Lizano said extreme heat is one of the main challenges facing marine conservation. He stressed that restoration and scientific monitoring are what allow reefs to become more resilient.

The threat reaches well beyond Costa Rica. In June, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration warned that El Niño could trigger a fifth global coral bleaching event, with the eastern Pacific at greatest risk. NOAA said El Niño could raise Pacific sea surface temperatures by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit), and put the chance of mass bleaching in the region between June and September at 60% to 90%.

The two most recent global bleaching events, in 2023 and 2025, affected 84% of the world’s reef area, according to NOAA. The Isla Tortuga project began in mid-2024 as a partnership between UNED’s Puntarenas campus, the National Learning Institute (INA) and tour operator Bay Island Cruises, which provides boats and logistics.

By June 2025, the team had planted its 2,000th coral and installed 43 nursery structures, and UNED reported that the cultivated corals were growing up to four times faster than corals in the wild.The relocation comes in a week of contrasting news for Costa Rica’s reefs. Days earlier, researchers raised coral larvae in Costa Rica for the first time. On land, El Niño has also been linked to the rainfall deficit that has left Guanacaste drying out this year.

Healthy reefs feed and shelter fish, protect coastlines and support the diving, snorkeling and fishing that coastal communities around the Gulf of Nicoya rely on. UNED warned that losing them would ripple through the marine species that depend on reefs for food, shelter and reproduction, and through the fishing and tourism built around them.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens Prison Modeled on El Salvador’s CECOT
World.content:
President Laura Fernández is scheduled to inaugurate Costa Rica’s new maximum-security prison at 12:30 p.m. Wednesday, but the facility will not receive inmates today. Justice and Peace Minister Gabriel Aguilar has said the first transfers to the Centro de Alta Contención y Crimen Organizado (CACCO), will take place at the end of this month.

The prison sits inside the La Reforma penitentiary complex in San Rafael de Alajuela, about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) from San José. According to the Justice Ministry, it can hold about 5,100 inmates in five housing modules, with 31,048 square meters (about 334,000 square feet) of construction on a 90,846-square-meter (22.4-acre) property.

Costa Rica built the facility from plans donated by El Salvador, and its design draws on its Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo, or CECOT, the mega-prison at the heart of President Nayib Bukele’s crackdown on gangs. CECOT was designed for about 40,000 people, roughly eight times Costa Rica’s new maximum-security prison.

Fernández has presented CACCO as the centerpiece of her government’s strategy against organized crime. In announcing the ceremony, she said her administration’s mission was to return peace to law-abiding people and that it would not rest until it did so.

The president said invitations went to Ombudsman Angie Cruickshank, Supreme Court magistrates, OIJ Director Michael Soto and Attorney General Carlo Díaz. She also invited Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose attendance had not been confirmed as of this morning.

The Justice Ministry has said one of the five units holds 1,020 people in cells built for 60 inmates each, fitted with triple bunks. The modules have their own guard posts, controlled access points, internal walkways, bathrooms, showers and separate sun yards.

Inmates will wear orange uniforms and will not be allowed to receive clothing from outside. Aguilar has said the garments, which have no pockets, elastic or drawstrings and are sewn with security stitching, are meant to make searches easier, prevent the concealment of phones, drugs or weapons, and help identify inmates in any escape attempt.

Women held at the Vilma Curling Rivera prison, better known here as Buen Pastor, sewed the uniforms with technical support from the National Learning Institute (INA), according to the ministry.

Daily life inside will be overseen by the General Regulation of the High-Containment Circuit, which started in August 2025. The ministry has said high containment adds restrictions designed to stop people tied to criminal organizations from coordinating activity from behind bars.

According to a constitutional challenge filed against the decree, the regulation limits inmates to one 10-minute phone call a week, bars access to radio and television and restricts intimate visits to once every two months. The regulation also prohibits visits by minors. Inmates may see their children only by video call, with narrow exceptions that require a social-work assessment and a specific authorization from the circuit’s management.

The government says CACCO will hold inmates it considers especially dangerous, including people linked to organized crime, drug trafficking and contract killings. Aguilar has said inmates already held under the high-containment regime at existing prisons will be the first to move. Officials have given different figures for the first phase.

In July, Aguilar said the first 2,500 inmates would be transferred once the building had been received and inspected. The government has since given a preliminary estimate of about 2,100 inmates for the first stage. Placement is supposed to follow technical criteria. The Ombudsman’s Office has pointed to Circular 1-2026 of the National Institute of Criminology, which sets the criteria for assigning inmates to high-containment spaces, and has said such placements cannot depend on the will or impulse of a political authority.

That question became a flashpoint two weeks ago, after the ministry published a video of Aguilar inspecting the 26 de Julio prison in Puntarenas. In it, he told several inmates they would be sent first to high containment and then to CACCO. The Ombudsman’s Office condemned the minister’s conduct and said the unilateral transfer orders violated the principle of legality and due process.

The Attorney General’s Office has since opened an investigation into Aguilar for alleged abuse of authority related to an inmate’s transfer to CACCO. Aguilar has not been charged and in an Oct. 10 statement, he denied that inmates were assaulted or mistreated during a separate operation at La Reforma.

Whether CACCO’s restrictions comply with Costa Rican law has not been decided. The Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV) admitted an unconstitutionality action against several articles of the decree in 2025. That challenge was filed by a Mexican inmate convicted of drug trafficking, who argues that the limits on visits, calls and education violate the Constitution and international human rights treaties.

The regulation stays in force while the court weighs the case, because admitting a challenge does not suspend the rule being challenged. Separately, judges have asked the chamber to rule on whether several of the decree’s articles are constitutional.

On Oct. 1, University of Costa Rica professor Ricardo Zeledón Zeledón filed an amparo, a petition asking the Constitutional Chamber to protect fundamental rights from a specific government action. His petition asks the court to stop the inauguration and any transfers and to order the building demolished. It also questions the project’s financing and the international cooperation behind it.

Court spokesman Alejandro Lizano outlined the request yesterday, when the case remained at the admissibility stage. The filing does not by itself suspend today’s ceremony. The National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture, which operates within the Ombudsman’s Office, went further on Oct. 1. After the Puntarenas video, it said CACCO should not begin operating because minimum guarantees and standards were not being met.

The Justice Ministry estimated the project’s total investment at $34.5 million when lawmakers approved its financing in 2025. The procurement record on the government’s SICOP purchasing system puts the cost at more than $33 million. The Legislative Assembly approved the first 40% of the funding in a midyear budget in September 2025, by a vote of 41 to 0. The government covered the remaining 60%, about $23 million, in the 2026 national budget.

Construction began in January during a visit by Bukele to Costa Rica. Then-President Rodrigo Chaves, now minister of the Presidency and Finance, promised the prison would be finished in 195 days, a deadline that passed on July 27. The ministry reported the work 95% complete on Sept. 21.

CACCO is the first new prison since CAI Terrazas opened in 2021, and it will be its largest. The opening is already affecting the rest of the system. The Justice Ministry suspended special visits, volunteer groups and attorney visits today at the prisons of the Western Complex in Alajuela and is rescheduling intimate visits and parcel deliveries planned for the day. The ministry asked inmates, their families and partner organizations for understanding.

The inauguration comes as Costa Rica’s prison population sits at a record high and as the government argues that criminal organizations must be cut off from running operations from inside existing prisons. How CACCO’s rules are applied to each person sent there, and how the Constitutional Chamber rules on them, will decide whether the country’s largest prison becomes a security model or its next major legal battle.

World.title: Snoop Dogg’s Costa Rica Promoter Says He Once Turned Down a Suitcase of Cash
World.content:
Update, Oct. 13, 7 p.m.: The December 3 concert has been canceled, and Stockwell’s lawyer says prosecutors will now seek pretrial detention for all 19 suspects. This article has been updated.

The promoter behind Snoop Dogg’s now-canceled December 3 concert in Costa Rica told prosecutors he once turned down an investment because the would-be investor arrived carrying a suitcase full of cash, as he looks to clear his name in a money-laundering investigation. Don Stockwell is one of the suspects in the investigation known as the Éxodo case, which authorities say centers on alleged money laundering and drug trafficking. He has not been convicted of any crime and denies wrongdoing.

In a formal statement to the Public Prosecutor’s Office following his arrest on October 7, Stockwell denied ever receiving money from drug traffickers or criminals, according to local reports published Tuesday. He told prosecutors that many years ago he rejected an investment offer from Elías AKL because AKL showed up with a suitcase of cash, more money than Stockwell said he had ever seen in one place. AKL was shot dead by hitmen in May 2017 outside a private school in Guachipelín de Escazú.

Stockwell also said he never suspected that money invested by Edwin Vargas García, known as “Sobrino,” came from criminal activity. He told prosecutors that cash payments are common in the entertainment business and that some investors prefer to remain anonymous, so neither raised red flags for him.

Investigators with the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) are examining whether a group allegedly led by Vargas used money apparently tied to drug trafficking to invest in live events. Michael Soto, a senior OIJ official, has said investigators link Stockwell and fellow promoter Hugo Barboza to three concerts that allegedly received funding from the organization, with about $859,000 tied to those events.

Vargas has been held at La Reforma prison in Alajuela since January 2025. An OIJ report filed in the case alleges he continued to direct an informal high-interest lending network, known locally as “gota a gota,” from behind bars in a prison system already holding a record number of inmates.

Authorities carried out 22 raids and arrested 18 people on October 7 in several communities in and around San José. Stockwell was released early the next morning. The Specialized Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime had said it would seek precautionary measures other than pretrial detention against him, citing his ties to the community and its assessment of procedural risks. On Tuesday evening, however, his lawyer, Daniel Brenes, said prosecutors would request pretrial detention for all 19 suspects in the case, although the request had not yet been formally filed. The hearing to set precautionary measures, which began Monday, was still underway and could last several more days, Brenes said.

Stockwell has publicly called the case a misunderstanding stemming from dealings with people he did not know well. He has said his conscience is clear and that he is ready to clear his name. The production company had said only days earlier that Snoop Dogg’s December 3 show at the Pedregal event center would go ahead. On Tuesday afternoon, it announced the concert had been canceled by mutual agreement with the artist and said ticket refunds would be processed automatically.

None of the suspects in the case has been convicted, and the investigation remains open.

World.title: Woman Sought After 74-Year-Old American Found Dead in Playas del Coco
World.content:
Costa Rican police are asking the public for help identifying a woman they are seeking in the death of a 74-year-old American man inside a condominium in Playas del Coco, one of Guanacaste’s busiest beach towns. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) has identified the victim only by his surname, Fleming. He was found dead with head injuries that investigators believe were caused by blunt objects.

According to the OIJ’s Liberia regional office, Fleming entered the condominium in Sardinal de Carrillo with a woman at about 4:50 p.m. on September 27. The woman left alone sometime later, and his body was found in the home hours afterward. The OIJ made its appeal public on Monday, more than two weeks after the death, and released security camera footage showing the woman.

Investigators describe her as light-skinned and slim, with black hair, and about 1.60 meters (5 feet 3 inches) tall. On the day of the incident, she was wearing sandals, blue denim shorts and a white bra-style top with chain-like details on the front. Street security cameras show a vehicle parking nearby and the woman getting out of the front passenger seat, according to information released by authorities. Investigators believe she later traveled toward San José, where they suspect she lives.

Preliminary information from the OIJ indicates investigators are examining whether the man’s credit cards were taken and used as a possible motive. Neighbors reportedly heard screams coming from the home. Local reports from the areas describe Fleming as a retired businessman who had lived in Playas del Coco for some time. Authorities have not released his full name.

No arrests have been reported. The woman is considered a suspect, but she has not been identified or charged. Anyone with information about the case can contact the OIJ confidentially at 800-8000-645.

World.title: Belize City man fined $200 for crack pipe but ends up with 3 years in jail over unpaid $10,000 drug trafficking fine
World.content:
Belize City man fined $200 for crack pipe but ends up with 3 years in jail over unpaid $10,000 drug trafficking fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man arrested with a crack pipe has found himself serving a three-year prison sentence after two unpaid fines from previous drug convictions caught up with him, including one dating back nearly a decade.

Erin Dillon Yacab, 28, a construction worker of West Street, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 on Tuesday, October 13, charged with possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug.

Police say Yacab was found with a metal pipe on Tigris Street on Sunday, October 11. He pleaded guilty and was fined $200 plus $5 court costs, payable immediately, or face one month in prison.

However, a review of his court records revealed two outstanding fines from previous drug convictions. The first, dating back to 2016, was a $10,005 fine for possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply, carrying a default sentence of three years. A second unpaid fine of $1,505 from 2018 carried an eight-month default sentence.

With the fines remaining unpaid, the Senior Magistrate ordered Yacab to serve three years in prison, with the shorter default sentences not adding to the three-year term.

Yacab was escorted to the Belize Central Prison on October 13, nearly ten years after the conviction responsible for his lengthy prison sentence.

World.title: Ruben Flores free after almost a year in prison unable to post bail on assault charge
World.content:
Ruben Flores free after almost a year in prison unable to post bail on assault charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who spent almost a year behind bars because he could not post bail has finally regained his freedom after the complainant in his common assault case failed to appear in court.

Ruben Flores was brought from the Belize Central Prison to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 14, where his trial was scheduled to begin before a Magistrate in Court #5.

However, the prosecution informed the court that the male complainant could not be located despite attempts by a process server to serve him with the necessary court documents.

With the complainant unavailable to testify, the prosecution was unable to proceed, prompting the Magistrate to dismiss the charge for want of prosecution.

Flores had been charged in connection with an alleged common assault dating back to October 2025. Although he had been granted bail, he remained incarcerated for almost a year because he was unable to meet the bail requirements.

The Magistrate informed Flores that his case had been dismissed and, with no other matters pending against him, he was free to leave.

The dismissal brings an end to nearly a year of incarceration for Flores without a conviction in the case.

World.title: Seasoned thief escapes jail time after stealing two cases of empties worth $22
World.content:
Seasoned thief escapes jail time after stealing two cases of empties worth $22

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Ladyville man with a lengthy history of theft convictions has avoided another prison sentence after pleading guilty to stealing two crates of empty bottles valued at just $22.

Eckert Anthony Fitzgibbon, 53, of Partridge Street, Ladyville, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Belize City on Tuesday, October 13, where he admitted stealing the bottles belonging to a woman.

The theft occurred on October 7, 2026, and involved one crate of empty Belikin bottles and another containing empty Guinness bottles, each valued at $11.

Despite his extensive criminal record, Fitzgibbon was fined $500 plus $5 court costs, payable by December 14, 2026, or face three months in prison.

The court heard that Fitzgibbon had numerous previous theft convictions dating back to 2007. The Senior Magistrate considered the age of his previous convictions in deciding to impose a fine rather than an immediate custodial sentence.

Fitzgibbon is no stranger to the courts. In November 2024, he was sentenced to one year in prison after pleading guilty to stealing $250 from a woman’s purse at a Ladyville gas station. That conviction was described at the time as his eighth for theft.

This latest case adds another conviction to his criminal record, although the exact total was inconsistently reported in the latest court account.

World.title: ‘Happy F*****g Birthday’: Four young men charged following birthday brawl in La Democracia
World.content:
‘Happy F*****g Birthday’: Four young men charged following birthday brawl in La Democracia

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A birthday celebration in La Democracia Village ended in violence, leaving a villager injured, a two-year-old boy reportedly struck by a bottle, and four young men facing criminal charges.

Michael Brandon, Malike Coote, Corey Jones, and a 16-year-old minor appeared before a Magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, October 14, charged with wounding and disorderly conduct following a fight near Angie’s Store on Saturday, October 10.

Police say 25-year-old fisherman Tyrone Gillett was attacked by several young men who allegedly punched him repeatedly and struck him in the head with a pint bottle. Gillett was transported to the Western Regional Hospital, where his injuries were classified as wounding.

During their arraignment, Coote and Jones pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, while Brandon and the minor pleaded not guilty.

Jones also attempted to plead guilty to wounding but told the court that Gillett had threatened him with a pint bottle and that he took the bottle away before striking him. He further claimed that the confrontation followed earlier threats and that his two-year-old brother had been struck by a bottle thrown during the altercation.

The Magistrate rejected Jones’ guilty plea after determining that his explanation raised a possible defence, and entered a plea of not guilty on his behalf.

Coote admitted punching Gillett but denied striking him with a bottle.

Coote and Jones were each fined $100 plus $5 court costs for disorderly conduct, payable by November 30, 2026, or face one week in prison.

The wounding charges remain pending against all four defendants, while Brandon and the minor must also answer to the disorderly conduct charge. The minor was additionally taken to the Belize City Family Court to face a separate aggravated assault charge.

All four are scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on December 9, 2026.

World.title: Two Belize City teenagers remanded to prison on firearm and ammunition charges
World.content:
Two Belize City teenagers remanded to prison on firearm and ammunition charges

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two 19-year-old Belize City men have been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after police linked them to an unlicensed 9mm handgun and 12 live rounds of ammunition.

Elijah Willoughby and Aaron Smith were jointly charged with keeping a firearm without a gun licence and keeping ammunition without a gun licence following a police discovery on Saturday, October 10, 2026.

According to court reports, police recovered a black Jericho 9mm pistol bearing a serial number, along with 12 live rounds of ammunition.

The two appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in Court #2 at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, October 13, where they both pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Due to the nature of the offences under the Firearms Act, both teenagers were remanded to the Belize Central Prison until their next court appearance on December 14, 2026.

World.title: International News: Pacific breaks record for powerful, long-lasting hurricanes
World.content:
International News: Pacific breaks record for powerful, long-lasting hurricanes

By Zoila Palma: The eastern and central Pacific has broken a record for accumulated cyclone energy, as powerful hurricanes continue to develop and last longer than usual.

Scientists say a strong El Niño, warmer ocean temperatures and favorable atmospheric conditions are contributing to the unusually active hurricane season.

Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach said the activity has intensified since Hurricane Odalys formed on September 20.

The region surpassed its previous accumulated cyclone energy record, set in 2018, on Sunday, while Hurricane Simon continued affecting the area off Mexico’s western coast. Klotzbach said the Pacific was also approaching a record for the number of days with a hurricane spinning.

Scientists attribute much of the activity to El Niño, which weakens wind shear in the Pacific, allowing storms to strengthen and survive longer. Ocean temperatures are also several degrees Fahrenheit above normal in parts of the Pacific, providing additional energy for storm development. Atmospheric scientist Kim Wood said both the eastern and central Pacific have been unusually active simultaneously this year.

The last five Pacific hurricanes—Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel and Simon—have all reached major hurricane status, with winds of at least 111 miles per hour.

Meanwhile, the Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet, with accumulated cyclone energy below 18 percent of normal for this time of year.

World.title: Soil Doctors train 20 farmers in practical soil management in Hopkins
World.content:
Soil Doctors train 20 farmers in practical soil management in Hopkins

By Zoila Palma: Certified Soil Doctors Sedella and Augustine of the Stann Creek District conducted their first farmer-to-farmer training at the Hopkins Cooperative, reaching 20 farmers as part of the rollout of the National Soil Doctor Training Programme.

The programme is implemented by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) under the Global Soil Partnership, in collaboration with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and Enterprise (MAFSE).

Building on their Training of Trainers at Central Farm, the Soil Doctors used hands-on demonstrations and Soil Doctor kits to teach farmers practical soil diagnostic techniques.

The training covered soil texture, pH and organic matter, along with sustainable soil management and climate-smart agricultural practices.

World.title: Ben apologizes following weekend incident; expresses gratitude to family and friends for encouragement
World.content:
Ben apologizes following weekend incident; expresses gratitude to family and friends for encouragement

By Zoila Palma: Social media influencer Benjamin Garcia has issued a statement following the incident that occurred over the weekend.

Garcia says that this incident has given him time “to reflect, not only on the events themselves, but also on the people who matter most to me, the responsibilities I carry, and the importance of the trust others have placed in me.

I recognize the seriousness of any incident involving a firearm and understand the concern and public discussion that the circumstances have generated.”

Ben says that beyond the headlines, he is a son, a family man, a friend, a colleague, and someone who has dedicated all of his life to building something meaningful through hard work and perseverance.

“Like anyone else, I have people who love me, believe in me, and depend on me. Knowing the worry and disappointment that the past few days have brought to some of those closest to me has weighed heavily on my heart.

To my family, friends, colleagues and clients, I sincerely regret the concern, uncertainty, and disappointment that this situation has caused,” he said.

Ben added that he has worked hard to build meaningful relationships, create opportunities, contribute to his community, and earn the confidence of those around him.

He further reassured his clients of his commitment to honoring his obligations, delivering the quality of work they expect, and maintaining the professional relationships they have built together.

Ben thanked everyone who reached out and offered words of encouragement and said that this incident served as a reminder of what really matters, his faith and family.

“I cannot change the attention or circumstances of the past few days, but I can determine how I carry myself moving forward.

With faith in God, humility in my heart, and a renewed appreciation for the people and responsibilities in my life, I intend to move forward with dignity and purpose,” he expressed.

World.title: Diddy rushed to hospital after prison fight with Dudus — report
World.content:
American rapper P Diddy and Jamaican drug lord Christopher 'Dudus' Coke a

American music mogul Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs was reportedly rushed to hospital on Wednesday after allegedly getting into a physical altercation with convicted Jamaican drug lord Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke.

According to a TMZ report, the confrontation reportedly erupted after Combs allegedly caused trouble that resulted in disciplinary action against fellow inmates.

During the alleged scuffle, Combs reportedly sustained a head injury and was subsequently transported to an outside medical facility for treatment.

Combs was sentenced last year to just over four years in federal prison after being convicted on prostitution-related charges involving two of his former girlfriends.

World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: ‘A wish list’
World.content:
Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes responding to an announcement in Parliament on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has described as a “wish list” an announcement by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals which will nearly double the bed capacity of the facilities they are replacing.

The facilities to be constructed are a new 250-bed Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, a 250-bed Falmouth General Hospital in Trelawny, a 150-bed Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover, and a 720-bed Kingston Public Hospital Campus at Orange Street, downtown Kingston.

“I must tell the honourable minister, that is indeed a very well put-together wish list,” Dawes said sarcastically as he rose to respond to Tufton’s 20-minute-long statement in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in which the minister told his fellow parliamentarians of the plans to construct the new facilities.

“We can rarely call it anything more than such because the weight of Cabinet approval is not a budget item,” Dawes added.

Tufton told the House that Cabinet had approved a partnership between his ministry and the National Reconstruction and Resilient Authority (NaRRA) for the works to be carried out.

It is being done in collaboration with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB).

Dawes, the Member of Parliament (MP) for St Catherine South Eastern, told the Parliament that all Jamaicans want better, safer, and more resilient hospitals.

“The challenge we have consistently had is that whenever this Government is tasked with delivering, we don’t know the cost, we don’t know the completion time, and we don’t know who is going to staff it.

And we have seen that happen over and over again, Dawes said.

He reminded the legislature that in the early 1990s under an IDB-funded project to improve hospitals, there was a special implementation unit in the Ministry of Health.

“This project to rehabilitate and construct major hospitals is going to be lumped with the Montego Bay Hip Strip development, the Vernamfield development, and any other NaRRA project that they deem fit,” he said.

The first-term MP pointed to the continued rising costs associated with the Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopment project and argued that patients in western Jamaica continue to suffer.

“In fact, patients all across Jamaica are suffering [and] the staff, they’re protesting almost weekly at this point.

And every time there is a protest or concern on social media we’re treated to tours of hospitals to come,” he said.

“This cannot be the status quo; we cannot continue to suffer while we hear about what is to come.

This Government has had 10 years to deliver and now they are delivering promises to come,” Dawes argued.

He said that the Opposition accepts that money must be spent on the hospitals that are being rebuilt, but said, “We would like to know how much money is going to be spent on the abandoned Black River Hospital, how much money are we sinking into these buildings that the minister has, quite honestly, said are unfit for inhabitation and occupation.” Dawes also argued that a hospital is not just a building and a bed, not [just] something to lie on.

“A hospital is service.

A bed without a nurse is a mattress,” he declared.

He lamented that there was nothing in Tufton’s presentation about a staffing plan and pointed out that by the health ministry’s own numbers Jamaica was experiencing an attrition rate of 500 nurses each year.

Dawes said the 47 nurses who arrived from Ghana recently are a welcome addition but that is a mere drop in the bucket.

In his statement, Tufton repeated that the climate-resilient facilities will be reconstructed and modernised by NaRRA.

He did not give a cost or timeline for construction.

“Together these projects will deliver some 1,370 beds inside modern, climate-resilient hospitals.

The three rural hospitals alone will raise beds from 260 today, to 650 beds, more than doubling the facility,” said the minister.

World.title: Jamaica Music Atlas active!
World.content:
Johnathon Kelly

Eager to share his enthusiasm for reggae music, Johnathon Kelly launched the Jamaica Music Atlas in August.

The website (jamaicamusicatlas.com) looks at the history of Jamaican music in 12 countries, among them the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada — home to some of the largest Jamaican Diaspora communities.

An information technology expert, Kelly used AI to gather data for the portal which he regularly updates.

It comprises almost 4,000 songs, 280 locations, and over 150 stories. “The response so far has been extremely encouraging.

What has been particularly rewarding is seeing interest come from well beyond Jamaica. Some of our strongest engagement and feedback has come from the United States and Europe, which really reinforces the fact that Jamaican music has a truly global audience,” Kelly told the Jamaica Observer.

“We have heard from music fans, members of the Jamaican Diaspora, researchers, and people who simply want to understand more about the history, culture, and stories behind the music.” Visitors to the website can discover reggae’s roots in each country featured.

For example, the first venues that played Jamaican music in the UK, the record labels, sound systems, artistes and producers who put reggae on the map there. There is similar comprehensive data for The Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Spain, Panama, Japan, Brazil, Cote d’Ivoire, and Nigeria.

“A major part of the vision is to make Jamaican music history accessible to different kinds of audiences.

Some visitors may want to do deep research, while others may want to explore a story, follow a musical journey or play a game,” Kelly explained. “The site is gradually becoming a much broader digital experience around Jamaican music rather than simply a collection of information.” In the two months since jamaicamusicatlas.com was activated Kelly has consistently added stories and features.

“We never intended Jamaica Music Atlas to be a static archive, so we have been steadily adding new ways for people to explore and interact with the material,” he said.

World.title: KSAMC urges water party restraint
World.content:
Patrons at a recent water party (File Photo)

THE Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) has urged water party organisers to carefully consider the timeliness and appropriateness of staging such events, as drought conditions persist and water restrictions threaten to become more stringent.

Speaking at the KSAMC’s monthly meeting on Tuesday, Deputy Mayor Lorraine Dobson, in the absence of Mayor Swaby, acknowledged the concerns of residents surrounding the issuance of licences for water parties.

She appealed to promoters to consider the plight of residents across the Corporate Area who are experiencing water shortages and have been urged to conserve, arguing that seeing water used for recreational purposes could cause frustration and distress.

“I therefore wish to make a direct appeal to the promoters of these events to act responsibly and with sensitivity to the circumstances confronting our residents.

I ask that they carefully consider the timing and manner in which these events are staged and ensure that their activities do not undermine the national call for water being experienced by members of our community,” said Dobson.

Water restrictions have been instituted by the National Water Commission (NWC) across Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine to protect depleted reservoirs amid an ongoing severe drought.

As of October 11, 2026, the Mona reservoir is at 36.3 per cent capacity, while Hermitage dam stands at 44.9 per cent capacity, leaving both critical facilities severely depleted despite recent rainfall.

Under the legal mandate, residents are strictly banned from using NWC-supplied water for any non-essential or unusual activities.

Prohibited actions include watering lawns, gardens, and farms; refilling swimming pools or ponds; washing vehicles with a hose; and washing down outdoor surfaces like roadways, pavements, or garages.

With no signs of the drought ceasing soon, Water Minister Matthew Samuda recently suggested that stricter regulations could be implemented.

Against that backdrop, Dobson explained that the KSAMC issues permits only to event planners who can provide evidence of a private water source.

However, she said the corporation recognises residents’ frustration and takes the responsible use of the increasingly scarce resource seriously.

“As an authority responsible for granting of permits for events within the municipality, we recognise the importance of exercising our regulatory responsibilities, responsibly in keeping with the national purpose to conserve water.

The KSAMC should not knowingly facilitate and even involve in the use of water supplied by the National Water Commission for recreational purposes in circumstances where such is prohibited,” she said.

“We have also taken note that the minister’s clarification that the current water prohibition order applies specifically to water supplied by the NWC and that promoters of water-based events are required to provide evidence of their water source where privately sourced water is being used,” added Dobson.

World.title: Central Kingston MP highlights big drop in murders
World.content:
Kingston Central Member of Parliament Donovan Williams making his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in Parliament on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

What was for a long time one of Jamaica’s most politically volatile constituencies, Kingston Central, which saw up to 50 murders per year, has recorded just four homicides since the start of 2026, Member of Parliament (MP) Donovan Williams has shared.

Williams, a second-term Jamaica Labour Party Government MP, spoke to the issue in the House of Representatives on Tuesday during his contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Constituency Debate.

“Major crimes are down, gang conflicts have plummeted, our murder rate is the lowest it has been when compared to previous years,” said Williams.

He pointed to the introduction of a zone of special operations (ZOSO) in the Parade Gardens community, noting that it has had an immediate impact.

“There was a time in Central Kingston when we were experiencing 50 murders per year across both police divisions that serve the constituency.

So far this year we recorded four murders across the entire constituency,” Williams said.

Highlighting that some communities were doing exceptionally well, he singled out Franklyn Town which, for the past two years, has had no murders.

He said that one murder has been recorded in the Allman Town community, one in Parade Gardens, and two in Rose Gardens.

The Rae Town community recorded a single murder in 2025 and none in 2026.

Williams’ report was specific to the constituency as Jamaica Constabulary Force data show that the Central Kingston Police Division, which expands beyond the riding, has reported eight murders so far this year, compared to 15 over the same period last year.

Williams told the Parliament that other major crimes have also plummeted.

“We still have some issues, we are working through them, but for the most part, we are doing exceptionally well,” he noted.

Our churches are open; our parties are in full swing.

Nightlife has returned to Central Kingston.

Our children are playing in the parks and in the streets and we intend to keep it that way,” he added.

“This is not the Central Kingston that we are accustomed to, this is not the Central Kingston I came and saw in September 2020,” Williams gushed.

He acknowledged the leadership of National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang, Commanding Officer Mishka Forbes of the Kingston Central Police Division, Commanding Officer Michelle Campbell of the East Kingston Police Division, and their predecessors who, he said, helped to lay the foundation of peace which now exists.

Williams also acknowledged the civic organisations that are playing their part in community engagement and peace initiatives such as Yard Empire, Social Development Commission, Project Star, Heavenly Culture, World Peace, Restoration of Light (HWPL), a UNESCOaffiliated non-governmental organisation, as well as the churches.

On the matter of the ZOSO, the two-term MP said the Jamaica Social Investment Fund has advised that an integrated infrastructural development plan has now been crafted for the zone and submitted to the Ministry of Finance for approval by the Public Investment Appraisal Branch (PIAB).

Williams said he was optimistic that the PIAB will approve the plan, especially given that the joint command has recommended the zone enters its build phase.

World.title: CHEQUES STILL COUNT
World.content:
THE Small Business Association of Jamaica (SBAJ) is calling for an extension of the timeline to phase out paper cheques as it warned that the pace of the transition could place additional pressure on micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) that still rely on the payment instrument for day-to-day business transactions.

Speaking in an interview with the Jamaica Observer this week, SBAJ President Garnett Reid said members across the association’s network of more than 700 businesses have raised concerns about the planned elimination of cheques — arguing that they need more time to adjust and access affordable alternatives before the payment method is completely withdrawn.

“Since the announcement of the phasing out, a number of our members have continued to ask us what will happen to those who use cheques. Right now, more than 20-30 per cent of them use cheques to settle transactions,” Reid told the Business Observer.

“We are not against the move to modernise Jamaica’s financial system, but the current schedule is too aggressive, particularly for a large number of small operators who lack the resources, digital infrastructure, and training needed to transition smoothly. What we are therefore calling for is an extension of the time frame by even a year,” he said, while noting that the extension would give businesses more time to adapt while the banking sector and other stakeholders strengthen the systems needed to support digital transactions.

Under the schedule established by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) and the Jamaica Bankers Association (JBA), the phased reduction in cheque clearing began on September 1, 2026, with cheques valued at $1 million or more no longer being accepted or processed. The threshold is scheduled to fall to $500,000 on March 1, 2027 and then $100,000 by September 1, 2027, before a complete elimination of cheques takes effect on March 1, 2028.

The BOJ, which has noted the phase-out as part of efforts to reduce systemic risks, said it will also encourage the settlement of high-value transactions through electronic channels, including the Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and Automated Clearing House (ACH) infrastructure.

Cheque usage locally, which has continued to decline steadily over the last two decades, saw volumes processed in 2025 falling 12.6 per cent to 2.4 million, as total value also declined 6.9 per cent to $444 billion. This compares with more than 8.4 million cheques valued at approximately $2.3 trillion processed in 2010.

Despite the decline, Reid said cheques remain important to some small businesses and as such, the transition must account for those that continue to depend on the instrument.

“Forcing micro-merchants into alternative routes like RTGS drives up ad valorem fees and transactional overheads that strip away the razor-thin profit margins of small businesses. We cannot strip a trusted financial instrument from the economy when the digital infrastructure remains broken,” he said.

SBAJ’s call comes amid recent legal challenges to the phaseout, which has seen at least two church groups stepping out recently to seek judicial review of the decision. The groups, in accusing the central bank of exceeding its legal authority, also said the planned phasing breaches the right of Jamaicans to equitable treatment. They have also similarly indicated that their members frequently use cheques to conduct business, pay bills, and settle debts.

The SBAJ said its concerns were further compounded by what has been a slow roll-out of the central bank digital currency JAM-DEX, which was introduced to support a more efficient and accessible payment system.

Reid said the pace of adoption, which has left some small businesses without practical alternatives to the payment methods they currently use, has also widened the digital divide between the push for financial modernisation and the readiness of merchants on the ground.

“We are in a digital era and SMEs are told every day to grow their digital footprint and increase digital acceptance… but I don’t think we’re all ready yet,” he said, pointing to the need for more training and support for business owners unfamiliar with digital payment platforms and online banking.

Highlighting gaps in the digital payment infrastructure, including limited access to compatible point-of-sale systems and digital wallets, the association further said these pose significant challenges for businesses seeking to make and receive digital payments across their supply chains. It stressed that merchants must be able to collect payments from customers, pay suppliers and purchase inventory using accessible and affordable options and in cases where digital currency is not widely accepted businesses will have to rely on alternative electronic transfers that usually attract higher transaction costs.

“We are modernising the top tier of the economy while leaving our grass roots businesses stranded. Right now, point-of-sale (POS) integration for JAM-DEX is incomplete and there are far too few active wallet providers in the market. Expecting a micro-merchant in rural Jamaica to instantly shift away from paper cheques to high-fee commercial options when they cannot even spend or accept JAM-DEX at local wholesalers is fundamentally unrealistic,” Reid said.

As part of the response, he urged the BOJ, commercial banks, and other stakeholders to work together to strengthen digital payment infrastructure, expand merchants’ access to digital wallets, and provide practical training to help business operators understand and use available payment options.

“Small businesses represent the backbone of the Jamaican economy. Modernisation should lift us up, not lock us out. We stand ready to collaborate with the central bank, but we will not sit quietly while our members are forced out of the financial system by an unforgiving timeline,” Reid said while stressing that the transition cannot be treated simply as a change in banking policy, but as a broader shift that must take account of the financial and technological realities facing small businesses.

World.title: BUTLER CRIES SHAME!
World.content:
Mona High Head Coach Craig Butler reacts during the rescheduled ISSA Walker Cup semifinal match against Jamaica College at Stadium East on October 10, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WHILE expressing happiness that Mona High will be playing in the ISSA Walker Cup final, Head Coach Craig Butler has called for serious intervention in Jamaica College’s football programme which he believes is being undermined by a “must-win” mentality.

Butler’s team was granted a place in the urban area knockout final against Kingston College after the competition’s governing body, ISSA, removed Jamaica College (JC) from the tournament after using Reggae Boy Jamone Lyle who was found to be a professional player.

ISSA’s rules state professional athletes are barred from participating in ISSA-run competitions.

Lyle played in last Saturday’s semi-final in which JC beat Mona 4-3 on penalties after a 3-3 draw in regulation and extra time.

After Mona lodged an official complaint, ISSA investigated and it was confirmed that the 17-yearold signed a professional contract in August with Jamaica Premier League club Waterhouse.

ISSA’s disciplinary committee met and ruled JC’s semi-final win null and void which meant Mona will play in Friday’s final.

JC issued a statement early Tuesday afternoon, saying it “had no knowledge of Lyle having entered into a professional contract” while also seeking clarity on the application of ISSA’s rules.

The school, however, stressed that it “remains committed to working respectfully with ISSA and other stakeholders” to uphold the integrity of schoolboy football and support the development of Jamaica’s young sporting talent.

However, Butler who played Manning Cup for JC during his high school days, told the Jamaica Observer that he’s concerned about the direction that the school has been heading in and is urging past students to step in and provide guidance.

“I’m disappointed in the way that I see my school, JC, that I love and how they have allowed the boys to just basically do whatever they want and it has to change at some point and I hope that this is a wake-up call,” he said.

“I hope that the past students, Kit and Kirk Kennedy, Chris Williams — all of the past students that came from our era will go back into the school again and start to contribute in terms of mentorship and make sure the boys know what life is about.

Because guess what? This little football thing that we’re playing, it’s going to go and after that, what happens? Where are these boys being left? What are they being left with? Are they being left with some education? Are they being left with social education? Are they being left with integrity?” Butler, though, says he has nothing personal against Lyle but believes rules must be followed.

“I think that’s a disservice to the player because he’s young and malleable and he’s going to listen.

I don’t, in any shape or form, blame the kid.

I really like him as well.

After the game was over, I hugged him and told him, great game,” he said.

“But to know that the player is ineligible and still use him is something that for me questions Jamaica College’s ethos.

When I went to JC, there was a lot of ethics and a lot of honour in how they did things.

We didn’t need to win at all costs.

We wanted to give good contributors to society and to use football as a vehicle to teach boys how to be men and to lead.

I think this winning at all costs mentality has to stop and I think that JC needed this wake-up call.” Butler says more of his compatriots need to be vocal about JC’s situation before it gets worse.

“Unfortunately, I’m a brave man so I go and ask the questions.

I’m not going to be like my friends that sit down and say ‘yeah, Bullhead, you’re right’ but when the time comes, they keep quiet,” he said.

“I’m not going to keep quiet because guess what? That could have been me when I was a kid.

When Jimmy Sinclair and all of my mentors back then who coached at the school told me the right way to carry myself and behave.

Of course, there have been many times that I have not listened and many times that I have got myself in trouble but I at least knew what was the right thing to do.

I was able to come back to the nuclei of that.

So, I love Jamaica College and because I love Jamaica College, I want them to wake up and who don’t like it, I don’t give a damn.”
