World.title: UK polling watchdog faces reckoning after Farage sting
World.content:
The polls had in fact been paid for by two undercover reporters posing as a wealthy American benefactor and his son. The pair had offered their support to Reform via Farage’s advisers Dan Jukes and James Orr.

At the time, the BPC said in a statement it was “clear there have been breaches” of the body’s rules and that it would seek further information from JL Partners. The BPC’s own rulebook states that polling companies must disclose who has commissioned their research and that those who fail to do so can be kicked out.

Three people familiar with internal BPC discussions — granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter — said members had since urged the industry body to dismiss JL Partners, arguing the pollster, which declined to comment for this piece, had committed a cut-and-dried violation of the rules.

However, the firm has not been expelled more than a month later — prompting concern among some members that the BPC is ill-equipped to deal with any serious misconduct.

One of the people cited above, from a rival pollster to JL Partners, said: “If the BPC isn’t able to kick someone out who’s so brazenly ignoring the spirit of the rules, it does beg the question: what’s the point of it?”

Crisis meeting

Jane Green, the president of the organization, laid bare the scale of the challenge facing the industry body at the behind-closed-doors meeting last week, according to a transcript reviewed by POLITICO.

World.title: Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
World.content:
The suspension comes as the EU seeks to step up deportations from the bloc — a leading pillar of EU migration policy, and the object of new legislation adopted earlier this month — and weeks before the European Commission is expected to propose expanding the mandate of the border agency, including its role in returns and reintegration.

Frontex cannot resume the program without additional cash. The agency asked the Commission for more funds, but is waiting for clarity on the EU budget for 2027, and the next seven-year budget starting in 2028, the emails said.

“There is no point in talking about a more ambitious European return policy without also talking about the resources needed to deliver it,” Frontex spokesperson Chris Borowski told POLITICO. “Ambition and funding have to go hand in hand.”

Borowski confirmed that the agency had suspended new cases, but stressed that individuals already been accepted into the program wouldn’t be affected and that Frontex would also continue to offer EU countries “other forms of assistance” on returns, such as operational and technical support.

“Returns do not end when a plane lands. Helping people rebuild their lives after returning to their home countries is an important part of making migration management work. It takes planning, people and money,” he said.

With 2,368 new cases per month on average, the agency took on significantly more migrants seeking reintegration support than it expected. Cases in September were 63% higher than Frontex’s target, according to Leijtens’ email to staff. In the first half of this year, the agency took on around 75% more cases than it did in the same period last year.

World.title: How Russia plans to revive its ties with Slovakia
World.content:
The IGC, which covers economic, scientific and technical cooperation, has been dormant since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last meeting was the commission’s 21st session, held in Bratislava on Nov. 12, 2021.

The meeting comes as Moscow finds openings in other international arenas. The U.S. has invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, while the International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and urged sports bodies to ease restrictions on Russian athletes.

Asked about the purported agenda for the IGC, the Slovak foreign ministry directed POLITICO to Blanár’s public statements after the Aug. 20 call. “We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár said at the time.

The Russian foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The renewed push for warmer Slovak-Russian relations follows Fico’s May 9 visit to Moscow, where he met Russia's President Vladimir Putin during Victory Day commemorations. It comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election, which cost Putin one of his closest partners in Europe and forced him to look elsewhere for EU allies.

Months before losing the election to Péter Magyar, Orbán rebooted the Russian-Hungarian Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which had been suspended for several years after the 2022 invasion. Magyar's government did not confirm to POLITICO whether the commission would go ahead next year.

World.title: How Putin’s favorite sport reopened the door to international contests
World.content:
“It’s clear that, considering how Vizer promoted the Russians and kept saying they were ‘good for us,’ [he has] definitely interests and connections in Russia. Russia’s ideas are everywhere,” the Ukrainian Judo Federation’s head coach Vitalii Dubrova said in an interview.

The International Judo Federation did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment on Vizer’s ties to Russia. The IJF also did not make Vizer available to reply to requests for comment.

While the IJF offered solidarity funding for Ukrainian judo in 2022 and instituted background checks on Russian and Belarusian athletes in 2023, in November 2025 it became the first major sports organization to fully reinstate Russian athletes — allowing them to compete under their national flag for the first time since the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022.

It was part of Moscow’s use of sports as a route back onto the global stage, from comebacks in major tournaments to broader Olympic rehabilitation — and a potential return at the 2028 Games, tacitly backed by Kirsty Coventry, president of the International Olympic Committee.

That has triggered alarm in Brussels, where top EU foreign policy officials are currently circulating ideas — from sanctioning athletes to cutting EU funds for sports federations that welcome Russia back — in a bid to slam the door on Russian reintegration, according to a European External Action Service document, dated Sept. 16 and seen by POLITICO.

While the Kremlin’s aggression against Ukraine continues unabated, Russia has nonetheless managed to retain influence at the top of international sports federations, including in chess, fencing and boxing. Moscow has found platforms to advance its soft-power agenda that have rankled Kyiv and European officials, who described how sport has “increasingly become a tool of political instrumentalisation by Russia and Belarus,” in the EEAS memo.

World.title: Why Ukrainian strikes on data centers are a real problem for Russia — and beyond
World.content:
The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy.

The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill.

Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia.

“To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov.

Joseph Jarnacki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences.

“These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO.

World.title: Macron and Merz hold keys to an EU budget deal — but may be too weak to use them
World.content:
Sealing agreement on the EU's long-term central budget, worth approximately €2 trillion, is the biggest challenge over the next few months facing leaders, all of whom must sign up to the final numbers. While it isn't just up to Macron and Merz, getting the chiefs of the bloc's two most powerful countries to overcome their differences would be a massive step in making all the pieces of the jigsaw slot into place.

But with Macron soon to leave office and Merz under severe pressure domestically, officials and diplomats in Brussels, Paris, and Berlin are playing down hopes of a Franco-German breakthrough this week.

"If the French and German leaders come hand in hand, I think that could change the game," an EU diplomat, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said. "You need [Italian Prime Minister Giorgia] Meloni and [Polish Prime Minister Donald] Tusk, but it starts with Merz and Macron."



While Merz and Macron may talk bilaterally during the summit, according to an Elysée official, there were no firm plans for a more formal sit-down, two EU diplomats said, adding they were expecting them to use the two-day meeting to hash out positions.

Domestic political weakness makes both leaders less likely to yield ground, three EU diplomats said.

Backfiring

For the French president, who leaves office next year, the fear is that making big concessions — like accepting cuts demanded by Berlin — could be weaponized by presidential candidates vying to replace him.

“Macron should not appear too conciliatory” in budget talks, said an ally of the French president. “It would backfire in the presidential campaign.”

World.title: New four-lane bridge between China and North Korea opens after a decade of delay
World.content:
A new four-lane road bridge linking China and North Korea finally opened on Thursday, 12 years late, enabling the Asian giant and its isolated nuclear-armed neighbour to substantially step up cross-border trade.

 

China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a vital diplomatic and political backer, although relations have not always been smooth with the ruling Kim dynasty.

Hundreds of people gathered on Thursday in the northern Chinese border town of Dandong, taking selfies in front of the 3,026-metre New Yalu River vehicle bridge before it opened.

Trucks bearing the nations' flags began moving in both directions late in the morning, with some of the North Korean vehicles decorated with flowers.

"It's great," one woman who came to watch told the AFP news agency in the town dotted with Chinese as well as Korean shops and restaurants, where residents were relieved the bridge had finally open.

"It's already been over 10 years. It's certainly going to be good for business," she said, without wishing to be named, accompanied by her friend and her dog.

Chinese flags are flown during the opening ceremony of the new China-North Korea Yalu River Bridge, 15 October, 2026 AP Photo

"I hope the standard of living in North Korea can rise to the level we have here," Dandong local Yu Shuyan, who before the pandemic had visited North Korea, said.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that the bridge symbolised Beijing's friendship with Pyongyang and that relations were "entering a new stage and opening a new chapter".

"Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, the successful opening of the bridge will not only strongly boost economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, but will also further facilitate people-to-people exchanges and tighten the bonds of affection between the two peoples," Li said by video link at the opening ceremony, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.

The structure was completed in 2014 but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported.

North Korea also sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic and train journeys between the East Asian neighbours only restarted in March after a six-year halt.

A TV screen shows an image of Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at a bus terminal in Seoul, 9 June, 2026 AP Photo

The new bridge is not the only border crossing between the two countries.

But the new structure will supersede the "extremely narrow" rail-and-road Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge downstream on the Yalu River, said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University.

"Previously, transporting heavy cargo such as industrial machinery, raw materials, construction materials and energy-related supplies required extreme caution because of safety concerns surrounding the ageing bridge," Lim told AFP.

"The new crossing will make such shipments much easier and more efficient," he said, calling it a "groundbreaking development" that will substantially increase cargo traffic.

Russia-North Korea bridge

The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.

Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.

China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in recent years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.

But Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.

A truck from Russia arrives in North Korea after crossing the first road bridge across their shared border, 7 September, 2026 AP Photo

China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China.

North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.

South Korea's unification ministry said that Seoul is "closely monitoring" the situation regarding the new bridge.

World.title: ‘They’re not dead yet’: Bleached corals recover in record time after touching healthy clones
World.content:
Dying corals may have found an unexpected lifeline: their neighbours.

 

Scientists at Stanford University have discovered a way to bring corals back from the brink of death by placing them in contact with healthy corals for just a few days.

Published in Science Advances, the study presents a promising new approach to restoring coral reefs as rising sea temperatures cause more frequent and severe coral bleaching events.

When water becomes too hot, corals expel the microscopic algae that provide much of their energy, an event known as bleaching, which leaves them vulnerable to starvation.

After bleaching events, it can take months or years for surviving corals to recover – but the scientists contend hope is not lost for them.

“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” says lead author Danny Collins, a PhD student at Stanford. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”

How scientists brought bleached corals back to full strength

The discovery happened by accident in 2025, when Steve Palumbi, a professor of oceans and marine biologist at Stanford’s Doerr School of Sustainability, noticed two pieces of coral that had fallen against each other in a laboratory tank. One was healthy while the other was bleached. But where the two touched, the bleached coral was beginning to regain its colour.

Collins then arranged 10 pairs of coral fragments, each containing a healthy and bleached piece from the same colony. Five pairs were placed in contact with one another, and the others were kept a few millimetres apart.

Within seven weeks, all five bleached fragments put in contact with their healthy clones had recovered. The ones that were kept apart had died.

Under a microscope, the scientists discovered the corals had fused together, creating tiny channels that allowed algae and nutrients to pass from one to the other. Within three days, beneficial algae had begun moving from the healthy corals into the bleached ones. After about a week, some had received enough algae to recover on their own.

In less than two months, bleached coral came back to life in a Stanford lab Danny Collins

Once inside the damaged corals, the beneficial algae began multiplying rapidly. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals,” says Palumbi.

During the second week, the algae doubled in number every four days – about 10 times faster than in wild corals – allowing the damaged corals to continue recovering even after they were separated from the healthy ones.

The finding marked a breakthrough in the lab. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a Stanford professor and one of Collins’ faculty advisors.

But the scientists say the technique isn’t ready for wide-scale application in the oceans.

The corals must be genetically identical for their tissues to fuse. In other words, every damaged coral would need a healthy copy of itself – an impractical solution for restoring whole reefs. But the researchers hope to find ways to deliver the beneficial algae without requiring direct contact or identical twins.

Coral reefs may be running out of recovery time

The revelation comes at a crucial time for coral reefs.

According to the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network’s latest assessment, the world's reefs have lost nearly 10 per cent of their living coral over the past four decades. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, it fell almost 9 per cent during a global bleaching event – the largest single-year decline ever recorded.

Global bleaching now occurs roughly every five to six years, leaving reefs less time to recover between bouts of extreme heat. The report warns that reefs will continue declining unless man-made emissions fall and threats such as overfishing, water pollution and coastal developments are curbed.

And while combining coral to help them recover from bleaching might save some of them, Palumbi stresses that it can’t protect them from rising sea temperatures.

“This is a recovery story. It doesn’t blunt heatwaves; it just helps the aftermath. There is still a huge need to reduce heatwaves and protect all of Earth’s life from rapid climate stress,” he says.

“Eventually, it can hopefully help the huge effort being put into restoration succeed better by helping those coral gardens survive heatwaves more completely.”

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 15th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Embryo gene editing is getting more precise, but how safe and ethical is the practice? | Euronews Tech Talks
World.content:
In the summer of 2026, two studies revived the debate on embryo gene editing, a technique that consists of manipulating the DNA of a human embryo for reasons ranging from better understanding human development to preventing children from developing certain diseases.

 

One study was led by Kathy Niakan at Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, and the other by Dieter Egli at Columbia University in the United States.

Both researchers employed base editing, a technique developed in 2016 to alter genetic material with greater precision than earlier methods. Both conducted their research on human embryos instead of mice, and both delivered results which caught the attention of many around the world.

Embryo gene editing is not yet a medical reality. Scientifically, modifying the genes of a human embryo is extremely challenging. In addition, no country allows the modification of cells that can be passed on to offspring.

With these studies, is society closer to the possibility of safely creating gene-edited babies? What are the ethical concerns surrounding this practice?

The studies

Using base editing, the Cambridge study targeted NANOG, a specific gene which was found to be essential for the formation of future bodies from an embryo.

“Base editing represents a significant advance on conventional CRISPR-Cas9 because it carries a far lower risk of causing unintended chromosome errors,” Kathy Niakan said in a press release.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Columbia’s research group tried base editing in three genes: one linked to high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease, and the other two related to haemoglobin production.

“By introducing such damage using editors, we are starting to understand how human embryos handle damage in their genomes. Long term, we hope to learn how to prevent genetic and developmental abnormalities during IVF to create more efficient, safer, and more affordable fertility treatments,” said Dieter Egli in a press release.

According to Robin Lovell-Badge, principal group leader and head of the laboratory of stem cell biology and developmental genetics at the Francis Crick Institute in London, the two studies are on the right path, but there’s room for improvement.

“The methods look much safer. But there's still work to do,” he told Euronews Next. “It looks like the levels of mosaicism are low, but not zero. So there's going to have to be more work done there,” he added.

Mosaicism is one of the main obstacles of gene editing. It happens when base-editor molecules fail to find and modify certain cells. This phenomenon could potentially cause the development of certain diseases.

The ethical debate

Although research on embryo gene editing might be advancing, several ethical questions remain unanswered.

“A question that very often pops up in regard to that is the tension between therapy versus enhancement,” Pascal Borry, professor of bioethics at the University of Leuven, in Belgium, told Euronews Next. “Where do we put the line? What is therapeutic? What is an improvement?” he added.

Borry also highlighted other ethical puzzles, ranging from the issue of consent to the problem of stigmatising a community already living with a certain disease.

In addition, he underlined that embryo gene editing might not be necessary: “There are many other alternatives to this technology, and I think it’s important to reflect upon that. And I’m thinking about the pre-implantation genetic testing,” he said.

Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is a medical test that takes place during in vitro fertilisation treatment to detect any abnormalities in the embryos.

Björn Heindryckx, professor at Ghent University in Belgium and principal investigator coordinating research in the infertility department, agrees with Borry on the non-necessity of using embryo gene editing to prevent certain genetic conditions.

Yet, he argues that this technique could still have benefits: “If we understand, and with this tool we can really test it much better, if we can get more insight into embryo development, it will give us more insight into certain forms of infertility.”

Badge, on the other hand, is less worried about the ethical implications of this technique. “I don't have a problem with doing it if it's safe and there's a good ethical reason for doing it. I think it's unethical to allow people to have children that have a genetic disorder if you can avoid it,” he explained.

According to Badge, countries should regulate the practice; however, they should not adopt a restrictive ban. “Let's say you want to fly to Mars. You're going to be in space for a long time; you're going to have an environment with very high levels of radiation. So you may want to be modified to deal with high levels of radiation,” he told Euronews Next.

Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

World.title: ‘Plot twist trips’: Why going off-script is the ‘ultimate travel flex’, according to Booking.com
World.content:
Fellow travellers, it’s time to forget about that all-too-comfortable beach break and plan to do something that’s, let’s say, not on your usual holiday agenda.

 

That’s the thinking behind the “plot twist trip”, one of nine trends identified in Booking.com’s travel predictions for 2027, which suggest holidaymakers are interested in “going off-script”.

Based on research from more than 28,000 travellers worldwide, the report’s findings show that people are rethinking where they are going, who they are travelling with, and how they experience the world.

Next year, travellers will “humble everyone who thought they had them figured out” and surprise themselves in the process with “a trip nobody saw coming”, said the online travel platform. And according to the data, 77% are interested in choosing a holiday specifically to do something "completely out of character”.

Booking.com said the reaction from others will be “part of the appeal”, with 36% actively wanting to surprise their friends and family with their holiday choices. “These trips are designed to disrupt the status quo, rewrite the story everyone thought they knew, and deliver the twist nobody predicted.”

In fact, nearly a third of respondents (29%) have deleted or avoided posting about a holiday “because it felt too predictable or ordinary”.

So, will 2027 finally be the year that they have something worth sharing on their socials? As Booking.com puts it: “The best souvenir? The look on everyone else’s face.”

From all-exclusives to a hotel in the sky

Beyond the plot twist trips, Booking.com’s predictions suggest that travellers want holidays tailored to their lifestyles and budgets.

Its “all-exclusive” trend sees 66% of respondents wanting packages that let them remove services they won’t use. "Moving forward, the most appealing travel package isn't the one that includes everything."

Meanwhile, “vibe check(in)” finds 81% of travellers would choose a destination primarily based on how they want to feel, rather than where they want to go.

Under “social currency”, money could shape the holiday guest list. Half of travellers have reconsidered who to invite on a trip because of spending differences and 38% have removed people from a travel group entirely. The kids may not make the cut either as 61% of parents are keen to travel child-free so they can spend more on themselves.

Venturing into the supernatural, 65% are interested in paranormal experiences and a “trip to the beyond”. Nearly half (48%) would seek an experience with the hope of speaking to someone on the “other side”.

While back in the working world, the “PTO: powered by AI” trend finds that 64% are interested in having AI cover their work while they’re away.

“Hotel in the sky” reflects demand for wellness in the air, with 89% of respondents saying they would take a long-haul journey if it guaranteed they would arrive rested and refreshed.

For “sweat synergy”, 66% of respondents who have travelled alone say a shared physical activity or challenge has led to a lasting connection or friendship.

Under “trailside therapy”, the new romantic getaway may be more about tough talks with your partner, rather than candlelit dinners. The data found that 47% would consider a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments, with walking and hiking among the activities that help couples tackle difficult conversations.

Bratislava in Slovakia Martin Katler/Unsplash

Top trending destinations for 2027

Alongside its predictions report, Booking.com has revealed 10 trending destinations for 2027, including three in Europe: Reims in France, Bratislava in Slovakia, and Pescara in Italy.

World.title: Deepening tech sell-off drags stocks lower as major markets slide
World.content:
Asian shares fell sharply ahead of European markets opening on Thursday morning with indexes in South Korea and Japan sinking, as a sell-off of technology shares deepened after US stocks fell on hotter-than-expected inflation data.

 

Meanwhile, US equity futures were lower.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 7.7% to 5,548.78. It was well below the 9,000 mark that it crossed in June at its all-time high driven by optimism over the global artificial intelligence frenzy.

Samsung Electronics slid 9.5% and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 11.4%.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.8% to 64,489.06. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 9.4%. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dropped 7.3%, and memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings lost 11.2%.

Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI boom, fell 3%. Its leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, dropped 2.2% ahead of its earnings report.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1% to 24,071.25. The Shanghai Composite index slipped 1.4% to 3,713.22.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.1% to 8,715.60.

Declines follow Wall Street losses

The declines followed losses on Wall Street on Wednesday. The S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.1%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite slipped 1.9% as AI-related stocks fell.

Nvidia lost 3.2%, Broadcom gave up 3.1%, and Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, declined 5.7%.

The US reported on Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, up from 3.4% in August and worse than what economists had expected.

World.title: Musk suggests US government behind slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system
World.content:
SpaceX boss Elon Musk said that any disruptions Ukraine reports in its use of the Starshield satellite communications system would be the responsibility of the US government, and not his company.

 

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk stressed, referring to US President Donald Trump.

Musk underlined the distinction between the Starshield system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but is not allowed to employ for offensive operations. Both systems were designed by Musk's SpaceX.

Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," but that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defence."

Fedorov then thanked Musk for his "continued support."

Ukrainian defence officials have suggested that Washington is behind the slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country's military strike Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.

Ukraine has also accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it about incoming missile strikes, with Kyiv hit by ballistic missiles for two nights in a row before air raid sirens could sound to warn people to take cover.

Meanwhile, Russia accused Ukraine on Wednesday of attacking two oil refineries in breach of the "energy ceasefire", a claim Kyiv dismissed as "fake", saying that other sites had been hit "but the refineries were not".

The row came as Kyiv dealt with the aftermath of an overnight Russian attack that killed at least one person and injured more than 20 others. A large fire broke out in a residential building after it came under Russian shelling. The strikes targeted the Darnytska CHP-4 plant, which supplies the capital with heating and electricity, according to Zelenskyy.

Russia said it had shot down 900 Ukrainian drones overnight, including 180 near Moscow.

Trump's election move?

Opposition Democrats in the US Senate and House condemned the Trump Administration over the reported interrupted connections.

Trump, facing key midterm elections next month, in which fuel prices are a major issue, has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the squeeze on supplies and the rise in prices at the pump.

A senior official in Kyiv confirmed that the United States had in recent days threatened to stop providing intelligence about Russian missile launches, which Ukraine uses to thwart attacks.

Trump denied doing so on Tuesday.

Meloni: Diesel deal is legitimisation for Moscow

In Rome on Wednesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said “It is a very risky choice” and “a legitimisation for Moscow while its bombs are still falling on Ukrainian cities”, referring to the US-Russia deal on the purchase of Russian diesel that was agreed last Friday.

Speaking in Parliament before heading to Brussels for Thursday and Friday’s European Council, Meloni warned of an “implicit weakening of the sanctions lever”, which she said runs counter to what has so far been done, including by the United States, “to push Putin to sit down at the negotiating table”.

World.title: AI in healthcare: from fighting epidemics to family doctors
World.content:
Since May, teams on the ground in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have been fighting the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. Every day, so-called health workers knock on doors and offer advice. They record recoveries and deaths and refer people with suspicious symptoms to medical facilities.

 

The knowledge of these health workers, whose notebooks reflect the condition of entire communities, has been digitised, according to a report by the AI company Anthropic.

Who has fallen ill? Who did the person have contact with, and where were they staying before they knew they were infected? To evaluate the answers and reports, Anthropic's Claude model was used. Among those involved in the study were CEPI, the WHO Regional Office for Africa and the national biomedical research institute INRB.

AI helps to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly

"A situation report is now produced within an hour instead of taking an entire working day," explains Dr Marie Roseline Darnycka Belizaire, Director for Emergency Preparedness and Response at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa. Artificial intelligence can help to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly and to target medical assistance more precisely, the WHO deputy director said on stage at the World Health Summits.

While analysing the data, potential outbreak hotspots were identified and preparations made, such as getting stocks of medical supplies to key hubs or high-risk areas.

That can be decisive in an emergency. The earlier health authorities respond to a potential outbreak, the better they can prepare and organise care. AI is intended to help process information from different sources more quickly and support decision-making by those in charge.

This positive example of how artificial intelligence can be used in healthcare illustrates a level at which AI can be deployed with relatively little risk. Experts, however, see far more possibilities for the future use of artificial intelligence.

The technology could improve diagnoses, relieve medical staff of administrative tasks and help to deploy scarce resources more strategically. At the same time, it raises fundamental questions: how reliable are the results? Can medical professionals understand how an AI arrives at a decision? And do patients really benefit?

AI as a support for overstretched healthcare staff

Demand for healthcare is growing worldwide. At the same time, many places lack staff, time and equipment. For Dr Thomas Zapata, Director of the WHO Academy in Lyon, this is a key starting point for the use of artificial intelligence.

"We have to think about a paradox we are currently facing. We have more health professionals worldwide than ever before, and we have unprecedented technologies at our disposal," Zapata said in a panel discussion at the World Health Summit. Yet, he added, there is still an enormous shortage of healthcare workers. "Demand for health services keeps on rising."

He sees AI as a way to narrow that gap. It is crucial, however, not to see it as an end in itself, but as a tool to be integrated into existing health systems.

"AI is an enabler, a means to an end. At the moment we are very fascinated by technology and AI, but I think we need to place it in the right context within the health system," warns Zapata. In his view, artificial intelligence fits in two areas. On the one hand, AI could change the way care is organised; on the other, training and continuing education for health workers must adapt to the new possibilities.

Ultimately, AI can of course help to reduce workloads, streamline administrative tasks, improve clinical decision-making and enhance diagnostic processes. For him, it is particularly important that the technology frees up time for what cannot and should not easily be automated: caring for patients.

Above all, the Ebola crisis in the Democratic Republic of Congo has shown that trust in local health systems is lacking.

That gives doctors more time for their patients

Automated processes can make a particular difference where healthcare staff work under intense time pressure. Dr Cecilia Mbaca, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE, knows these challenges from more than 15 years on the front line.

For her, three questions are crucial: can AI support clinical decision-making? Can it take over repetitive tasks? And does it help to tailor care more closely to the individual needs of patients?

"If AI does this work very well, that leaves more time for the personal aspects of care, so that we can ask questions, listen, examine patients and refer them on to the next level of care," explains Dr Cecilliah Mbaka, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE as well.

She herself spent more than 15 years working on the front line, with little support, limited resources and a heavy workload.

In epidemics in particular, it is not just about medical data. Trust within the population also plays an important role. People must be able to trust that they will be protected and properly cared for in a health facility. In affected communities, this trust can be decisive in whether people seek medical help in time.

It is estimated that around 50 percent of deaths in villages in the DRC occur outside medical facilities, according to epidemiologist Maximilian Gertler. The local health system is under pressure and was not prepared for the Ebola outbreak. Thousands of protective suits are needed every day to shield nursing staff from contamination. Germany recently increased its aid by 21 million euros.

AI can therefore support the organisation of care. On its own, however, it cannot ensure that people trust medical facilities. As AI experts themselves criticise, the path leading to a diagnosis is still often opaque.

The transparency problem: how does AI arrive at its diagnosis?

Modern AI systems can analyse large volumes of data and detect patterns that humans might miss. Yet in many cases it remains unclear exactly how they reach their results.

Dr Thomas Thesen, Professor of Medical Education and Informatics at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth University in the United States, describes the problem like this: "They are extremely good at recognising patterns, but they are really bad at explaining to us what those patterns actually are." Chatbots and large language models such as Claude or ChatGPT have what he calls an explanation problem. In this respect, artificial intelligence remains a black box.

This so-called black-box problem is particularly relevant in the healthcare sector. When a system provides a diagnosis or treatment recommendation, medical professionals need to be able to judge whether it makes sense in the specific case. A result on its own is not always enough; the path leading to it also has to be traceable.

"That is the problem of explainability. They cannot explain in human-understandable language how they arrive at these conditions."

This black-box issue concerns not only transparency but also responsibility: who is liable if an AI provides a wrong recommendation? That is why, for Dr Mbaka, it is crucial that AI does not simply spit out results, but genuinely supports decision-making.

Expert: AI must not replace learning in training

Artificial intelligence can also help in training medical professionals, for instance by making information more accessible or assisting with repetitive tasks. But when it comes to learning itself, Thesen, the professor of medical education and informatics, also sees risks.

He points to a study that compared searching for information via conventional search engines with using an AI chatbot. The students who used the chatbot ended up with more superficial knowledge that was less firmly anchored.

"These so-called desirable difficulties are actually very important for the learning process. And if you outsource all the cognitive work of learning to a chatbot – which may be highly efficient – you do not actually learn anything."

Anyone who needs to retain knowledge in the long term should not, in his view, let an AI take over every mental step. Especially in medicine, it can be crucial to make the right decisions even when technological support is not available.

Thesen therefore also recommends using AI primarily where it reduces workload. Where the aim is to understand knowledge and retain it in the long term, independent learning must continue to have its place.

World.title: India news: Supreme Court likely to hear Rahul Gandhi's Election Commision plea
World.content:
10/15/2026 October 15, 2026 Rahul Gandhi's key petition on mass voter deletions listed in Supreme Court today

The Supreme Court is slated to hear a petition filed by India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition lawmakers over a sweeping exercise which has so far purged over 130 million names from the country's electoral rolls.

A list of cases to be taken up on Thursday by a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kanta shows the petition named "Rahul Gandhi and others versus Election Commission of India and others."

The plea was filed on Monday at the end of a protest march to the Supreme Court that saw Congress' Gandhi rallying thousands, including members of the opposition INDIA bloc, student leaders, activists and civil society, through a heavily barricaded part of the capital.

The protest was the latest in a series of demonstrations calling for India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The poll body, whose neutrality has come under scrutiny, rejects the allegations and says the exercise, called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Modi's party has also dismissed the accusations and deems the protests as attempts to "create anarchy."

Meanwhile, neither Modi nor Kumar have publicly addressed the issue.

Gandhi's petition seeks an interim suspension of the nationwide revision of voter rolls, along with an audit of voter deletions and safeguards against deletions without prior notice.

World.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping
World.content:
New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.

India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies.

New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday, killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike.

The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships.

The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can diplomacy deliver safety?

Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels.

"Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW.

India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received.

Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts.

Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement.

"India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW.

How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Working with other powers to reach a deal

He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa.

"A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar.

India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear.

Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns.

"The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW.

"India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement.”

Will India face a higher import bill?

Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes.

"Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said.

The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs.

"A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Brazil to shorten workweek in win for Lula ahead of runoff
World.content:
Brazil's Senate approved cutting the workweek from 44 to 40 hours. The move could give President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva an edge over his opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 25 runoff.

Brazil's Senate on Thursday approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the working week to five days from six without a salary cut, likely providing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with an edge ahead of Flavio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff on October 25.

Lula is expected to sign the shorter workweek into law next week.

Brazil's leftist leader has taken a number of steps in recent days to shore up support before the runoff, including new fuel tax cuts, extending existing subsidies and pledging to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses to the federal government and others.

But the pledge to trim the workweek turned into a top promise that Lula hoped to deliver on before the runoff.

Brazil election: Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"6x1" reform receives overwhelming support

The new amendment, known as the "6x1" reform, could benefit more than 37 million workers, according to the government.

"The end of the 6x1 is more than a change in the workday. It's more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow, take care of yourself, and enjoy life," Lula wrote on X.

"Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve time to live. It's a victory for workers. It's Brazil ready for more," he said.

But the legislation still leaves out a large number of people in the shadow economy, like freelancers and delivery drivers.

Lula, a former trade unionist, worked on the proposal to reduce the workweek with his government over the course of the year.

Bolsonaro backs "6x1" reform after opposing it

Flavio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator and the eldest son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, had long opposed the legislation. But Flavio Bolsonaro reversed course on Tuesday to say that he'll back the bill because it has so much support.

Many businesses opposed the bill because it would raise their costs, and Bolsonaro previously argued for estabilishing a flexible payment regime where individuals negotiate their pay with their employers.

He repeatedly called the legislation election-motivated.

In the first round of elections earlier this month, Bolsonaro dealt Lula a bruising defeat, finishing ahead with 47% of the vote, though short of the 50% needed for an outright majority.

The campaign in Brazil has been dominated by voter frustration over high street crime, the strength of Evangelical churches, the high tax burden for businesses and economic dissatisfaction.

World.title: North Korea says it tested cruise missiles to be launched from sub
World.content:
North Korean state media said the military test-fired cruise missiles designed to be launched from submarines. Pyongyang has ramped up weapons launches in recent weeks.

North Korea said Wednesday it test-fired cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines to test the readiness of the country's underwater combat systems and strengthen the Navy's capabilities.

North Korea's state media said it carried out the tests in waters off the east coast of the Korean peninsula.

A North Korean state media report described the weapons as strategic, implying an intent to arm them with nuclear warheads.

But the report did not specify whether they were launched from an actual submarine or an underwater test platform.

North Korea has pushed ahead with modern missile submarines and both ballistic and cruise missile developments.

People in South Korea watching the news about North Korea having fired ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on October 12 Image: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS

Pyongyang has tested various weapons in recent weeks to sharpen its military deterrence against the United States and South Korea, but it is not ​yet believed to ‌have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation.

What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What to know about North Korea's relations with South Korea and the US

The latest development comes two days after the North Korean state media released photos of the North Korean leader, Kim Jong Un, visiting a new military museum in an undisclosed location in the country.

The museum displayed an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of reaching the US, photos released by KNCA state media showed.

Kim has made clear that boosting his country's nuclear arsenal was his key priority. Denuclearization, as the US has pushed for, is off the table in this case.

Relations between the North Korean leader and US President Donald Trump also appear to have quieted since the two haven't met in recent years.

US President Donald Trump, during his first term, met Kim three times. Earlier in the week, Trump, alluding to a trip to Asia next month, said he might meet Kim on the trip.

North Korea has put a halt to all coordination with South Korea and has removed all references to reunification with the South from its constitution.

World.title: Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access
World.content:
Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated. President Zelenskyy has asked Elon Musk to "switch" it back on.

Ukraine confirmed on Wednesday that its military has been cut off from full access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite system , which reportedly interrupted some missions overnight.

"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said Presidential Adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov.

"Our defense forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added.

"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.

Ukraine presses allies on intelligence sharing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Starlink cut-off coincides with Trump's 'energy ceasefire'

That political situation refers to US President Donald Trump's recent decision to lift sanctions on buying Russian oil.

Trump has also criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy— saying he needs to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure and that he should be replaced because "he won't make a deal" with Russia.

Oil and gas prices have skyrocketed this year due to the US and Israel's war on Iran.

Russia has meanwhile continued to target Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure as winter approaches.

Trump over the weekend insisted, without providing evidence, that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire." But Moscow and Kyiv have both denied this.

On Tuesday evening, Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv power plant. Ukrainian officials said the Starlink outages had coincided with overnight Russian attacks.

Ukraine: Russian strikes continue as ceasefire questions remain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy in UK asks Musk to turn Starlink back on

During a visit to the UK on Wednesday, Zelenskyy called on Starlink owner Elon Musk to fully restore the system.

"So they switched off. It's their decision," Zelenskyy said in an interview with UK journalist Piers Morgan.

"I hope that it's a mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to do it, to switch (it) on."

In a post on X, Musk later said that any "limits on speed or usage" are ultimately decided by the US military and the president.

Musk's post was in response to an earlier post from Ukraine's former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," while thanking Musk. This has not been immediately confirmed by standing Ukrainian military officials.

SpaceX move slowed down Ukrainian drones

Ukrainian troops use Starlink to conduct drone operations and internet terminals supplied by Elon Musk's company are key to operating long-distance strikes.

Presidential Advisor Beskrestnov said SpaceX had cut off access to its military-grade version of Starlink above 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour), adding that Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our ‌observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of ‌just 110–120 ​km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," a Reaction Corps representative told Reuters news agency.

Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said such limitations significantly complicate logistics and ​drone operations.

Ukraine has used Starlink terminals as an alternative to radio control for its drones as well as for ground communications since shortly after Russia launched its invasion.

Starlink's resistance to electronic jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters that drop supplies for Ukraine's frontline troops.

Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a key Donald Trump supporter, has, however, repeatedly shifted his stance on Ukraine since the early days of Russia's invasion.

In August, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to create an alternative to Musk's Starlink, in concert "with a European country."

Zelenskyy recieves warm welcome in UK

Arriving in London on Wednesday for talks at 10 Downing Street, Zelenksyy received a strong show of support amid the tensions with Washington.

"You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain ... we are behind you and that will not change," said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

When asked by Piers Morgan about Trump's recent turn towards Russia, Zelenskyy said it was "pity" to lose a "⁠strong partner." "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ​side, not our side."

The Ukrainian president received a strong show of support from UK PM Andy Burnham Image: Alberto Pezzali/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Washington continues to share intelligence, for now

There has not yet been any follow-up from the US or Starlink regarding the speed restrictions in Ukraine, a senior Ukrainian official told DW.

"We view this as a signal regarding further restrictive measures," the official said under condition of anonymity.



The official confirmed Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv, for now, amid concerns that the US will use vital battlefield intelligence as a bargaining chip.

World.title: Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
World.content:
Serhii Kuznietsov is accused of attacking civilian infrastructure in the 2022 sabotage of the Russian gas pipeline to Germany. His lawyers called Nord Stream a military target, and said their client is sworn to secrecy.

The trial of a former Ukrainian special forces officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, opened in the northern German city of Hamburg on Wednesday amid considerable public and press interest.

Kuznietsov is accused of leading the September 2022 sabotage operation that put the undersea Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines linking Russian to Germany out of action. The pipelines remain inactive four years later, with no sign of plans to ever reactivate them as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine heads into its fifth winter.

Prosecutors accuse the Ukrainian of participation in a war crime by targeting civilian infrastructure, but his defense lawyers on Wednesday argued that the case should be dismissed entirely on multiple grounds.

The defense lawyers argue that the case should be thrown out entirely, saying their client is forbidden from speaking with them or anybody else about the case Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

What did Kuznietsov's lawyers say on opening day?

A team of three lawyers representing Kuznietsov questioned the premise of the trial in court.

One of Kuznietsov's lawyers, Nicola Canestrini, argued that it was not valid to try the officer on war crimes charges for an attack on civilian infrastructure.

He argued that the pipeline, which provided half of Germany's natural gas imports prior to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, was ultimately a "Russian weapon," given the importance of energy revenues for funding Moscow's military.

"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked the court.

After the charges were read out, the judge asked Kuznietsov if he wanted to comment, and he said that he did not.

His lawyers argue that this silence extends beyond not speaking in court and say this should be the main grounds for dismissal.

They say Kuznietsov is sworn to secrecy by his home government in Ukraine and so is unable to discuss his case or potential exonerating evidence with anyone, including his legal representatives.

"He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers," defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court. In German law, Meyer-Lohkamp argued: "Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted."

A small group of demonstrators stood outside the court on Wednesday arguing that the wrong party to the war in Ukraine was on trial Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

What was the mood in court in Hamburg?

DW's Matthew Moore was on hand in the court in northern Germany on Wednesday.

There is huge interest in this court case, Moore reported. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told Moore they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."

Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.

"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Based on investigative reporting and a Bojan Pancevski book on the sabotage published this year, Kuznietsov coordinated a small and unlikely team made up not of professional spies or soldiers, but rather people with relevant specialist skills like deep-sea divers and explosives experts Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

Geramny's Wadephul: 'We will deal with any outcome'

The case has been highly politically awkward for Germany — a staunch supporter of Ukraine despite investigators pursuing a trail that led to Kuznietsov and other suspects.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly denied any Ukrainian involvement in the operation, and had also resisted Kuznietsov's extradition to Germany after his arrest in Italy last year, arguing that there was no case to answer.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul declined to comment on the trial on Wednesday, saying that the most important thing for now was for the case to proceed with no political interference or restrictions.

"We will deal with any outcome, and we will, of course, take it into account in our political calculations," he told a press conference in Berlin.

Nord Stream sabotage trial begins in Hamburg To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Court dates for the trial are currently scheduled through February of next year but this could be subject to change in either direction.

With additional reporting from DW's Matthew Moore in Hamburg.

World.title: How Trump's diesel deal with Russia will impact the United States and Ukraine
World.content:
US President Trump's diesel deal with Russia has alarmed Ukraine and its allies. What is he hoping to achieve at home, and what does the deal mean for Kyiv and Moscow?

Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow.

And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.

'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'

Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."

He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.

All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.

Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.

"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.

The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.

"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.

Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.

'No concrete military benefits for Russia'

The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.

He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.

"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.

Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European alternatives to US intelligence

A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.

While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.

As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.

Support for Ukraine across both US parties

Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.

Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.

There is broad bipartisan support for Ukraine in US Congress Image: Valerio Rosati/Visually/picture alliance

"Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.

He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."

Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian

World.title: Japanese journalist arrest in Russia's Far East draws rebuke from Tokyo in latest diplomatic spat with Moscow
World.content:
A journalist for a Japanese newspaper was arrested on suspicion of spying in Russia's Far East. A geopolitical rivalry over disputed islands in the region has recently caused tension.

Japan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Russia's ambassador after a Japanese journalist was arrested by Russia's FSB security agency on suspicion of espionage.

What do know so far?

The journalist's arrest comes amid a dispute in a dispute between Russia and Japan over the four southernmost islands of the Kuril Island chain, which are controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo. The archipelago in the northwest Pacific is near the Russian island of Sakhalin where the man was arrested.

Russia's Federal Security Service announced the arrest on Tuesday and claimed the journalist, who works for the northern Japanese Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was gathering information about Russian defense capability on behalf of Japanese intelligence.

In a statement, Japan's Foreign Ministry lodged a "strong protest" against Russia for "detaining this Japanese national and issuing unilateral statements regarding the matter, while the Japanese government has not received any explanation concerning the detained national as yet."

On Wednesday, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo called for Russia to treat the detainee fairly and humanely, while asking Russian authorities for more information about his arrest.

Kihara added that Japanese officials have been unable to contact the man, his condition is unknown, and Moscow had not responded to Tokyo's requests for access.

"We'll do everything we can for the protection of the Japanese citizen," he said.

Russia claims Japan using journalists as spies

Russian authorities identified the journalist as Yuki Imai. The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper has not yet confirmed the journalist's identity, saying it is still gathering details of what could have led to the arrest.

The newspaper said the man had been reporting in Russia on a journalist visa and was supposed to leave on Monday.

In footage on Russian state television, a man is seen being placed in handcuffs by three masked men in black uniforms, and then being accompanied by FSB agents onto a plane. The man is then seen in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for two months.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova claimed that Japan is using accredited journalists in Russia to gather sensitive security information.

Kimitake Nakamura, head of the European Affairs Bureau at Japan's Foreign Ministry, said he has asked Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to quickly arrange a meeting between the detained journalist and the Japanese government.

Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Japan-Russia Kuril Islands dispute

The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.

Bilateral tensions were aggravated by Japan joining Western sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

The dispute reignited in August after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the Kurils for the first time, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling the visit "absolutely unacceptable." Putin was only the second Russian leader to ever visit the islands

Russia has also increased its military presence on the islands in recent years, including by deploying missile systems, expanding air fields, and using the islands for live fire drills.

In Wednesday's Foreign Ministry statement, Nakamura reiterated Japan's territorial claims over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which Tokyo calls the "Northern Territory."
