World.title: Network disruptions and intelligence blackout: Is the U.S. deserting Ukraine? | Explained
World.content:
The Story So Far: Ukraine, engaged in a war with Russia for more than four years, on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) reported network connectivity issues, affecting defence infrastructure and weapons system, arising after the U.S.-based Starlink system “slowed down”. Ukrainian officials and analysts have alleged intentional disruption of services of the system owned by Elon Musk and have also accused the Donald Trump administration of holding back intelligence and leaving the country in the dark against Russian advances. The reported network disruption comes days after the U.S. President announced a deal to procure diesel from Russia and declared an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kiev, saying that the warring parties have agreed to stop attacking energy facilities.

What are the issues reported with Starlink?

The low-earth orbit satellite system by SpaceX, a dream project of the billionaire Mr. Musk, provides Internet connectivity to more than 160 countries and claims to be able to reach remote areas with far more reliability than other network systems. Following Russia’s invasion in 2022, Mr. Musk has deployed Starlink satellites over Ukraine and have sent over thousands of receivers to enable uninterrupted communications for military personnel, even in the frontlines, government officials, and civilians.

Ukraine also have access to Starshield, a modified and secure Starlink network developed for the Pentagon which is tailored for military operations. While Mr. Musk has claimed that the two are separate entities, both Starlink and Starshield use the same base technology. The Pentagon funds the use of Starshield in Ukraine under a classified contract managed by the U.S. Department of Defence.

Ukrainian troops have used Starlink and Starshield to communicate as well and control crucial defence and offence assets during the war, especially in drones and missile-defence systems. The systems can provide livestreams from the front lines. Enable remote control of drones and other weapons and help track assets. However, all these facilities took a hit last day when assets reported bad connection or no connection while moving faster than 160 kilometre per hour.

The New York Times reported messages among military units on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) warning soldiers operating vehicles or drones about the slowdown of Starlink services. It also reported Ukrainian soldiers as saying that the restrictions affected weaponised drones targeting Russian logistical routes and occupied territories.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukraininan weapons expert and an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said in a social media post that defence forces did not receive any warnings on the restriction and the move has led to the “failure of several missions”. He said that the slowdown affected long-barrage missions and frontline logistics but added that the bigger problem was the effects of defence systems.

Russia’s jet-powered attacking drones, Shaheds, move at speeds close to 200 kilometre per hour and the slowdown of Starlink has made it impossible for Ukrainian missiles to catch up to it. The restrictions effectively tied Ukraine’s hands while Russia, from where Mr. Musk had earlier withdrawn Starlink coverage, was left free to go on with its war. The restrictions “obviously cannot be a coinccidence and are related to the current political scenario,” the Zelenskyy adviser said in his post.

Why is the U.S. being accused of the disruption?

While U.S. has been a Ukraine ally since the beginning of the invasion, the highly unpredictable President Trump has gone wayward in his policies on wars. Weeks after signing into law an Act enabling 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil to cut funding for Moscow, Mr. Trump last week announced getting diesel from Russia, a move aimed at satisfying his vote base ahead of the November midterms. The President also announced the “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.

However, Mr. Zelenskyy remains skeptic over this truce as he accuses Russia of not abiding by it and continuing to attack Ukrainian powerplants. Analysts have pointed out that Mr. Trumps ceasefire only covered oil refineries, of which none in Ukraine are currently operational. This makes Mr. Trump’s truce an attempt to keep his diesel flow uninterrupted while Russia moves on with its tactics of cutting of energy for Ukrainians ahead of the winter. Mr. Zelenskyy, in a social media post, said the strikes were “entirely deliberate”, adding that “Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect” to the U.S.

Adding to the allegations of U.S. moving to Russia’s side came the reported shutdown of intelligence sharing between Washington and Kiev, as military personnel in the frontline said they were unaware of a barrage of ballistic missiles from Russia on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) night. Mr. Zelenskyy said dozens of ballistic missiles were fired at Ukraine on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) night, one of the largest such attack since the war began, cutting off power for more than 6 lakh people.

While Mr. Trump has denied Ukraine’s charges on stopping intelligence sharing, Axios reported that U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had threatened Ukraine of the same if Washington’s proposals were not accepted. A U.S. official denied the threat and said that the envoys merely conveyed that the “U.S. was a strong partner providing munitions and intelligence” and that Ukraine therefore “should not take actions that hurt Americans”.

Mr. Musk late on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) night responded to Starlink issue, and appeared to pass the blame to the administration, strengthening Ukraine’s charges, while replying to a post on X by former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Federov, in which he claimed that Starlink connections appeared to be back to normal in the country. Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government, Mr. Musk said, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately the President. He also sought to separate Starshield from Starlink, saying that the latter was a commercial service for civilian use or defensive activities and cannot be engaged for offensive purposes.

World.title: Mayawati demands regularisation of contractual employees working in Uttar Pradesh departments
World.content:
The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) president, Mayawati, on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) demanded the regularisation of contractual employees working under various government departments in Uttar Pradesh, urging the State government to include them in its recruitment plans of one lakh permanent jobs.

In a post on X, BSP chief said, “Recently, the Uttar Pradesh government has announced it will provide government jobs to one lakh people within the next six months, but it would have been better if the people who have been working temporarily for years in all the government departments should also be included in the permanent job scheme,”.

The BSP chief added that the party is against the exploitative system of outsourcing and contracting, especially in the government system.

“In any case, the BSP is against the exploitative system of outsourcing and contracting, especially in the government system, and that is why the party demands that, in order to restore government jobs, it would be appropriate if all the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) contractual workers who have been serving continuously for the past several years under the NRHM are also regularised in the health department. They have been on a dharna near the Honourable Shri Kanshi Ram Ji Eco Garden in Lucknow for the past several days in support of their demands for regularisation, etc,” said Ms. Mayawati.

World.title: Why J&K Waqf Board’s push to uniform Friday sermons triggered a political storm | Explained
World.content:
The Story So Far: The J&K Waqf Board, headed by senior BJP leader and chairperson Darakshan Andrabi, held a meeting on October 11 at its office in Srinagar. It was attended by imams (prayer leaders) and khateebs (preachers) of hundreds of mosques and shrines affiliated with the Board. Ms. Andrabi informed the meeting about the creation of a core committee of Islamic scholars and preachers to decide on a uniform topic for Friday sermons in Jammu and Kashmir. Ishtiyaq Mohi-ud-Din, an Executive Magistrate at the Board, disclosed that the Board was pushing the idea for the past one month and a directive was already in place “to broach only one topic in sermons”. He also sought views from the religious persons on incorporating non-Waqf mosques under the new uniform sermon. J&K has both Waqf-affiliated and non-affiliated mosques and shrines. Ever since Ms. Andrabi took over the reins of the Board in March 2022, scores of family-run shrines were also taken over by the Board like Ziyarat Shareef Rayil Gund, Dargah-e-Faiz Panah, Mir Syed Taj-ud-Din Hamdani, Ziyarat of Hazrat Sultan-ul-Arfeen, Seer Hamdan Shrine etc. Both the management and financial control were taken over of such shrines across the Union Territory (UT), in a rare bid.

Why does Andrabi want uniform sermon?

Ms. Andrabi suggested the need for a uniform Friday sermons was to “forcefully and unitedly” raise concerns of the society, which included waywardness, late marriages, drugs etc. She argued that the pre-selected topics by the core committee of Islamic scholars will be an impactful way of addressing social issues plaguing the community. This is a departure from the history of mosques in J&K. All mosques and shrines in the past were free to decide on topics to be touched upon in Friday sermons, which has two parts: one that deals with local and contemporary issues and two, where sermon delivered by Prophet Muhammad is recited, ahead of the congregational noon prayers attended by thousands of worshippers every Friday. Traditionally, these sermons would touch upon both political and social issues in Kashmir. Mosques and shrines in Kashmir also have a history of rallying political movements. In 1931, the speech by Abdul Qadeer Khan at the Shah-e-Hamdan Shrine resulted in an upheaval against the Dogra rule in Kashmir. The Jama Masjid in 1964 turned into the platform to mobilise people over the theft of holy relics from the Hazratbal shrine. In the 1990s, anti-India rallies were held from most of the shrines in Kashmir. Ms. Andrabi’s bid is seen by many as an attempt to de-politicise religious places in Kashmir, which saw three decades of armed conflict, and limit their role to social issues, which the core committee of the Board will pre-approve. BJP legislator R.S. Pathania supported the move of the Board’s religious leaders.

Who is Darakshan Andrabi?

Ms. Andrabi, 52, is one of the senior members of the BJP in Kashmir. She has been a loyal worker to the party even though she has not won any elections in the UT. In 2016, Andrabi was first appointed as a member of the Central Waqf Council by the Ministry of Minority Affairs. She was later also appointed as chairperson of Education and Women Welfare Committee of the Union Ministry of Minority Affairs and Member of the Maulana Azad National Education Foundation. In 2019, as the Centre ended special status of J&K, the J&K Waqf Board was brought under the Central Act. In 2022, the Union Minority Affairs Ministry appointed Ms. Andrabi as chairperson of the Board under clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 14 of the Waqf Act-1995 for five years. The Central Act brought the legal and administrative framework governing the Waqf “in alignment with the applicable national framework”. According to the Board, preservation of religious places in J&K carries a responsibility far greater than maintaining physical structures; it means protecting the spiritual environment and religious traditions that have shaped communities for centuries. She ended “Dastabandi (turban fastening)” of political leaders and removed the families traditionally associated with the shrines. Prior to 2019, the Chief Minister of the State would be the ex-officio Chairman of the Board and, if he happens to be a non-Muslim, an eminent Muslim from the Council of Ministers, was to be appointed as the Chairman. Currently, the elected government of Omar Abdullah has no role in the affairs of the Board.

Why are J&K regional leaders riled up over uniform Friday sermons?

Most regional parties and top religious leaders have criticised the move of the Board to introduce a system of uniform Friday sermons. J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah termed it as “an unacceptable attempt to interfere in the religious affairs”. He said the BJP-appointed Chairperson must “immediately halt this misplaced attempt to please her masters”. Kashmir chief cleric Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, also head of a pan-J&K conglomerate Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulema, said the State or the government cannot assume the authority to determine religious discourse and script speech to be delivered, or interfere in matters of faith and religious practice. This amounts to forcible State intrusion into the religious sphere, which is against law and principles of freedom of religious practice, he said. Kashmir’s grand mufti Naser Ul Islam objected to the Board’s move, saying “religious sermons are an integral part of Islamic guidance and must be approached with due regard for Shariah, the principles of Islam, and the religious responsibilities of Imams and Khateebs”. He said matters concerning Islamic teachings and religious guidance must not become instruments of political influence. “The autonomy of religious institutions and the dignity of the pulpit must be respected,” he added. Former J&K Chief Minister and Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti said it was a bid to push the BJP agenda on the lines of Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in J&K. Leaders of the J&K Peoples Conference (JKPC), Awami Ittehad Party (AIP) and J&K Apni Party also opposed the move.

What is the status of the Waqf initiative?

Ms. Andrabi denied any interference in religious affairs or issuing any formal order. She ruled out any role of the Chairperson or Waqf officials to decide on the Friday sermons. She said it was on the suggestions of the religious scholars and preachers that the subject came up for discussion. She said the Board will have a core committee of scholars and preachers and they will get to decide and not politicians on sermons. Though there is no formal order, the creation of a Board-appointed core committee of scholars to choose the topics for Friday sermons has the ball rolling. Maulana Raiyaz Ul Haq Noorabadi, senior cleric who heads the Hazratbal shrine, backed the narrative of Ms. Andrabi and denied “any government circular or agenda behind the meeting of religious scholars”. He reiterated that Islamic scholars would decide sermon topics in consultation with each other, “keeping in view the prevailing circumstances and social issues”. However, there are many religious leaders in the Jammu province who publicly opposed the Board’s move to thrust down uniform sermons “without consultations and against the provisions in Islam”.

World.title: At Ashvita’s, explore history of Madras through art
World.content:
“Thou still unravish’d bride of quietness, Thou foster-child of silence and slow time.” It is almost impossible not to recall John Keats’s Ode on a Grecian Urn as I enter Ashvita’s art collection, showcasing art from 19th and 20th-Century Madras. Here, time, with all its charm, is frozen in art that outlives the artists.

Starting with Tanjore paintings and kolu dolls arranged in one corner, the exhibition ends with a display of analog photographs from RK Studio. Each piece, a work of art, represents a fragment of time in history.

Layers of history are embedded in Tanjore paintings — a classical South Indian art form that evolved over centuries, with Thanjavur emerging as a thriving creative centre under Nayak rule and Telugu-speaking Raju community artists settling there to become its main creators. “Later, under Maratha rule, the style truly began to glow,” says Rithik Pramod, co-curator of the exhibition Between Tradition and Modernity, adding, “The Marathas blended their love of rich decoration with local traditions, bringing in the refined raised relief (gesso), glass beads, lavish gold foil and gemstones we recognise today.”

Despite their rich history, the art forms remain deeply personal. Most paintings depict deities such as a young Krishna and are created on wooden panels, with raised relief work and gold foil. These artworks hang in most Chennai households, where families worship them as their chosen deities.

Colour also acts as a hidden historical language in Tanjore paintings. The extensive use of gold leaf is not merely decorative. It also catches the flickering light of an oil lamp in a dimly lit puja room, lending the paintings a divine glow.

Rithik says the same about kolu dolls displayed in front of Tanjore paintings. “To a foreigner, a doll may be just a painted figure. To a family, it may be a grandmother’s gift, standing on the same step every Navratri. So whether a family is protecting a centuries-old Tanjore painting or passing down a traditional kolu doll, they are not just saving an antique. They are keeping faith, regional history and family identity alive in their own living rooms.”

Further along, the exhibition explores Chennai’s colonial past through portraits by European artists. These mostly include hand sketches of Madras and portrait paintings by George Chinnery and John Joseph Fonceca. “The official written records of Madras are full of administrative ledgers and Government decrees. They tell us about the business of the Empire, but very little about what the city actually looked and felt like. Art fills that gap,” Rithik says.

Among the European artworks, the portrait of Helana Oakeley particularly stands out. “The painting depicts Helana Oakeley, her family and their domestic staff in their home, surrounded by lush, jungle-like gardens, offering a peek into their life. Their paintings make me feel that documenting Madras through European perspective was important to them,” says Sruthi Srinivasan, co-curator of the exhibition.

Nearby, oil portraits by Indian artists,Bhavani Charan Law, M Pachappa hang on the walls, capturing members of privileged communities who could afford to commission such works, which serve as documentation of their community, preserving its image for future generations.

Portraiture evolved further with the advent of photography. Subjects no longer had to sit for hours to have their portraits painted. Instead, photographs could be taken, enlarged, retouched with colour, and framed.

Analogue photographs from the 1980s also had a place in the exhibition on tradition and modernity. Drawn from the archives of Malavika Sarukkai and the KR Nathan studio, Royapettah High Road , they offer a glimpse into the evolution of photography in Chennai. “Photography is also an art; with the right lighting, right angle, the picture captures and documents the subject,” says Rithik.

“When we preserve these artworks, we are holding onto a blend of everything people have held dear across generations: deep faith, master craftsmanship, artistic knowledge, family traditions, and the legacy of the patrons who kept the art alive,” he adds.

The exhibition is open from Monday to Friday, 10am to 6pm, at Ashvita’s till November 22.

World.title: Lavanyavati: Reframing lavani through documentary theatre
World.content:
A woman in a nine-yard sari, anklets tinkling as she dances to the beat of the dholki — for many, this is the image of lavani. But how much do we really know about the woman behind that image?

This will be the central question of Lavanyavati (a performer of lavani), a documentary theatre production by Kali Billi Productions which will be performed at The Lab @ Shanta on October 1.

Lavani, an art form from Maharashtra, was traditionally performed by women from communities such as Bhatu, Kalwat and Dombari, many of whom are from nomadic or OBC (Other Backward Class) communities. Historically, while the performers have mostly been women, in spaces such as tamasha and sangeet bari, the audiences have largely been men from dominant communities.

Years ago, when Savitri Medhatul, founder, Kali Billi Productions, began researching lavani, she realised that its portrayal in popular culture was skewed, with lavanyavatis often being labelled as vulgar or perceived as the ‘other woman’. She felt this narrative needed to change. Savitri along with a team of six, will be performing at the Lavanyavati.

“To counter such fictional narratives woven around lavani artistes, the production has been built around research, oral histories, interviews and personal narratives, using a non-fiction format,” says Savitri, explaining the choice of documentary theatre.

“Lavanyavatis have been perceived either as vamps or victims. I wanted to challenge both these ideas and show that lavani women are independent, intelligent, and artistic entrepreneurs. The problem was never the women, but the larger patriarchal society,” she says.

At the heart of lavani is shringara rasa (emotion of love). While the form can be burlesque, Savitri believes its texts can be viewed through a feminist lens, allowing the performance to be seen as an expression of agency and empowerment rather than exploitation.

For her, encountering traditional lavani artistes through dramatised stage performance and conversation is key to changing perceptions of the form. “Once you meet traditional lavani artistes, you understand that the portrayal of them in popular media is wrong. But it is important to have that encounter.” Through Lavanyavati, the group hopes to facilitate that encounter by bringing the artistes’ narratives to urban, middle-class, and upper-middle-class audiences, thereby changing the way lavani is perceived. The production has previously performed in Goa, Mumbai and Delhi

“Everybody talks about the pride of lavani, but nobody talks about the sustenance of these artistes,” says Savitri, adding that Government support and patronage are necessary if the traditional form is to survive.

Over the years, Savitri has also observed positive changes in the way lavani has accessed and perceived. The form is no longer confined to the communities that have traditionally performed it, with lavani workshops drawing people from diverse backgrounds across Maharashtra. The growing interest in learning and performing the form, she says, offers hope for its sustenance.

The association of lavani with vulgarity has also begun to shift, with the form finding newer audiences through Hindi cinema and other popular platforms. For Savitri, the growing interest is a positive sign.

ThroughLavanyavati, she hopes to take that conversation further. “It’s like a domino effect. Through the performance, I hope it will spark more conversations about lavani keeping it alive,” she says.

Lavanyavati, a documentary theatre production by Kali Billi Productions, will be presented at The Lab@Shanta on Thursday, October 1, at 7pm.

World.title: The time when Travancore said no to longer Onam holidays in Keralam
World.content:
Nowadays, it is taken for granted that the Onam holidays would run into several days. But it was not always so, reveal old records from the time before the modern-day State of Keralam was formed in 1956.

Questions were raised and answers given in the Travancore Sri Mulam Assembly (a precursor to the current State Legislative Assembly) in the 1930s over a demand that the number of public holidays for Onam be raised to 10 as was the case with the Christmas-New Year break. Back then, the government took the stand that the number of holidays cannot be increased as there were already a “sufficiently large number of holidays in the year.”

Assembly records preserved from those days show that a number of members, notably T.P. Velayudhan Pillai representing Tiruvalla, had persistently raised the issue in the Sri Mulam Assembly. The replies were given by the then Chief Secretary to government Rao Sahib, Dr. N. Kunjan Pillai, who defended the government’s stand. What seems to have irked some members was that the Christmas-New Year holidays in December lasted 9 to 11 days, while it was not so for Onam although Thiruvonam day was a public holiday.

In May 1935, Velayudhan Pillai wanted to know whether the government was aware of the representations made in both Houses of the Legislature – Sri Chitra State Council and Sri Mulam Assembly – that the number of public holidays for the Onam festival be raised to 10. Kunjan Pillai replied in the affirmative. When Pacode A. Narayana Pillai, representing the Vilavankode constituency (now in Tamil Nadu), asked whether the government was aware that Onam was an important ‘national festival’ for the whole State, the Chief Secretary replied: “That is a matter of opinion. This subject was discussed in one of the sessions in the Assembly last year and since then it has been under consideration.”

In the July session the same year, when Velayudhan Pillai brought up the matter again, Chief Secretary N. Kunjan Pillai replied that “Such holidays cannot be increased.” When the former stubbornly stuck to his guns, the Chief Secretary replied that “there are already a sufficiently large number of holidays in the year and government dooes not therefore think it necessary to increase the number any more.” Back then, there were approximately 108 holidays in a year, counting Sundays.

The Chief Secretary also had a justification for the longer year-end break. “As the honourable members may know, Christmas is only on one day, though the holidays are called Christmas holidays. They are not intended for Christmas. That is the best season when the officers can go for a change. So government thought it would be better to increase the number of holidays during Christmas so as to allow the officers to have the chance of going out for a change [sic].”

The records show that the government reaffirmed its stand in January 1938 as well.

Some years before the above exchange in the Sri Mulam Assembly, A.R. Menon (who later became the first Health Minister of Kerala) raised a question in the Cochin Legislative Council in November 1926 regarding the Onam leave permitted – “wholly or partly” – that year to medical officers of the General Hospital, Ernakulam. The indication from the records is that the query was meant to ascertain whether the hospital was left without a civil surgeon.

Diwan Bahadur Dr. V. Verghese replied: “Wholly – nil. Partly – seven. Dr. T. Verghese did duty for Capt. A.R. Puduval for 2 days. The Chief Medical and Sanitary Officer was looking after the work of both the Civil Surgeon during their absence [sic].”

Cut to the 21st century Keralam. While school holidays last for around 10 days, the holidays for public offices are not that many still. In 2026, the holidays for public offices during the Onam week last from August 25 to August 28, as per the official list published by the Keralam government’s General Administration Department. August 26 is First Onam and Milad-i-Sherif (birthday of Prophet Mohammed), August 26 is Thiruvonam, August 27 is Third Onam, and August 28, Fourth Onam as well as the birth anniversaries of the social reformers Sree Narayana Guru and Ayyankali. These holidays are followed by the weekend.

World.title: Assamese film Rador Pakhi wins special jury award at Moscow festival
World.content:
Guwahati

The Assamese feature film Rador Pakhi (morning sunshine) has received a special jury award at an international festival for women-made films in Moscow.

Director Bobby Sarma Baruah and co-producer Sulakhyana Baruah received the Super Mama Award at the festival held in the Russian capital from July 8 to 12.

The producers said on Tuesday (July 21, 2026) that the recognition marked an important milestone in the film’s journey across national and international film festivals.

Before featuring in the competition section of the International Film Festival—Made by Women in Moscow, Rador Pakhi was selected for the NFDC (National Film Development Corporation) Film Bazaar Co-Production Market and later premiered in the Indian Panorama section of the 55th International Film Festival of India in Goa in 2024.

It was subsequently selected for the Asian Spectrum section of the 21st Third Eye Asian Film Festival in Mumbai, the 23rd Pune International Film Festival, and the Indian Competition section of the 16th Bengaluru International Film Festival in 2025.

In 2025, the film was also selected for the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne, the 20th International Film Festival of Thrissur, and the Mosaic International Film Festival in Canada.

The director said the film was inspired by the real-life journey of writer Sarmistha Pritam, who is based in central Assam. The film revolves around Jyoti, an aspiring writer from Assam who is diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy at a young age. Despite facing severe physical challenges, her determination to live independently and pursue her dreams forms the emotional core of the film.

“Receiving the recognition (Super Mama Award) on an international platform is truly an honour and a proud moment for our entire team,” Ms. Sarma Baruah said.

Ms. Sarma Baruah produced Rador Pakhi along with Sulakhyana and Basanta Kumar Baruah. Sulakhyana also plays a key role alongside Kamal Lochan, Arun Nath, and Bina Patangia.

World.title: Slaves, a new production by The Madras Players, is a translation of writer Sujatha
World.content:
In a distant corner of the internet, there exists a review on Wordpress by blogger VishyTheKnight (from 2018) who calls Sujathavin Nadagangal, an 830-page collection of Tamil plays by writer Sujatha, absolutely unputdownable.

He summarises everything he enjoys and does not in this detailed blogpost and among the first play he lists as his favourite is Adimaigal (Slaves). He notes that Sujatha, who is most known for sci-fi novels, paints interesting perspectives of his subjects despite choosing dramaturgy, a genre that he is not always known for. Vishy comments, “this play is different, because it is complex, the characters are flawed, and it is impossible to do the good-and-bad binary thing here. Sujatha is clearly breaking new ground here, at least in the Tamil theatre scene (sic).”

Interestingly, during a chat in his Venus Colony apartment, director and vocal artist PC Ramakrishna seems to share similar thoughts about the author’s ability to write characters with grey shades. “This is a story about a patriarchal tea estate owner who rules over his nephews with an iron fist. I feel like this is something people might really engage with because it talks about property disputes. What happens to the property when the patriarch falls in love? I enjoy it when people go back with strong opinions after watching a play. I am looking forward to seeing that happen again on October 24,” he says, announcing his latest production, Slaves, set to be performed by The Madras Players at Narada Gana Sabha.

The cast involves some familiar names who have frequented Chennai’s stages and some novices including the likes of Balaji K Moorthy, S Ram, Karthik Sundar, Prasanna Ramachandran, and Anuradha Ramesh.

Ramakrishna says that there has been a steady attempt to build a rapport on stage through rehearsals that have been spanning over two months. This vocal artist whose deep baritone has captured the imagination of several Tamil folks, has been in the theatre space for 60 years now and adds that tweaks at rehearsals are central to building a good production. It is why he invites friends and family over to watch. “It’s the feedback at this time that is crucial,” he adds.

Ramakrishna says that the inspiration to translate this play and perform it arose because of a conversation between a journalist who had recommended Sujatha as his potential subject. “I knew him in the capacity of a sci-fi author but not as a playwright. When I was recommended to read Adimaigal, I found the process of translation easy because it was already written in the format. This is different from the other plays I have dramatised like [writer] Chudamani’s work,” he says, adding that the latter was rewritten to fit a play format.

In his long career, PC Ramakrishna has also been responsible for run-away hit productions like Water, an English dramatisation of Komal Swaminathan’s Thanneer Thanneer. He has also directed Sujatha Vijayaraghavan’s Kamalakshi, a story about a devadasi dancer and the oppressive system she is part of. “I am drawn to plays that have strong women characters. It is probably because of the women in my life,” he says, adding that his mother, wife, and daughter play a pivotal role in shaping his outlook towards life. “In Slaves too, the plot takes a turn because of a woman,” he says.

Ramakrishna says that in order to write, one must consistently consume quality works. It is why he reads as extensively as he does and why he has been able to hold his own in his career working with greats including the likes of Girish Karnad. His ability to pull together an interesting cast has also contributed to his success, he says. “Everytime I read books (he reads multiple at the same time), I’m always thinking about what would make for a good play,” he says.

What’s next? That is work-in-progress. For now though, there is Slaves.

Catch Slaves at Narada Gana Sabha on October 24, at 6.30pm. Tickets prices start from ₹120. Book tickets at mdnd.in

World.title: At least 4 killed, 20 injured as school roof collapses in Peshawar: Rescue 1122
World.content:
PESHAWAR: At least four people were killed and 20 injured on Thursday when the roof of a private school collapsed in Peshawar’s Dir Colony, Rescue 1122 said.

In a statement, Rescue 1122 spokesperson Bilal Ahmed Faizi said rescue personnel had transported around 20 people, including students and teachers, to hospitals. Four people had died in the incident, he said, citing Lady Reading Hospital.

A rescue operation is underway.

An earlier statement by the agency said that more than 10 children had been provided first aid and taken to hospitals. It added that several children were feared trapped under the rubble.

More to follow.

World.title: World Bank sees ‘moderate’ progress in Pakistan's tax reforms
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The World Bank on Wednesday rated its two loan programmes in Pakistan, worth around $670 million, as ‘moderately satisfactory’ with ‘substantial risk’. The programmes are intended to support macroeconomic stability, improve service delivery and increase the tax-to-GDP ratio to 15pc in five years.

In its public disclosure, the Washington-based lending agency rated the overall implementation of the $700 million financing for the Pakistan Public Resources for Inclusive Development — Multiphase Programmatic Approach (PRID-MPA) as ‘moderately satisfactory’. It assigned a substantial risk rating to the loan, which became effective on June 19, 2025. One of the programme’s key objectives is to increase Pakistan’s tax-to-GDP ratio from 12.3pc in June 2025 to 15pc by June 2030.

The rating is based on high political and governance risk, and moderate to substantial risks across macroeconomic, sector strategies and policies, institutional capacity, fiduciary, and environmental and social standards. Overall risks have been described as ‘substantial’.

The MPA operation became effective on May 14, and an advance disbursement of $164.52 million was made on June 29. Despite these risks, the bank noted strong progress across most of the disbursement-linked indicators, “reflecting continued momentum in the reform programme”. It said the government was operationalising the technical assistance component and related implementation arrangements, following refinements to project activities and cost allocations.

Washington-based lender flags substantial risks to $670 million programmes

The two sides — the government and the World Bank — are now working closely to advance preparatory activities and mitigate the impact of delays in approval timelines on fulfilment of effectiveness conditions and reform implementation.

The World Bank has reported to the government for correction the delays on account of the constitution of the governing council of the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics and the appointment of the chief statistician — a key lapse in programme conditions.

Under this, the chief statistician position should not remain vacant during the programme implementation, and an existing government official may not be formally delegated the role of chief statistician. The condition has been delayed because the position has been vacant since Sept 24, 2026, the bank said.

The bank has also assigned a moderate-to-substantial risk rating to the $70m Connected Punjab Programme for political, governance, macroeconomic, and fiduciary reasons, effective from the start of the current fiscal year and running until June 2031.

This is despite the bank conceding that the programme benefited from “strong ownership at the highest levels of the Government of Punjab”.

The programme focuses on three mutually reinforcing results areas: broadband access and connectivity; digital service delivery and artificial intelligence (AI) readiness; and enhanced cashless transactions.

The Punjab Information Technology Board (PITB) has secured provincial government approval, demonstrating strong institutional preparedness. Next steps include advancing the AI Oversight Committee, Data Governance Framework, personal data protection strategy, and cybersecurity strategy as foundations for responsible AI adoption.

The PRID-MPA was approved by the WB board of directors on Dec 19, 2025, while describing it as an innovative, national programme supporting federal and provincial reforms to mobilise domestic revenue and enhance spending quality and leverage data and digital tools for improved services.

World.title: Pakistan worst hit by hunger in South Asia
World.content:
• Economic instability erodes household purchasing power; heavy rains, floods trigger acute crop losses

• ​South Asia remains in the ‘serious’ category; ​global hunger rises after two decades

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recorded the highest score in South Asia on the 2026 Global Hunger Index released on Wednesday, reflecting a worsening food security crisis driven by economic instability, climate shocks and global conflicts.

Published jointly by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and the Swiss organisation Helvetas under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, the report reveals that progress in South Asia has largely stagnated, with conditions in Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorating since 2018.

In Pakistan, economic instability and sharp food price inflation have eroded households’ purchasing power and constrained access to food. Undernourishment in the country has climbed from low in 2018 to medium, while child wasting has risen toward the high threshold.

Across South Asia, the situation remains serious with a regional score of 23.5. Although the region’s score has fallen substantially from an alarming 37.5 in 2000, most of that progress occurred before 2018.

While Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved from the alarming to the serious category since 2000, child stunting remains very high.

Pakistan’s stunting rate continues to fall, whereas Afghanistan’s has edged up since 2018. Child mortality rates in both nations have declined from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels today.

The report warned that high levels of acute food insecurity will persist across the region. Heavy rains and flooding caused localised crop losses in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures negatively affected Afghanistan’s 2026 cereal-growing season.

According to Food and Agriculture Organisation estimates, 218 million people in South Asia, including Iran, were undernourished between 2023 and 2025, representing roughly one-third of the global total.

Globally, hunger is rising again after nearly two decades of progress. The 2026 global score stands at 18.1, worsening from 17.6 in 2018.

Hunger has increased in 32 countries since 2018, and 57 countries are on track to miss achieving even low hunger levels by 2030.

Three of the index’s four indicators — undernourishment, child stunting and child wasting — have worsened, while only child mortality has continued to decline slightly.

State-based armed conflicts, now at their highest level since World War II, alongside frequent extreme weather events, are major drivers of this reversal.

The war in Iran and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait are driving up fuel, transportation and fertiliser costs.

Meanwhile, Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea export restrictions threaten higher wheat prices, making basic supplies unaffordable in the Global South.

Compounding the crisis, international spending on food security has fallen to 2016-2017 levels, forcing cuts to aid programmes and emergency rations. The report urged governments to reverse funding cuts for humanitarian assistance and data collection to prevent and manage future crises.

Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

World.title: Lawmakers, govt differ over Discos’ privatisation
World.content:
• Muhammad Ali claims CCI nod not required, says Discos caused over $30bn in losses over 15 years

• Panel seeks records of council’s decisions, other consultations

• Questions Rs2.6tr federal spending on devolved subjects

ISLAMABAD: The propo­sed privatisation of power distribution companies (Discos) stirred controversy on Wedn­esday, as a Senate panel maintained that the matter constitutionally fell within the domain of the Council of Common Interests (CCI), while the government’s top privatisation official insisted that no fresh CCI approval was required.

Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatisation Muhammad Ali told a subcommittee of the Senate Functional Committee on Devolution that no new CCI approval was needed for the privatisation of Discos. He added that the companies had caused losses of more than $30 billion over the past 15 years.

He said the CCI had approved the privatisation of three power generation companies and nine distribution companies in 2011. It also approved the National Electricity Policy on June 21, 2021, which recommended that the government explore various privatisation options to improve the efficiency of state-owned entities where applicable. Both decisions remained valid, he said.

On the validity of the decisions, the law division, in a Sept 25, 2026 letter, reconfirmed that in light of the 2011 CCI decision, fresh approval was not required for the privatisation of Discos.

Accordingly, the privatisation division maintained that no fresh CCI approval was required in light of the 2011 decision and the 2021 National Electricity Policy, Mr Ali said.

The adviser told the subcommittee that legal and procedural requirements for the privatisation process had been fulfilled.

He said the National Electricity Policy 2021 had been formulated after obtaining recommendations from the provinces and that the privatisation programme had subsequently been approved, with further work undertaken during 2023-24.

Referring the matter back to the CCI at this stage could cause significant delays, affect investor confidence and adversely impact the financial position of power distribution companies, he argued.

Highlighting substantial losses faced by the power sector due to electricity theft and operational inefficiencies, he stressed that privatisation was necessary to improve performance and reduce burden on the national exchequer.

Responding, subcommittee convener Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro emphasised that the constitutional position and role of the CCI could not be overlooked.

He questioned whether the proposed privatisation was consistent with the constitutional distribution of powers under Article 157, observing that electricity distribution and related matters involved provincial interests.

Referring to previous judicial decisions and privatisation initiatives, he stressed the importance of transparency and protecting provincial interests, and asked authorities to provide relevant decisions and supporting documents for examination. He said provinces, being represented in the CCI, should have an opportunity to consider matters falling within their domain.

Officials informed the committee that the CCI had taken 11 relevant decisions and that, according to available record, no province had formally recorded reservations. They assured that relevant documents and details of provincial consultations would be shared. The minister reiterated that all necessary legal requirements had been met and referring the matter back to CCI was not considered necessary at this stage.

The chairman reiterated that the committee’s examination was intended to ensure constitutional compliance, transparency and effective parliamentary oversight, and directed authorities to furnish decisions and supporting documents so the matter could be assessed in light of the Constitution and previous judicial pronouncements.

He said constitutionally the matter was related to CCI and necessary documents must be submitted to examine the process from all aspects.

The subcommittee met under the convenorship of Senator Ghumro to review federal expenditure on ministries, institutions, organisations, statutory bodies and corporations retained by the federal government despite provincial matters following the 18th Constitutional Amendment. It also examined compliance reports and status of matters concerning the CCI.

The meeting was attended by Senators Jan Muhammad Buledi and Poonjo Bheel, secretaries of cabinet, CCI, Establishment Division, special secretary establishment, additional secretary establishment and senior officers.

At the outset, the report of the Auditor General of Pakistan (AGP) and the Accountant General on expenditure incurred by the federal government on ministries relating to provincial subjects was taken up.

The chairman observed that despite 16 years since the 18th Amendment, concerns persisted regarding federal expenditure on devolved subjects, including education and health, which had been notified as provincial matters by the Implementation Commission.

Referring to Articles 168 and 169 of the Constitution and the legal framework governing the audit of public expenditure, he questioned the authorisation and constitutional basis for expenditure of approximately Rs2.6 trillion on the health and education ministries over the past 16 years.

He termed the expenditure of Rs2.6tr by the federal government on the two ministries, which he said had been de-notified in 2010, a misuse of taxpayers’ money, arguing that the Centre could spend only on federal subjects.

He said the amount could rise to several trillion rupees once expenditure on other ministries created for provincial subjects was included.

Mr Ghumro expressed concern that the details sought by the committee had not been submitted within the stipulated timeframe and stressed that parliament was the primary authority for authorising public expenditure, and that such expenditure should be confined to federal subjects.

He maintained that expenditure from the Federal Consolidated Fund could not be authorised for devolved provincial matters. AGP officials explained that the audit process was guided by budgets approved by the competent parliamentary forum and acknowledged certain limitations in coverage.

World.title: Israeli settlers set fire to mosque in occupied West Bank
World.content:
MIKHMAS: Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque and graffitied its outside walls on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank village of Mikhmas, Palestinian sources and the Israeli military said.

Atta Kanaan, a Palestinian resident of Mikhmas who lives 50 metres from the mosque, told AFP that he heard the sound of breaking glass shortly after midnight on Wednesday and immediately went to the building.

“A fire was burning fiercely, and we called the fire brigade. Young men rushed to help us with fire extinguishers, and we managed to contain part of the fire before the flames engulfed the entire mosque,” he said.

Israel’s military told AFP that soldiers were dispatched to Mikhmas following a report of graffiti and arson at the mosque, as well as damage to a vehicle.

“No suspects were identified,” it said, adding an investigation had been opened.

AFP video footage showed that the fire had burned down the mosque’s interior carpeting and blackened the walls.

An AFP journalist reported that slogans were spraypainted in Hebrew on the exterior walls, including “just because we are quiet doesn’t mean we are asleep”.

Settlers also set fire to a car, Kanaan said, adding that in recent weeks villagers had formed night-watch patrols out of fear that settlers might torch homes, particularly those on the outskirts of the village.

Rouhi Fattouh, president of the Palestinian National Council, described the arson attack on the mosque as “a barbaric act and a dangerous escalation in settler terrorism”.

Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

World.title: Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly passes ‘amended’ Local Govt Act 2026
World.content:
• Clears path for local bodies polls delayed for over two decades; election date to be announced after governor’s assent; municipal corporations set up in Gilgit, Skardu, and Chilas; 17pc quota reserved for women

• House also approves bill to establish GB Information Technology Board

GILGIT: The Gilgit-Baltistan (GB) Asse­­mbly on Wednesday cleared the way for the region’s first local bodies elections in over two decades by passing the amended GB Local Government Act 2026, while also approving a separate bill to establish an Information Technology Board.

During a session chaired by Deputy Speaker Malik Kifayatur Rehman, the assembly first approved the amended GB Local Government Act 2026 by a majority vote. The legislation aims to hold local bodies elections that have not been conducted in the region for more than 20 years.

Gilgit-Baltistan Minister for Local Bodies Zulfiqar Ali Murad introduced the amended draft in the House to seek its passage.

Although the assembly had previously passed the act with a majority, GB Governor Syed Mehdi Shah returned the bill for reconsideration after raising objections to several points.

Opposition members raised objections when the amended bill was tabled, asking the treasury benches for more time to study and consider the draft. However, the majority of the assembly members favoured the bill, and Deputy Speaker Rehman announced its passage over the opposition’s dissent.

Speaking on the floor of the House, Mr Murad stated that the act was reintroduced only after the governor’s objections were removed and the revised draft was approved by the GB Cabinet.

Under the new act, municipal corporations have been established in the cities of Chilas, Gilgit and Skardu, where elected members will choose mayors and deputy mayors.

Additionally, union councils and district councils have been established across all districts, with a 17pc quota allocated for women in all local bodies. The passage of the bill follows months of administrative deadlock over local polls.

The dispute emerged after Chief Election Commissioner Raja Shahbaz Khan unilaterally scheduled elections for Aug 2, causing friction with the chief minister, who was not consulted.

The chief minister insisted on conducting the elections under a new 2026 act, while the election commissioner intended to use the previous 2014 act. The election commission subsequently postponed the polls.

Official sources state that a new election date will be announced once the governor signs the amended bill into law.

Separately, the bill to establish the GB Information Technology Board was unanimously approved. Under the legislation, the chief minister will serve as the board’s chairman, while a minister or adviser will act as its vice chairman.

Speaking on the occasion, Chief Minister Amjad Hussain Advocate said the board is being established to address long-standing information technology and telecommunications issues and to upgrade internet connectivity faced by residents across the region.

The chief minister told the assembly that governance, tendering, tax collection and other departmental functions are being shifted online.

“The board will invite foreign investors, bring stakeholders to GB from other provinces, and establish IT parks and other facilities for locals, particularly the youth, to ensure their easy and high-speed access to the internet,” CM Hussain said, adding that the board will be inaugurated by the prime minister.

World.title: Two wings of Karachi police clash over custody of suspects
World.content:
• SIU officials intervened in District Central police sting operation to arrest suspected kidnappers, sources say

• City police chief orders inquiry

KARACHI: Authorities on Wednesday ordered an inquiry into a public confrontation between personnel of two wings of Karachi police over the custody of four suspected kidnappers in North Nazimabad on Tuesday night.

A brief statement said Karachi police chief Azad Khan took notice of what it described as a “tussle” between District Central police and the Special Investigation Unit (SIU) and directed South DIG Syed Asad Raza to conduct a detailed inquiry.

While the statement did not contain any details about the “tussle”, residents of District Central witnessed an open display of firearms, exchange of gunfire and physical confrontation between the two police units over the custody of four suspects who had allegedly kidnapped a trader.

Police sources told Dawn that the trader, who was travelling with his minor son in his car, was kidnapped on Monday within the jurisdiction of the Taimuria police station and the abductors dropped off the boy.

They drove him through several areas for three to four hours, using different roads and routes, withdrew cash from ATMs using the trader’s bank cards and later released him.

As the Taimuria police registered a case, district Central investigators arrested the alleged mastermind on Tuesday afternoon and during interrogation at a police station, he disclosed the names of his accomplices, the sources said.

As part of their strategy, the investigators, led by the Shadman DSP, brought the alleged mastermind to a restaurant in North Nazimabad and asked him to call his accomplices there. Four suspects arrived at the restaurant, and the investigators were waiting for their fifth accomplice to arrive to arrest the entire gang.

In the meantime, some men in plain clothes arrived at the restaurant in a car and tried to take away the suspects without realising that a sting operation was underway. They were intercepted by District Central police personnel. The men in plain clothes identified themselves as SIU officials and refused to hand over custody of the four suspects.

A scuffle broke out between the two police teams and apparently the SIU personnel called in additional members of their unit. The confrontation escalated on the main road and they exchanged gunfire, which triggered fear and panic among residents.

The Nazimabad SHO and his team arrived at the scene and persuaded both sides to move to the police station rather than continue fighting on the road.

Talks between District Central police and SIU officials continued for around two hours and the two sides agreed that their senior officers would “settle” the issue of the custody of the suspects.

The sources said that the Shadman DSP and two members of his team were allegedly taken by SIU personnel to their office in Saddar, where they were reportedly manhandled.

They said the SIU maintained that its personnel had traced and arrested the suspects with the help of technology, while District Central police contended that the SIU officials had arrived under “suspicious circumstances” without informing the local police.

The District Central police managed to get the custody of the four suspects and brought them to the Taimuria police station.

According to the police statement, the Karachi police asked the South DIG to ascertain all aspects of the incident, record statements of the police officials concerned, assess all available evidence and submit a report.

Published in Dawn, October 15th, 2026

World.title: Police on high alert as Peshawar CCPO visits Bara
World.content:
PESHAWAR/KHYBER: With the police remaining on high alert, Peshawar Capital City Police Officer (CCPO) Dr Mian Saeed Ahmad visited Bara tehsil in Khyber tribal district on Wednesday to monitor the law and order situation.

They said the security situation in Bara Bazaar and surrounding areas was being continuously monitored, while the CCPO was personally overseeing it.

In a statement issued from his office, Dr Ahmad said there was effective coordination between Peshawar and Khyber police as well as other law-enforcement agencies to protect public life and property, government installations and sensitive places.

“Maintaining law and order and providing a safe environment to citizens is our top priority. There will be no compromise on the rule of law, so violators of the law will be dealt with strictly,” he said.

The CCPO said legal action would be taken against those who damaged government property, committed vandalism or caused unrest. He said that the police were fully alert and were utilising all available resources to protect citizens and establish the writ of the government.

Dr Ahmad urged people to cooperate with the police and administration in maintaining law and order and that Peshawar police, in coordination with Khyber police, were committed to maintaining peace in the area.

Also, a tense calm prevailed in Bara tehsil of Khyber district on Wednesday after the police barricaded Bara Bazaar from all sides sealing all entry and exit points.

Police officials said additional personnel had been deployed in Bara Bazaar.

They said CCPO Dr Mian Saeed Ahmad visited the site of Tuesday’s clashes between police and PTI protesters.

A statement issued by the office of the district police officer in the Shakas area of Jamrud said security had been tightened and measures taken to maintain law and order in Bara Bazaar and surrounding areas. It said Khyber and Peshawar police were closely coordinating with other law-enforcement agencies.

Sources said the local PTI leadership had advised supporters and sympathisers to refrain from staging protests following Tuesday’s violent demonstration in Bara.

They claimed that local MNA Iqbal Afridi and MPA Abdul Ghani had gone into hiding.

Police booked 15 PTI supporters for demonstrating in Jamrud.

The situation remained peaceful in Landi Kotal, with all roads, including the main Peshawar-Torkham Highway, open to traffic.

On Tuesday, five PTI workers were injured during a protest in Bara tehsil that turned violent after participants torched government buildings and clashed with riot police.

Sources said angry protesters set fire to the nearby Nadra office and part of the Rescue 1122 building.

PTI workers were injured during clashes with police and the firing in the air, with the party leaders accusing police of directly firing at protesters.

Police denied the allegation. The injured workers were taken to a local hospital, where their condition was stated to be out of danger.
