World.title: FACT CHECK: Comelec did not set barangay, SK polls for December 14
World.content:
The Comelec flags a circulating graphic as fake. Under Republic Act No. 12326, the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections are scheduled for November 13, 2028.

Claim: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) announced that the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) would be held on December 14, 2026.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post in the group “Duterte Legacy” that was published on October 8 carried the claim with a caption that reads, “Confirmed!”

The attached graphic mimics a Comelec announcement, displaying the poll body’s seal and the heading “Official Announcement.” It states: “This is to confirm the scheduled date for the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE). Despite any varying information, the scheduled date on record is December 14, 2026.”

Its text further states: “PAALALA: Ang opisyal na petsa ay maaaring magbago ayon sa batas. Manatiling nakatutok para sa anumang opisyal na bagong anunsyo mula sa COMELEC.”

(Reminder: The official date may change according to law. Stay tuned for any official new announcement from the Comelec.)

As of writing, the post had drawn 763 reactions, 136 comments, and 140 shares.

The facts: The Comelec did not announce a December 14 BSKE. On October 10, it warned the public that the circulating graphic was fake and urged the public to rely on the poll body’s official website and social media accounts for election-related announcements.

The graphic cites no law or Comelec resolution establishing December 14 as the election date. It provides no resolution number and merely directs readers to the Comelec website. The use of the poll body’s seal and official-looking design does not establish its authenticity.

Under Republic Act (RA) No. 12326, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on September 24, the next BSKE is scheduled for November 13, 2028. The law postponed the elections from the previous schedule of November 2, 2026.

Petitions before the Supreme Court seek to block the new law and compel the Comelec to hold the elections in 2026. The poll body has said that RA 12326 remains in effect because the Court has not issued a temporary restraining order.

Date change: The BSKE was initially scheduled for December 1, 2025. In August 2025, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed RA 12232, postponing the elections to November 2, 2026, and setting a four-year term for barangay and SK officials.

Senator Francis Escudero then filed Senate Bill No. 2387 in August 2026, seeking to extend the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years, amending RA 12232.

Escudero’s proposed measure was subsequently enacted as RA 12326. The law provides for elections every five years, on the second Monday of November, beginning in 2028. (READ: How often have barangay, SK elections been postponed?)

Fake dates: The shifting election schedules have fueled misinformation online. Rappler previously fact-checked a claim that the postponement had already become law before Marcos signed it, as well as another claiming that the elections would be held this coming November 28. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar, who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies from the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Microsoft, partners disrupt phishing kit ecosystem behind cybercrime operations
World.content:
Microsoft and its partners dismantle three parts of a wide-ranging cybercrime marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man

MANILA, Philippines – Microsoft worked with Japan’s National Police Agency and a host of partners, including cybersecurity companies and global nonprofit organization Health-ISAC, to dismantle part of the operations of a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace responsible for creating and selling phishing kits — or accounts, hosting services and tools for building fake websites and online identities.

In an October 14 blog post, Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC dismantled three parts of that marketplace’s infrastructure: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man.

Steven Masada, general counsel and general manager of Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, said YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have since January 2026 “collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone.”

He added, “These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.”

While YAM Store provided the infrastructure, the phishing kits sold on the marketplace, including CoGUI and Iron Man, provided bad actors with access to ready-made templates allowing them to impersonate trusted organizations. With the templates in hand, criminals could quickly send email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries, and countries in an effort to get people to click on phishing links.

Masada explained that the phishing kits allowed for impersonation attempts across a spectrum of organizations, from government agencies to banks, retailers, and parcel delivery services from various countries and in numerous languages.

Masada added, “YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on.”

A more technical breakdown of the phishing infrastructure that complements the Microsoft blogpost is available on Microsoft’s security blog. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandro Marcos leaves father’s party, joins Lakas
World.content:
KEY POST. Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos leads the floor after being elected House majority leader on July 28, 2025.

The congressman's office has kept the move low-key, providing no press release or photo handout of the oath taking

MANILA, Philippines – House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos has left Partido Federal, the party of his father President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and joined Lakas CMD, the party of his uncle and mentor, former speaker Martin Romualdez.

A source told Rappler that the younger Marcos took his oath before Lakas member and Camiguin Representative JJ Romualdo at the House of Representatives on Monday, October 11.

Marcos’ office has kept the move low-key, providing no press release or photo handout of the oath taking. Former president and Pampanga 2nd District Representative Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, was said to be present at the event.

No reason has been given for his party transfer, which comes weeks after its president Romualdez was arrested for plunder in connection with the flood control and overall national budget corruption scandal.

The party hasn’t distanced itself from Romualdez despite the controversy, and repeated calls for impartiality and due process after his arrest.

Lakas remains the biggest contingent in the House, with around 60 members, although its numbers are down from its peak of more than 100 members in the 19th Congress.

The lower chamber’s second largest delegation, National Unity Party, isn’t far behind, with around 50 members.

Rappler has reached out to both Lakas and PFP for comment, but they have yet to respond. – Rappler.com

World.title: At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be
World.content:
MOVECEBU. Advocates, educators, and media representatives talk about the city’s liveability and how citizens can help make Cebu better for everyone during Rappler’s #MoveCebu roadshow panel discussion, 'How Citizens Can Build a Better Cebu,' at the University of San Carlos Downtown Campus in Cebu City on October 14, 2026.

'A liveable Cebu is one where no one is left behind,' says urban poor community leader Lourdes Bueza

CEBU, Philippines – “If we want a liveable Cebu, we need to stop thinking as only a city but start thinking we are a Metro Cebu,” Yumi Espina, convenor of the Movement for Liveable Cebu said during the Sugbo Alang Sa Sugbuanon (Cebu for Cebuanos) public forum on Wednesday, October 14.

Espina spoke during the #MoveCebu roadshow at the University of San Carlos (USC) in Cebu City where more than 200 participants from civil society groups, youth-led initiatives, and academe gathered to get a better understanding of what makes a liveable city.

It coincided with Cebu facing environmental and societal challenges — from waste management issues following the Binaliw landfill incident to struggles brought by heavy flooding in the metropolitan’s major urban and residential hubs.

“This forum was almost canceled because of the suspension of classes that was announced by the city mayor, ironically, because of poor air quality in so perhaps, it is one of the underlying causes why we must reflect on the issue of liveability,” Owen de La Victoria, OIC chair of the USC Department of Political Science, said in his welcome remarks.

In the days leading to the forum, the air quality in Metro Cebu dropped to very unhealthy levels due to localized emissions, made worse by unfavorable weather conditions, according to the Environmental Management Bureau in Central Visayas.

Espina listed the five major factors that make cities liveable: stability, healthcare, culture and environment, education, and infrastructure. Climate change and urbanization are the ultimate challenges to liveability, he added.

UNDERSTANDING. Architect Yumi Espina of the Movement for Liveable Cebu breaks down the watershed system of Cebu and its links to the heavy flooding felt in the metropolitan areas. Photo by Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

“We experience flooding not just because rain is heavy but because urbanization has changed our waterways,” he said, citing the experience of La Paloma Village in Barangay Labangon in Cebu City which became a catch basin because of urbanization.

Espina presented the recommendations of the Cebu City Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP). The CLUP recommended the creation of a mass transit line, a “green belt” along the metropolitan’s major watersheds, and a “green loop” for the shift of urban development wherein urbanization moves eastward from the capital to Mactan Island.

The problem, Espina lamented, is that civil society groups are often left out in the discussions of developmental policies that the government and private sector typically have.

“What we need is a genuine partnership among government, business, and civil society, and an engaged citizenry that is willing to participate, speak up ,and hold institutions accountable,” Espina stressed.

As a reactor, Cebu City Councilor Joel Garganera conceded that the city government could have done so much more in promoting liveability with better planning and management.

“We are like in a dark room — blind and looking for a path out,” he said.

Defining a liveable Cebu

When asked how they would define liveable Cebu, speakers, reactors, and concerned citizens responded during the forum and on Muni in the Rappler app.

On the app, resident Asia Katrinah Atendido said that a liveable Cebu should be walkable, with walkable sidewalks that are not only used to park cars or any vehicles, serving the people and not vehicles

For University of the Philippines Cebu student Crispin Ginicez Caballero, a liveable Cebu would have continued improvement, expansion, and proper implementation of public transportation initiatives.

UP College of Communication, Art, and Design Dean Crina Tañongon emphasized the significance of empowerment in pushing for a liveable Cebu, adding that the academe must ensure that learners have the space to develop critical thinking.

CONNECTING. ‘Students must ask why this is happening and that would lead to deeper understanding…it would be grounded on the shared realities that we face,’ UP College of Communication, Art, and Design Dean Crina Tañongon said.

Community leaders present during the forum pointed out how much of the lived realities of struggling Cebuanos showed a “grim picture” of the metro’s direction towards liveability.

Rebecca Herbese of Pangisda Cebu pointed out that small fisherfolks in Lapu-Lapu City struggled to find their own space amid campaigns for land reclamations and the presence of large fishing vessels within municipal waters.

“Mahimo lang liveable ang atong lugar karon kung ang atong mga katawhan dili na mag-antos sa kalisod (A place can only be considered liveable if the people no longer suffer from hardships),” Herbese said.

Joan Lucañas of urban poor rights group SILHIG said that Mandaue City residents feel left out in consultations for resettlement programs. She stressed the importance of creating a liveable city with the urban poor being seen as part of the population rather than a hindrance to the interests of developers.

United Fisherfolks and Urban Poor of Cebu City coordinator Lourdes Bueza asked: “Is empowerment just for the educated? Are the poor to be left out in that empowerment Cebu wants?”

“Ang liveable Cebu kay kanang wala mabiyaan (A liveable Cebu is one where no one is left behind),” Bueza said.

Community at the center

Rappler’s managing editor Miriam Grace Go shared the importance of putting community at the center of a city’s campaign for liveability.

“Cebu has had citizens who have been courageous enough to study the masterplans, to talk to residents, to engage with the residents…they all tell us the necessities of consultations, planning, and action,” Go said.

Go hoped that Cebu’s experts, journalists, and concerned citizens would share the discussions on liveability questions outside Cebu.

“Rappler is here to expand the awareness of its all-citizens-approach…to bring Cebu’s experience onto a larger stage so the other regions and communities will see that these are the same liveability challenges they are facing,” Go added.

The forum was organized by MovePH, Rappler’s civic engagement arm, in partnership with the University of San Carlos, the University of the Philippines Cebu; and Cebu Citizens Initiative and Movement for Liveable Cebu. It was supported by the government of Canada through its Canada Fund for Local Initiatives and by the Journalism for Nation Building Foundation.

Rappler officially launched the #PadayonCebu chat room on Rappler’s Muni at the public forum. Join the conversation on making Cebu liveable here. – Rappler.com

World.title: Mother of drug victim killed over mistaken identity clings to hope for justice
World.content:
GRIEVING. A grieving Lorna Pepaño lights a candle in memory of her son, Christian, who was mistakenly gunned down by unidentified “riding-in-tandem” perpetrators in Quezon City on May 18, 2020 – amid the Covid-19 pandemic.

MANILA, Philippines – “Kahit justice delayed, justice denied, umaasa pa rin kami (Even if it’s justice delayed, justice denied, we’re still holding on to hope),” said single mother Lorna Pepaño whose son, Christian, was a victim of extrajudicial killing in 2020.

Pepaño, 72, recounted the killing of her son during the fourth truth-telling session of the Philippine Truth Commission on October 9.

Christian, 39, was shot four times by riding-in-tandem gunmen in Quezon City on the early evening of May 18, 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Pepaño, Christian headed outside to buy her maintenance medicine for hypertension. An hour later, a neighbor told her that her son was shot dead just blocks away from their house.

RECOLLECTION. 72-year-old Lorna Pepaño, a single mother, becomes emotional as she recounts the death of her son, Christian, during the fourth truth-telling session of the Philippine Truth Commission on October 9, 2026, at the Pope Pius XII Catholic Center, Manila. Rhen Peñada/Rappler

The perpetrators allegedly mistook her son for their supposed victim because they were wearing the same clothes.

“Ginaya [ng mga hinahabol ng ‘riding-in-tandem’] ‘yong damit ng anak ko, kaya ‘yong anak ko ang na-target (My son was targeted because the person the riding-in-tandem was pursuing wore the same clothes),” said Pepaño.

The perpetrators initially fired four shots at Christian, but the latter still managed to run away. Unfortunately, they caught up with him in the streets of Barangay Holy Spirit, where he was killed.

“Hindi po ako ‘yon…. Hindi po ako ‘yon (It’s not me…. it’s not me),” were Christian’s last words before he was mistakenly shot death, Lorna recounted.

“Pare, hindi siya ‘yong target natin. Mali (He’s not our target. We got it wrong),” Pepaño recalled the perpetrators’ belated realization.

She added: “Bakit? Nagbase ba sila sa damit? Kaya isinisigaw ko na hindi ganoon ‘yong anak ko. Porke’t ganoon ‘yong damit niya, suspect na?”

(Why? Did they just base it on clothes? That’s why I’m insisting that my son is not who they claim to be. Just because of his clothes, he’s already a suspect?)

The day Christian was killed, Pepaño said she saw the perpetrators and their supposed target loitering outside their residential compound.

“Sumisilip sa compound namin pero ‘di ko pinapansin kasi wala naman akong pakialam sa kanila kung ano man sila. Hindi ko naman iniisip na mapapatay ‘yong anak ko na wala namang kinalaman sa mga sitwasyon na iniisip nila. Masakit…. Ang dami kong ‘bakit’ na tanong na walang sagot,” Pepaño added.

(They were peeking in our compound, but I ignored them because I didn’t care whoever they were)I never thought my son would get killed over the situations that they accuse him of. It hurts… I have so many why’s that were never answered.)

NOT FORGOTTEN. An empty chair memorial for Christian Pepaño. A good son to his mother and brother to his siblings, Christian was supposed to buy his mother’s hypertension maintenance medicine before he was gunned down in Quezon City on May 18, 2020. Rhen Peñada/Rappler

Christian’s killers have yet to be tracked down.

Established on May 27 this year, the Philippine Truth Commission is an independent, civilian-led institution that documents violations and extrajudicial killings connected to the war on drugs campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte. The commission brings together testimony, records, research, and public truth-telling sessions for policy advocacy and institutional reforms.

Duterte, who faces three counts of crimes against humanity, is currently detained in the International Criminal Court at The Hague, Netherlands, after his arrest in March 2025.

Lack of probe, cycle of killings

Forensic pathologist and truth commissioner Dr. Raquel Fortun said she was skeptical about the issued death certificate to Christian’s family. Like other drug war victims, Fortun and her team also conducted n examination of Christian’s remains.

Signed May 20, 2020, or two days after Christian’s death, the death certificate claimed that the victim had only around two minutes to live after receiving the fatal gunshot wounds to his head and trunk.

“‘Pag tiningnan ‘nyo ‘yong injuries niya, I doubt tumagal siya ng isang minuto sa grabe nang tama niya (If you take his injuries into account, I doubt he even lasted a minute due to the gravity of the shots he sustained),” Fortun argued.

Not only that, Fortun was also surprised by the doctor’s decision to put “homicide” as the victim’s manner of death. She explained that even doctors do not usually put “homicide” in cases involving gunned-down victims.

Despite the lack of police reports and forensic evidence, Fortun was able to confirm that Christian died of multiple gunshot wounds to the head and trunk.

“Pinagyayabang ng PNP (Philippine National Police) na meron silang IDs, raid lists, and then hitlists…. May laman ba ‘yong database nila (The PNP boasts they have IDs, raid lists, and then hitlists…. Does their database contain anything)?” Fortun questioned the PNP’s lack of evidence in the said incident.

“Kaya tuloy-tuloy ang patayan kasi walang imbestigasyon (Killings persist because there are no investigations),” Fortun added.

FINDINGS. Forensic pathologist and truth commissioner Dr. Raquel Fortun presents her team’s findings on the remains of the late Christian Pepaño during the truth-telling session. Rhen Peñada/Rappler

The Philippine Truth Commission is set to have its first conference on November 23, to release its first report on its independent investigations and documentation of Duterte-time killings. – Rappler.com

Rhen Peñada, a Rappler intern, is a junior information technology student from the Polytechnic University of the Philippines-Santa Rosa, Laguna campus. He is a former staffer of his school paper, “Ang Alpas.”

World.title: [Good Business] Rethinking enterprise as a force for good
World.content:
The challenge is not simply to declare that business should be a force for good. It is to make that commitment visible in how capital is invested, people are treated, and growth is pursued.

What does it mean for a business to do good? Is it enough to create jobs, donate to communities, or support social causes? Or should we examine something more fundamental: how a business earns, whom it serves, and what its success makes possible for others?

These questions were at the heart of the Business as a Force for Good (BFG) Summit 2026, held on October 9 at Makati Shangri-La. The discussions challenged a familiar assumption that profitability and social impact belong to separate agendas. More importantly, they invited business leaders to consider whether their purpose is reflected not only in their stated values, but also in their everyday decisions.

One idea offered by Ramon R. del Rosario Jr. provides a useful starting point: identify an unmet societal need, then build a sustainable business to address it. This two-step approach presents social challenges not simply as problems for philanthropy to solve, but as opportunities for enterprises to create lasting value. Yet recognizing a need is only the beginning. The harder task is building a business that can respond to it effectively, responsibly, and over time.

This distinction matters because good intentions alone cannot sustain meaningful impact. An enterprise may have a compelling mission, but without sound financial management and operational discipline, its ability to serve people remains fragile. Conversely, a profitable business may still fall short of being a force for good if its growth does little to address the needs of the communities around it. Purpose and performance must therefore reinforce one another.

The summit’s conversations about impact investing brought this challenge into sharper focus. If underserved communities represent significant unmet needs, why does so little capital reach enterprises working to address them? Expanding shared prosperity requires more than individual companies with admirable missions. It also calls for an ecosystem in which investors, businesses, civil society, and government can work together to direct resources toward meaningful and sustainable outcomes. Trust and collaboration are not peripheral concerns; they help determine which ideas receive the opportunity to grow.

But even a well-funded enterprise must ask a deeper question: what kind of progress are we pursuing, and for whom?

The discussion on Pamamahalang Pilipino offered a distinctly Filipino perspective through concepts such as kapwa, the recognition of shared personhood, and loob, the inner values that shape our choices. (READ: [Good Business] Kaloob and kapwa: Agrabah Ventures on co-creating a bountiful tomorrow)

These ideas challenge organizations to look beyond employees as units of productivity or communities as markets to be served. They encourage leaders to recognize the people behind business outcomes and consider whether their decisions contribute to a more dignified and humane life.

This perspective also changes how success is understood. Growth can be measured in revenue, expansion, and market share, but its wider significance lies in the opportunities it creates. Can employees build secure futures for their families? Can smaller suppliers participate in the value chain?

Can more Filipinos access education, livelihoods, and the resources they need to thrive? These questions bring social impact closer to the core of business strategy.

Screengrab from a Business as a Force for Good forum social media post.

The launch of Ventures for a More Humane World: A Handbook for Social Entrepreneurs in the Philippines, by Dr. Raymund Habaradas and Professor Ian Benedict Mia, reinforced the importance of equipping enterprises to turn their intentions into practice. Social entrepreneurship requires more than compassion; it needs knowledge, viable business models, and a supportive network that allows solutions to endure and grow.

Ultimately, rethinking enterprise does not mean treating profit as the enemy of social progress. Profit can sustain an organization, fund innovation, and extend its reach. The question is whether these capabilities serve a purpose beyond accumulation alone. When businesses take responsibility for the effects of their decisions, success becomes more than an internal achievement: it becomes a means of creating opportunities for others.

The challenge is not simply to declare that business should be a force for good. It is to make that commitment visible in how capital is invested, people are treated, and growth is pursued.

For every business leader, the question remains: “What need can our business meet, and how can our success help others thrive?” – Rappler.com

Madriella L. Mendoza is the Communications/Business Development Officer of the PHINMA–DLSU Center for Business and Society. She works on communications, public relations, business development, and initiatives that advance the Center’s mission of promoting business as a force for good. She may be reached at madriella.mendoza@dlsu.edu.ph.

World.title: What is lung adenocarcinoma, the cancer diagnosed in Pope Leo?
World.content:
PRAY. A woman holds a rosary and a card portraying Pope Leo outside Gemelli Hospital, where the Pontiff is being treated for lung cancer following surgery to remove part of his right lung, in Rome, Italy, October 14, 2026. REUTERS/Yara Nardi

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, often found in non-smokers and typically grows slowly

VATICAN – Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said.

Here are some facts about the disease.

What is it?

Adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that forms in glandular cells, which produce substances such as mucus. In the lungs, it develops in cells lining the air sacs and is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the category that accounts for about 80%-85% of lung cancers. Adenocarcinoma represents roughly 40% of all lung cancer cases, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

It is typically found in the outer parts of the lungs and tends to grow more slowly than some other forms of lung cancer, increasing the chances of detection before it has spread.

Who gets it?

Smoking remains the main risk factor. However, adenocarcinoma is also the most common type of lung cancer among people who have never smoked. The pope is not known to have been a smoker.

Symptoms

Early-stage disease often causes no symptoms and may be discovered during scans performed for other reasons. As the cancer progresses, symptoms can include a persistent cough, shortness of breath or wheezing, coughing up blood, chest, shoulder or back pain, unexplained weight loss and fatigue.

The Vatican has said the tumor was found during a routine health check. Leo said on Sunday that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.

How is it treated?

For patients whose cancer is confined to the lung, surgery offers the best chance of a cure.

The standard operation is a lobectomy, as occurred on Tuesday, in which an entire lobe of the lung is removed. Doctors consider it the preferred treatment when the tumor is limited to a single lobe because it maximizes the chances of removing all cancerous tissue while preserving as much lung function as possible.

Depending on the stage of the disease, treatment can also include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted drugs and immunotherapy. The Vatican has not given any information yet on what follow-up treatment the pope might need.

Prognosis

Doctors say prognosis depends heavily on the stage of the cancer and whether it has spread beyond the lung.

The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumor or whether lymph nodes were affected, making it impossible to assess Leo’s individual prognosis at this stage.

According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate for non-small cell lung cancer is 67% when the disease remains confined to the lung. The rate falls to about 40% when the disease has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes and to about 12% when it has spread to distant organs.

However, it says people being diagnosed now may have a better outlook than these statistics suggest because of improving treatments. Medical experts also caution that outcomes vary widely depending on tumor size, lymph node involvement, a patient’s age and overall health.

(This factbox drew on information posted online by the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, the National Library of Medicine and the American Cancer Society.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo back on his feet after shock cancer diagnosis
World.content:
VATICAN AND AI. Pope Leo looks on on the day of the weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, on September 23, 2026.

Blood tests and a chest X-ray show normal post-operative results, the Vatican says, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy

VATICAN – Pope Leo‘s recovery from surgery is progressing as expected and he has begun walking in his hospital room and eating normally, the Vatican said on Wednesday, after doctors announced the 71-year-old pontiff was being treated for lung cancer.

World leaders, Catholics across the globe and senior cardinals at the Vatican have offered prayers for Leo after he had part of his right lung removed in an operation on Tuesday, October 13.

Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on Wednesday, October 14, showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said, adding that the pontiff had undergone respiratory physiotherapy.

The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.

Leo normally follows a very busy schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17 and the Vatican press office said on Wednesday that “nothing has changed” regarding the planned trip.

However, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said on Wednesday that the dates could change because of the amount of time his recovery would take.

The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.

Prayers for Leo

A prayer was recited for Leo to have a good convalescence and complete healing during an open-air Mass in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday following the surgery.

The pope has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during Tuesday’s operation in an effort to eliminate all cancerous tissue.

Human lungs have five lobes — three in the right lung and two in the left.

The operation lasted about 90 minutes and was completed without complications, the pope’s lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, said late on Tuesday.

The Vatican has not disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.

Dr. Serena Ricciardi, a lung cancer specialist at Rome’s San Camillo Forlanini Hospital, said that if the cancer had not spread to Leo’s lymph nodes, the surgery may have been sufficient for treatment.

“If there are no further issues or lymph node involvement, we could consider the surgery curative,” she told Reuters. “The disease has been completely removed.”

Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.

Engagements canceled until next week

The Vatican said this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and that all his public engagements had been canceled until October 20.

The Mass on Wednesday was the closing act of an assembly of bishops called by Leo to discuss the Church’s family life teachings, the largest gathering of Church leaders so far during this papacy.

Filipino Cardinal Luis Tagle led the service in place of Leo. The pope last week approved Tagle as the dean of the Church’s College of Cardinals, in the first selection of an Asian cleric to the elite role.

Political leaders offered messages of support.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the pope, an American who was born in Chicago.

“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” he said on X. Rubio met Leo at the Vatican in May.

US President Donald Trump, who has criticized the Roman Catholic Church leader, said on Wednesday he hoped that Pope Leo would “get better fast.”

“I want to see Pope Leo get well,” Trump told reporters. “I just want to wish him well, get better fast.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar’s Opposition Leadership Is Holding Back the Resistance
World.content:
Myanmar’s resistance coalition has lost the political and diplomatic war but not the military campaign. The main reason lies less in the junta’s strength than in what I call an “insurgency-industrial complex” that has grown around the opposition.

This international ecosystem of diaspora communities, exiles, dissidents, donors, rights-based organizations and Western governments, with the National Unity Government (NUG) at its center outside the country, is geared towards fighting a military dictatorship rather than defeating it and governing Myanmar in a different way.

Unless the resistance regroups around leaders inside the country and mounts a convincing battlefield turnaround, perhaps led by drone warfare, Min Aung Hlaing will keep consolidating his grip even as the fighting goes on.

It is critical to separate Myanmar’s two wars. After staging elections last December and January, Min Aung Hlaing has reinvented himself as a pseudo-civilian president. Since assuming the presidency in April, he has made eight foreign trips. China, India and Russia have received him, as have four Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states in three months, namely Laos in July, Thailand in August, Vietnam and Cambodia in September, and this month in Malaysia.

Counting Myanmar itself, nearly half of ASEAN now deals with him at the top level. Each visit lowers the diplomatic cost of the next. ASEAN, which has kept him out of its leaders’ summits since the 2021 coup, is now under pressure to readmit him. Once in motion, political engagement generates its own momentum towards normalization and eventual recognition. The political war more or less has been lost.

The military war, on the other hand, is not lost. The armed forces do not control most of the country. Ethnic armed organizations remain strong and continue to take the fight to the military in borderland states, while People’s Defense Force (PDF) units are still holding on in the central dry zone. Neither side has clearly won on the battlefield.

Yet the resistance had its chance and missed it. By mid-2024, resistance forces held more than half of Myanmar’s territory. The military was pinned down in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw and appeared close to being toppled. But the coalition of ethnic armies, PDFs and the NUG lacked the cohesion and bold thrust to take over. Its battlefield tenacity was not matched by political capability.

When Beijing saw that the resistance did not have what it took to seize control, it backed the junta, leaned on the ethnic armies along its border to stand down, and endorsed the election roadmap. The tide turned, and here we are.

Why did the resistance falter when it mattered most? The NUG has been weak and ineffective, but the deeper reason is structural. Donations, aid and grants flow into the insurgency-industrial complex.

These funds sustain offices, salaries, jobs, scholarships, residencies abroad and a way of life. Its currency is opposition and its output is advocacy. A resistance victory would end its funding model and require some of its leaders to return home to govern a broken country of 55 million people, with all the risks that entails.

Put this way, the insurgency complex almost needs a military dictatorship to fight against. For many in the diaspora and among critics who live outside the country, it is not about winning and taking over the country but about keeping a four-decade struggle going. To be sure, many exiles and dissidents are authentic and sincere and have paid a heavy personal price.

At issue are incentives, not intentions. And these incentives work squarely in Min Aung Hlaing’s favor. An opposition led from abroad keeps the contest outward-facing and predictable, and it allows the regime to portray its enemies as foreign-funded “terrorists” detached from the people.

It does not help that global standards on human rights and democracy have sagged, and international aid has been slashed systematically, from the dismantling of American aid programs to deep cuts by the United Kingdom and European donors. The moral pressure that once isolated Myanmar’s generals has weakened.

The only way to change this narrative and shift direction is a resistance counteroffensive, led mainly by the PDF and the ethnic armies still willing to topple the regime. The battlefield is where the resistance still holds cards, and the decisive weapon is the first-person-view (FPV) drone. FPV drones have already allowed small, motivated units to hit armor, outposts and supply lines. Scaled up and coordinated, a drone-led campaign against strategic towns and corridors could deliver the key victories needed to convince Beijing and ASEAN that Min Aung Hlaing is not a safe bet for them because he cannot control the country in the long run.

But a counteroffensive requires a different leadership. The resistance needs to regroup away from the NUG and towards those who are actually fighting inside the country. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has been the most successful fighting force in the civil war. Its commander-in-chief, Major General Tun Myat Naing, has the battlefield record and standing to serve as the resistance’s overall military commander. Meanwhile, PDF commanders must be brought into the top leadership, not treated as foot soldiers for exiled politicians.

Their fighters came of age during the decade of opening from 2011 to 2021, with mobile phones, jobs, travel, foreign investment and elections that counted. They want that country back. Their objective is to retake Myanmar, while the insurgency-industrial complex’s goal is to oppose the regime and keep fighting the military dictatorship to no end.

A leadership rooted inside the country would also be the kind of interlocutor that Beijing and ASEAN could take seriously, one with control over territory and troops rather than offices and press releases. That is precisely what was missing in mid-2024.

Unless there is a clear and convincing military turnaround in the resistance’s favor that is accompanied by a more capable leadership from inside the country, Min Aung Hlaing will continue to consolidate politically and diplomatically. Neighbors and major powers will deal with whoever looks set to last—right now that is Min Aung Hlaing.

Until the fighters inside lead the leaders outside, the resistance may win more battles but will keep losing the regional and international politics of the civil war.

Thitinan Pongsudhirak is a professor of comparative and international politics at Chulalongkorn University’s Faculty Of Political Science and a non-resident associate with the Southeast Asia Centre at the London School of Economics.

This article first appeared in the Bangkok Post.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Escalates Assault on Free Press Critical of Its Rule
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime has intensified its threats against independent media critical of its rule, vowing to eliminate outlets and journalists regardless of their location.

An editorial in the junta’s mouthpiece Kyemon on Monday urged the “elimination of any destructive element inside or outside the country,” echoing the Home Affairs Ministry’s threats last week.

On October 6, Deputy Home Affairs Minister Major‑General Min Thu told parliament the regime has opened cases against independent media outlets The Irrawaddy, Mizzima, DVB, Myanmar Now, and Khit Thit under the Counter‑Terrorism Law, Telecommunications Law, and Penal Code. He claimed the regime was coordinating with international law enforcement including Interpol and Aseanapol to detain staff working for these organizations.

Interpol bans any interventions on political grounds while Aseanapol’s focus is limited to transnational crimes.

The Kyemon editorial stated that anyone inside or outside the country who “disrupts peace, stability, and development, undermines national sovereignty, prestige, and unity, or obstructs the administrative mechanism must be eliminated.”

Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing branded outlets reporting his military’s mass-killing of civilians as “nation‑destroying media” during his October 13 trip to Dawei, claiming they were misleading the public. “Those outlets do not want to see national development,” said the president, whose February 2021 coup plunged the country into turmoil.

The putsch was followed by a brutal crackdown, targeting not only peaceful protesters but also media documenting the military’s abuses. The regime revoked licenses, raided offices, and arrested scores of journalists, forcing independent outlets into exile. After establishing itself as one of the world’s worst jailers of journalists, it is now seeking to target exiled media.

Independent media groups emphasize that journalism is not a crime and note that Interpol does not act on political requests. “Interpol does not intervene in political or religious cases. Only genuine criminal matters are considered,” said Toe Zaw Latt, secretary of the Independent Press Council of Myanmar. He added that while the regime may attempt to link reporting with criminal activities, such requests are weeded out by Interpol. “So, there is no need to worry, but we should still monitor the situation carefully.”

Lower House Speaker Khin Yi—who as former dictator Than Shwe’s police chief led deadly crackdowns on pro-democracy demonstrators—has advised the Home Affairs Ministry that criminal cases must be concocted to pursue arrests abroad.

The junta’s warning comes as its propaganda apparatus struggles to discredit the resistance movement while concealing its own war crimes. Circulation of regime newspapers has sharply declined since the coup, and junta news outlets have been barred from multiple social media platforms.

A Yangon street vendor said demand for state‑owned newspapers is practically non-existent, except for once a month when lottery results are printed.

The junta’s threats come as it faces ongoing international isolation. ASEAN has barred Min Aung Hlaing from summits since the coup for failing to implement its peace plan, while he is wanted on an international arrest warrant issued by Argentina over the Rohingya genocide. Rights groups have repeatedly called on Interpol to arrest the coup leader during his overseas trips.

On Wednesday, the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) and its affiliate, the Exiled Myanmar Journalists Network (Exiled-MJN), condemned the regime’s threats as a blatant abuse of international policing mechanisms.

“Myanmar’s junta will stop at nothing to try to legitimize itself in the world’s eyes and to expand its repression against the brave and determined media and journalists who continue to expose its gross violations against its own people,” IFJ stated.

According to MJN records, at least seven journalists have been killed by the regime since the coup. The International Centre for Not-for-Profit Law has documented at least 227 journalists detained by the junta, with at least 20 still in jail.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Burn Church in Bhamo, KIA Says
World.content:
Myanmar military forces burned a Christian church near Bhamo on Monday evening as the regime continues its campaign to recapture the Kachin State town, according to Colonel Naw Bu, a spokesperson for the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).

“They [the regime] burned a Christian church in Three Mile Village on the way to Momauk,” Naw Bu told The Irrawaddy. “There have been periodic clashes in that area.”

He added that there has been frequent fighting between regime troops and KIA-led forces around Light Infantry Battalion 47 and near Bhamo University.

The KIA and its allies launched an attack on Bhamo in late 2024 and captured the majority of the town in 2025. This year, however, it has lost some ground there to the regime, which has been reinforcing its troops in preparation for a counteroffensive.

Naw Bu claimed resistance groups still control a large part of the town. The Irrawaddy could not independently verify the claim.

Citing residents, local media reported that the arson attack on the Kachin Baptist Convention-run church followed heavy regime casualties in the face of fierce resistance defense.

Human rights activists condemned the torching of the church.

“This is a violation of freedom of religion; we condemn it,” Jacob from Kachin Human Rights Watch told The Irrawaddy. “The regime does not respect international laws and continues to violate them.”

He said the regime and allied militias have used religious sites for military purposes, carried out drone attacks on churches, and detained religious leaders. “Religious rights in Kachin State are being increasingly violated,” he said.

Mervyn Thomas, founder president of Church World Service, an international Christian human rights group, said the attack was a “grave crime” and a “clear violation” of international laws and freedom of belief, while calling on the international community to cut off the regime’s access to aviation fuel and military equipment.

In September, the regime-allied Shanni Nationalities Army used the compounds of a Baptist church and a Catholic church in Indaw as a military training ground and an office, sparking criticism from ethnic Kachin residents.

The regime and its allies conducted a suicide drone attack on another church in Mohnyin Township in October.

The regime’s attacks on places of worship do not discriminate by faith, however. Myanmar Witness in April said it documented over 300 airstrikes on religious sites, including churches, monasteries and mosques, between January 2024 and December 2025. Nearly 90 percent of them were conducted by the regime’s air force, with Sagaing Region and Shan State the worst-affected areas.

In August, 14 civilians were killed in Sagaing Region’s Myaung Township when the regime launched an airstrike on a Buddhist temple that was hosting around 100 people for a meditation retreat.

World.title: Myanmar’s Spies: A History of Surveillance, Power and Purges
World.content:
Myanmar: The Making of an Intelligence State

By Andrew Selth

ISEAS Publishing, Singapore, 2026

609 pp. US$48

This book is bound to become a classic. Never before has any international scholar described and analyzed the history of intelligence in Myanmar, from the days of the kings, through colonial rule, to democratic and military-dominated governments after independence. And no one would be more qualified to do this study than Andrew Selth, an Australian academic and former diplomat who has written extensively about Myanmar for several decades. The Burmese kings sent spies across the eastern as well as western borders before invading armies captured the old Siamese capital Ayutthaya and the old Arakan kingdom. And they developed what a British historian, quoted by Selth, has described as “a powerful and sophisticated internal espionage system” when the country was threatened by European colonial powers.

A new, entirely different intelligence apparatus emerged after the British conquest in the 19th century. In 1896, a Criminal Intelligence Bureau was formed within the headquarters of the Burma Police, and its duty was quite specific: to monitor domestic dissent and “deal with cases of a political nature.” A Special Branch of the police continued that work throughout the colonial era, and its work became especially important after the Saya San rebellion in the 1930s, which also prompted the British to send in military police officers from India.

In the years after Myanmar’s independence in 1948, Selth outlines how the new government created five main intelligence agencies, of which the Military Intelligence Service (MIS) became the most powerful, and even cooperated with foreign intelligence services. Some officers were trained by the British, and then chiefly to spy on Myanmar’s growing communist movement. The CIA also provided training on the US-held island of Saipan in the Pacific. Among those receiving instruction was “Spectacles Tin Oo,” who became a close associate of the dictator General Ne Win and, as such, one of the most feared men in the country. He collected intelligence not only on political dissidents but also, and perhaps primarily, on officers and the ranks of the military, on whose loyalty the Ne Win regime relied for its survival.

Tin Oo (not to be confused with General Tin Oo, one of the founders of the National League for Democracy) and his inner circle of followers eventually became too powerful, acting like a state within a state, which led to his downfall in July 1983 and a purge of the entire intelligence apparatus. The near vacuum that ensued has been seen as the reason why North Korean agents managed to infiltrate Yangon and, in October that year, detonate a bomb that killed 17 visiting South Korean officials and four Myanmar nationals.

With MI Tin Oo behind bars, Ne Win needed a new officer who could rebuild the country’s intelligence services, and that was his trusted protégé, Khin Nyunt. His Directorate of Defense Services Intelligence (DDSI) soon had agents all over the country, and surveillance—and repression—of the population at large became of utmost importance during and after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising. According to Selth: “The DDSI already was the largest and most powerful intelligence agency in Myanmar before 1988, but under the SLORC [the State Law and Order Restoration Council] it dramatically increased in size, sophistication and territorial presence. The refashioning of the SLORC into the State Peace and Development Council in 1997, possibly on the advice of an American public relations consultant, does not seem to have resulted in any significant changes to the intelligence structures and procedures that were set in train after the uprising.”

Selth provides detailed descriptions of how Khin Nyunt’s DDSI and its affiliated agencies were structured, and how they operated. Now, foreigners, among them diplomats and others who were suspected of having contacts with the pro-democracy movement, also became targets of its surveillance. But like MI Tin Oo before him, Khin Nyunt grew too powerful for comfort, and he was eventually ousted in October 2004 along with almost his entire intelligence apparatus. New intelligence outfits had to be created, and those were placed more directly under military command to avoid a repeat of what happened in 1983 and 2004.

During Burma’s decade of relative openness, from 2011 to 2021, the intelligence services remained wholly autonomous from the governments in Naypyitaw, and that separation became even more obvious during the years when the NLD—after an election in 2015—was allowed to appoint most ministers. I experienced this firsthand when I visited the country on many occasions between 2012 and 2019. I was under constant surveillance, and the intelligence agents often didn’t even bother to hide it.

Selth also describes how various opposition forces have treated suspected informants for the various intelligence services. In 1992, the All-Burma Students’ Democratic Front’s section in Kachin State killed 15 of their own comrades on suspicion of being spies. In 2021, 25 unarmed prisoners were executed by Karen rebels. In both cases, the opposition groups had depended on faulty intelligence, which their own agencies had provided.

Anyone who wants to understand how successive military-dominated governments have survived, and on what traditions Myanmar’s intelligence services were built, has to read this book. It contains a 43-page bibliography, which is the most extensive I have seen in any book about Myanmar. The book also lists, for the first time, military intelligence chiefs since 1959, regional military commands in 2024, and the various intelligence agencies that shaped today’s Myanmar. Its subtitle, “The Making of an Intelligence State,” could not be more appropriate.

World.title: China Sentences Myanmar Scam Clan Members to Death
World.content:
BEIJING—A Chinese court sentenced three members of a criminal gang to death on Tuesday for operating a network of brutal scam centers in Myanmar’s Kokang region on the border with China, while jailing dozens more.

China has stepped up cooperation with Southeast Asian nations to crack down on a vast industry that has flourished in the region in recent years to fleece people out of billions of dollars.

Those conducting the online scams are sometimes willing con artists. Others are trafficked foreign nationals—many Chinese—tricked into work and held in prison-like compounds.

Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court said in a statement on Tuesday that it had sentenced Wei Huairen (aka Wei San), Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang to death for their involvement in the “Wei family criminal gang”.

The gang was involved in crimes including drug trafficking, organizing prostitution, operating illegal casinos, telecommunications fraud and the murder of at least two Chinese citizens, the court said.

Wei Huairen was identified as one of the group’s leaders and found guilty of several crimes including murder, the court said.

The gang’s operations netted more than 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion).

Another three gang members were handed life sentences, while 55 more were given prison terms ranging from 24 years to three years and three months, the court said.

Analysts describe the Wei clan as one of the “four families” running crime syndicates in Kokang.

China’s state broadcaster CCTV on Tuesday called them the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar,” having created an “iron triangle of political, military and business criminal activities.”

It described the gang as operating 14 “large-scale” scam compounds and luring “large numbers” of Chinese to Myanmar through fake promises of high wages.

Police had also discovered remains of victims bound with iron chains and with bullet holes in their skulls, CCTV said.

Members of the Wei family were first indicted in October 2025.

In January, China executed 11 people, including members of the “Ming family criminal gang.”

The following month, four members of the notorious Bai clan were executed for crimes including “fraud, intentional homicide, intentional injury, kidnapping [and] extortion.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Beached in Battle for Sittwe
World.content:
Fierce battles have erupted around rebel-held Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Kaladan River delta, where regime forces keep trying to land troops despite heavy losses.

Local sources say scores of regime solders were killed or captured in the first three days of fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) defends the strategic outpost while laying siege to the state capital Sittwe across the water.

AA troops recently seized regime sentry bases at Amhyint Kyun Village at the entrance of Sittwe.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed six gunboats and a dozen speedboats backed by airstrikes and artillery fire from Sittwe in an effort to seize the island.

But AA fighters are entrenched there because it allows them to attack regime naval bases and ships stationed throughout the delta and along the coast.

Sources close to the AA said regime troops are reduced to trying to land troops with speedboats after three of their larger ships were hit by AA fire on Oct. 8, with two sustaining serious damage.

“Despite the casualties, they keep on coming,” one source told The Irrawaddy.

As many as 50 regime soldiers managed to reach the shore in the first two days of fighting but were either killed or captured, sources said.

As of Monday the regime had been unable to gain a foothold. Soldiers are reportedly being forced to advance under threat of being shot by their own commanders if they refuse.

“I’ve heard they are using conscripts as cannon fodder,” another source said.

Last month, the regime launched an offensive to retake lost territories in Rakhine, dispatching three columns to AA-held Ponnagyun north of Sittwe. Nearly one month later all three columns have been repelled, and the regime is retreating in Sittwe Township itself, according to the sources.

AA troops have captured four more outposts and are pushing at the gates of Shwe Mingan naval base and Sittwe Regional Operations Command, they added.

The attack on Nga Pyi Island was apparently launched because the regime sensed the danger of an imminent siege of its Sittwe stronghold, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

“Regime navy vessels in Kaladan have repeatedly been attacked by AA drones and artillery from Nga Pyi, so the military wants to get control of the island,” said a Pauktaw resident.

Meanwhile, residents across Sittwe, Pauktaw, Ponnagyun and Rathedaung townships say the regime is bombarding the area daily and firing heavy artillery. “Every day, a dozen aircraft come and strike,” a Sittwe resident said. “Artillery units in Sittwe launches daily volleys toward Nga Pyi.”

Fighting is also intensifying in the state’s other major regime stronghold of Kyaukphyu, which is home to massive Chinese investment projects. There the AA has overrun two regime outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base. The military is reinforcing positions as far afield as Chin State as well as the Rakhine borders of Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady.

Except for Sittwe and Kyaukphyu and the sparsely populated island of Manaung, the AA now controls all of Rakhine as well as Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State.

World.title: Running for Cover: The Limits of Early Warning in Rakhine Air War
World.content:
In the week after the Sept. 28 massacre on Kyauktaw’s Indian market that killed 50 people and injured at least 58 others, Rakhine State endured another wave of aerial attacks. Local media reported at least nine bombing incidents across the townships of Ponnagyun, Rathedaung, Pauktaw, Kyauktaw, Thandwe and Kyaukphyu that killed at least another 12 civilians and injured more than 37 others. Some strikes hit locations where displaced people were sheltering.

The attacks were part of a wider pattern. The UN says aerial attacks killed more than 190 people in Rakhine in 2025. ACLED, an independent global conflict monitor, says Rakhine has suffered Myanmar’s highest reported casualties from airstrikes on local markets, recording at least 11 such attacks and 49 deaths even before the Sept. 28 massacre.

The immediate question for civilians under air attack is how they can know where a military aircraft is heading and reach safety in time.

Communities in Rakhine have improvised ingenious early-warning networks. To understand how they work, I spoke with six residents in Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U and reconstructed the warning timeline leading up to the Sept. 28 massacre.

A military jet is sometimes airborne one or two hours before an attack. What people often cannot know is where it will strike until the bombs have already begun to fall.

Watchers, channels and loudspeakers

The locals told me how warnings reach civilians in areas under Arakan Army (AA) control. What emerges is a kind of relay network: volunteer scouts track aircraft leaving airfields; their reports appear on public Telegram channels with takeoff times, directions and regions at risk; and in some communities those alerts are then announced through sirens and loudspeakers.

Warnings begin with a beeping alarm, followed by a spoken announcement. One Mrauk-U resident said at least three locations now broadcast such warnings, a system that began three or four months ago and can sometimes give people 10 to 15 minutes to find cover.

The timeline of Sep. 28

A reconstruction based on posts from a volunteer air-scout channel and the AA’s account of the strike times clearly shows the problem.

A Telegram channel with about 13,000 subscribers reported a fighter jet leaving Naypyitaw toward the southwest at 10:16 a.m., and another from the same airbase in the same direction at 11:08 a.m. Both alerts covered Rakhine, Ayeyarwady, Magwe, Bago, Karen and Chin. At 11:36, the channel reported another jet leaving Meiktila, with Mandalay, Rakhine, Magwe and Chin potentially at risk.

Yet the warning narrowed too late. An observation that a jet was circling over Kyauktaw at 12:10 was posted at about 12:13. A second observation, saying the aircraft was still circling at 12:15, appeared at about 12:16. But the AA says the first bomb struck at 12:10 and the second at 12:14.

The scouts were quick, but their information still had to pass from observer to channel operator before reaching the public. Even a few minutes matter. By the time the warnings narrowed down the target to Kyauktaw, the attack was already underway.

What’s more, phone and internet services have been severely restricted in much of Rakhine for years, and many residents cannot reliably access Telegram alerts. Repeated alarms can also cause warning fatigue.

“We can never assume where the jets are heading based only on the direction they take off in,” one resident told me. “Sometimes they appear to be flying toward another city, then turn back to drop the bombs.”

Ground observers may also lose track of sudden changes in course or altitude. The problem is not simply the speed of the volunteers, but the limits of the available information and ways to relay it.

What should change

International support should go beyond diplomatic statements. Donors, humanitarian organizations and local authorities should invest in warning systems that do not depend entirely on internet access, including radio networks, sirens and community warning posts. Air raid drills and clear protocols could reduce warning fatigue, while tiered alerts could distinguish a general aircraft warning from an imminent local threat.

Similar systems have been used elsewhere. In Syria, volunteer aircraft spotters fed flight information into warning networks that used social media, radio and street sirens to give civilians several minutes to seek cover.

The responsibility for the attacks lies with the Myanmar military. But local authorities can reduce civilian exposure by breaking up large commercial hubs into smaller neighborhood trading points, adjusting market hours to avoid peak crowds, taking any locally observed patterns of air patrols into account, and mandating the provision of proper shelters near hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.

Shelter is especially important for displaced families. Two people who fled Sittwe for Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U told me that many displaced people can afford only basic rented housing or makeshift accommodation, which offer no proper protection from airstrikes. Even a timely warning has limited value if there is nowhere safe to reach.

Historically, communities under heavy bombardment have adapted. During the Vietnam War, for instance, communities in North Vietnam built collective shelters, trenches and tunnels, while authorities adjusted school, work and market hours to reduce large daytime concentrations of people. Such measures cannot stop an air campaign, but they can reduce exposure.

International statements of concern will continue. But for civilians on the ground, the immediate challenge is to turn an early alert into a warning they can actually use. Closing the gap between knowing that a jet is airborne and knowing where it is heading may not prevent an attack. But it could give more people enough time to reach safety.

Khine is a researcher from Rakhine State with a decade of experience in peace processes, conflict issues, and human rights documentation. She is pursuing a master’s degree in Human Rights and Democratization at Mahidol University.

World.title: Philippine President Hails Diplomatic Engagement with Myanmar’s Regime
World.content:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has hailed recent visits by Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis.

In an interview with The Straits Times published Saturday, Marcos claimed credit for a recent engagement by various ASEAN governments with the putschist regime of Min Aung Hlaing.

Marcos conceded that ASEAN’s previous insistence on its Five-Point Consensus peace plan for Myanmar and refusal to engage with Myanmar’s regime at the political level were “absolutely correct.” But he added they were “not working.”

“Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else,” he told the daily.

This prompted the Philippines during its 2026 chairmanship of the bloc to propose a “new approach” at the ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May, he said without going into detail.

He then pointed to coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Malaysia and Cambodia as signs of progress, describing them as “shoots coming out of the ground” that had “not happened before” and would eventually lead to a “complete resolution.”

“Asked if ASEAN was moving towards recognizing the Myanmar government, Marcos said the grouping has to move towards that if it is going to play a part in resolving the conflict in the country,” the Straits Times wrote.

Since appointing himself president in April and rebranding his regime, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, while reportedly being invited to Indonesia and Brunei.

However, the diplomatic engagement Marcos cited has yet to lead to any reduction in violence on the ground. In some cases, Min Aung Hlaing’s trips coincided with aerial massacres on civilians at home.

In the latest major atrocity, a military airstrike on a crowded market in Rakhine State on Sept. 28 killed at least 50 people, while further air raids in the state targeted locations where displaced people were sheltering. A week later the putschist leader was being welcomed in Kuala Lumpur.

ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus consist of ending violence, beginning dialogue among all parties, appointing an ASEAN special envoy, and ensuring that humanitarian assistance those in need. It was adopted in April 2021 in response of the military coup. However, the regime led by Min Aung Hlaing has since ignored the framework, and most recently the regime’s new rubber-stamp Parliament rejected it altogether.

The conflict since the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people and internally displaced about 3.8 million as of June 2026.

“Shaking hands with war criminals is a threat to humanity,” Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, told The Irrawaddy. “We are watching to see whether the ASEAN leaders will show accountability if their re-engagement with the regime does not work out.”

Some ASEAN members are standing firm. Timor-Leste, the bloc’s newest member, has supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement and initiated legal proceedings against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. And Singapore, which stands to take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, affirmed this summer that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

World.title: From Reading Culture to Reading Competence: What PISA 2025 Tells Kazakhstan
World.content:
Kazakhstan has set itself an ambitious goal: to become a reading nation. In May, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree placing the development of reading culture among the country’s national priorities. The policy includes new libraries, a national digital library platform and a Reading Nation concept for 2027–2031. These are welcome developments. The latest international evidence also suggests that Kazakhstan needs to think carefully about what it means to be a strong reader.

The latest OECD PISA results for Kazakhstan provide an uncomfortable starting point. In PISA 2025, Kazakhstan’s average reading score was 385, compared with an OECD average of 461. Only 36% of Kazakh 15-year-olds reached at least Level 2 in reading, compared with 69% across the OECD. Almost no students in Kazakhstan reached the highest reading levels.

The more revealing number may be 36%. At Level 2, students should be able to identify the main idea of a moderately long text, locate information using several criteria and reflect on the purpose of a text when directed to do so. Higher levels demand increasingly complex skills, including comparing sources, recognising implicit meaning, separating fact from opinion and judging the reliability of information. PISA therefore gives us a picture of how confidently young people can use reading to make sense of unfamiliar information.

Kazakhstan’s reading difficulties are also longstanding. According to the OECD, reading performance has remained relatively stable since the country first participated in PISA in 2009. Kazakhstan scored 390 that year. Sixteen years later, it scored 385. The pattern stretches across several generations of students and predates the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent arrival of generative artificial intelligence.

Research conducted inside Kazakhstan offers some clues about what may be happening. Akhmetova, Imambayeva and Csapó examined more than 1,500 Grade 6 and Grade 8 students and found something that complicates the common claim that young people simply lack interest in reading. Around 85% of the Grade 6 students and 79% of the Grade 8 students reported that they enjoyed reading. Yet the relationship between positive attitudes towards reading and actual reading achievement was relatively weak.

Encouraging young people to pick up books clearly has value. Frequency alone tells us little about how readers respond when a text becomes difficult, unfamiliar or open to several interpretations. Students also need strategies for deciding what deserves attention, how different pieces of information fit together and when a claim should be questioned.

Their related work on reading strategies also identified weaknesses in how students approach texts, including deciding which sections deserve closer attention and using information from tables and figures to support understanding. Modern reading increasingly requires young people to move between an article, a graph, a website and several competing claims before deciding what information can be trusted.

Evidence from teachers presents a more encouraging picture. In 2025, Sarmurzin and colleagues surveyed 117 Kazakh literature teachers and interviewed experienced practitioners, finding a growing emphasis on reading comprehension, critical thinking, technology and more student-centred approaches. Teachers also identified continuing problems with curriculum coherence and the relationship between some reading materials and students’ everyday experiences.

Teacher preparation appears less settled. Research published in 2026 involving 254 final-year preservice teachers from five Kazakh universities found that 72% were uncertain about the distinction between functional literacy and traditional reading comprehension. The researchers also identified limited preparation in informational texts and critical digital reading, particularly among students preparing to teach Kazakh language and literature.

Greater professional support would help teachers respond to an increasingly complex reading environment. University programmes and professional development can give teachers more opportunities to work with inference, source comparison, evidence evaluation and critical digital literacy. Released PISA tasks can also show the kinds of reading processes students find difficult and provide useful material for lesson design and discussion.

There is an important limit to how far this should go. PISA measures particular forms of reading, and education should avoid turning those measures into a complete definition of what good reading looks like. Teaching students primarily to succeed on PISA-style tasks could narrow the curriculum and encourage another form of test preparation without necessarily creating more thoughtful or engaged readers. Reading also involves imagination, curiosity, emotional engagement, interpretation, enjoyment and the experience of spending time with ideas that do not lead towards a correct answer on an assessment.

PISA is most useful as a diagnostic tool. Its results can reveal weaknesses in areas such as inference, comprehension and source evaluation, while reading education itself should remain considerably broader. The aim should be to develop young people who can approach many kinds of texts with confidence, from novels and poetry to news reports, scientific arguments and digital information.

Kazakhstan could also make reading a clearer responsibility across the school curriculum. A history student comparing conflicting accounts of an event is practising reading. A science student deciding whether evidence supports a conclusion is doing the same, as is a geography student combining information from a map, graph and written report. Across these subjects, questions such as “How do I know this?”, “What evidence supports the claim?”, “What has been left out?” and “Which source should I trust?” can help students treat reading as a way of thinking rather than simply retrieving information.

Schools also need to protect space for sustained reading. Young people now encounter enormous quantities of written material through social media, messaging platforms, websites and increasingly AI systems. Much of this information arrives in short fragments. Regular opportunities to stay with longer and more demanding texts, discuss them, annotate them and return to difficult passages should remain part of school life. Sustained attention is itself becoming an important educational skill.

Generative AI adds another layer to this reading environment. AI can summarise a chapter, explain an argument and produce an answer within seconds. Students need strong skills for deciding whether that summary is accurate, what it has left out and whether the evidence supports the answer. One useful classroom activity might involve comparing an original article with an AI-generated summary. Students could identify missing qualifications, check claims against the original source and discuss how the meaning has changed. Used in this way, AI can support deeper reading.

Kazakhstan’s 2026 decree on developing reading culture already provides a framework for moving in this direction, particularly through its emphasis on reading in the era of artificial intelligence. Continued investment in books, libraries and positive reading cultures remains valuable. The next stage should connect that access more directly with how young people understand, question and use what they read.

A reading nation needs citizens who can stay with difficult ideas, recognise weak evidence, compare competing accounts and reach informed conclusions. It also needs readers who find pleasure in language, become absorbed in stories, encounter unfamiliar perspectives and sometimes read without being asked to extract a measurable skill from the experience. These abilities and experiences develop gradually through years of purposeful reading across classrooms, subjects and languages.

The PISA score of 385 should be treated as more than a position in an international ranking. It offers a useful warning about the depth of reading skills many young people currently possess and gives policymakers and educators a clearer sense of where attention is needed. Kazakhstan has already committed itself to becoming a reading nation. The next stage is to create the conditions in which young people can read widely, read carefully, enjoy what they read and learn to think for themselves through the process.

The author is Michael Jones, an writing and communications instructor, School of Social Science and Humanities, Nazarbayev University (Astana).

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kuwait’s Jazeera Airways Eyes Resumption of Direct Flights to Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Kuwait’s airline Jazeera Airways is interested in resuming direct flights to Kazakhstan once regional conditions stabilize, potentially restoring a route suspended after its launch in 2021.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Kuwait Yerzhan Yelekeyev discussed restoring direct air connectivity with Jazeera Airways CEO Barathan Pasupathi, the Kazakh Foreign Ministry reported on Oct. 13.

The officials explored opportunities to expand cooperation in civil aviation, tourism and trade. Yelekeyev emphasized that resuming flights would boost tourist flows, strengthen business ties and facilitate exports of Kazakh products to Kuwait.

Jazeera Airways reaffirmed its interest in the Kazakh market, saying it would consider resuming flights when the regional situation stabilizes and operating conditions become favorable.

The airline launched direct flights between Kuwait City and Almaty in 2021, but suspended the service later due to the regional situation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Claims Two Golds at U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Greco-Roman wrestlers have secured two gold medals at the U23 World Wrestling Championships on Oct. 14 in Las Vegas, with Aibek Aitbekov and Yusuf Ashrapov winning their finals and Temirlan Turdakyn advancing to the title bout.
