World.title: ‘Nostalgic exploitation’: South Ossetia’s new president sends schoolchildren to collect rosehips
World.content:
An initiative by Marat Kambolov, the new president of South Ossetia, to get schoolchildren to collect rosehips has drawn public criticism.

Photos and videos shared on the president’s official Telegram channel and in the media show children picking berries from thorny branches with their bare hands. In some images, they are even wearing school uniforms with white shirts. One girl is wearing a lace apron.

Kambolov came up with the idea in a fit of nostalgia for his own schooldays.

“When I saw how many rosehips we had this year, I immediately remembered Khaznidon, a village in North Ossetia. As children, we often ran up the mountain to collect them. It was a normal thing for us: climb higher, gather rosehips and bring them home.

“Of course, back then we didn’t think about vitamins or their health benefits. We simply grew up close to nature and made use of what it gave us. That is why I suggested organising this activity for our schoolchildren,” the president explained.

According to Kambolov, after he issued the relevant order, around 1,500 pupils in Years 8–11 across South Ossetia went out to collect rosehips. They gathered around 250kg in total, which the authorities will “distribute to medical facilities, educational institutions and social care homes”.

“Rosehips are a useful product, rich in vitamin C. People here have always collected them, dried them and brewed them into tea. But for me, this is about something else, too. I want our children to know their land, to see what it has to offer, to go into the mountains and understand that even something as simple as spending a few hours collecting rosehips can be worthwhile.

“We used to run into the mountains to collect them when we were boys ourselves. Years have passed, but rosehips still grow on our hillsides. And it is good to see the next generations collecting them now,” Kambolov said.

However, local bloggers did not share his enthusiasm for passing traditions down through the generations. They criticised the president’s idea as an example of exploiting schoolchildren in the Soviet style.

Blogger Sidamon, for example, wrote that he was curious to know “what genius came up with the idea of sending children to collect rosehips in brand-new school uniforms, when just a couple of months ago Kambolov ordered 10,000 roubles [around $119] to be allocated for their purchase?”

The fact that the children wore school uniforms also led the blogger to suspect that they collected the berries during school hours — or, more precisely, instead of attending lessons.

The author of another Telegram channel recalled taking part in “voluntary-compulsory activities” as a child. However, he said, at least “they organised them more competently back then”:

“At the appointed time, we would arrive at school in work clothes. They would put us on a bus and take us to the apple orchards, where we would be given all the equipment we needed.

“They could at least have given the schoolchildren in the photos some gloves. Anyone who has ever picked rosehips knows exactly why they have ‘thorn’ in their name.”

A teacher at a school in Tskhinval said the school administration had informed pupils in advance that they would collect rosehips on Saturday. She insisted that pupils from her school wore sportswear and gloves.

“That girl in the lace apron apparently didn’t know about it. I don’t know how she ended up there in her school uniform either. She isn’t from our school,” the teacher added.

She suspects the education ministry passed the president’s order on to schools, which then carried it out as they saw fit. In any case, she believes such mishaps are hardly surprising given the chaos surrounding the change of power.

“There is such confusion at our ministry. The government has resigned, and everyone is worried about keeping their jobs. No one knows who is responsible for what.”

The mother of one schoolchild, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said she disapproved of the practice of using children as an unpaid workforce. She was unhappy that the school had sent children to collect rosehips without consulting their parents, but said she “didn’t pursue the matter”.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: New Russian trade ban on Georgian goods: why now, and what risks do Georgian experts see?
World.content:
Russian embargo on Georgian goods

Russia has banned imports of products from seven Georgian companies. Alongside this decision, Moscow has again demanded that Tbilisi guarantee it will not use force against the occupied regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali, and agree to the demarcation of what Russia calls state borders.

Some Georgian experts believe Russia is using Georgia’s economic dependence as a lever for political pressure.

Meanwhile, the Georgian government says it does not know why Russia has imposed the trade restrictions and expects Moscow to reverse its decision.

These developments take on particular significance against the backdrop of the policies pursued by the Georgian Dream party. For years, the government has justified maintaining economic ties with Russia and refusing to join international sanctions on the grounds that this protects Georgia’s national interests. Experts, however, argue that this policy has failed to shield Georgian companies from Moscow’s unilateral trade decisions.

The key questions are why Moscow has acted now, what it may be seeking from the Georgian government, and how far this economic pressure could go.

What happened: ban targeting seven companies

A document issued by Russia’s consumer protection watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, and dated 9 October 2026, announces the temporary suspension of imports and sales in Russia of products from several Georgian companies. News of the decision emerged on 10 October.

The restrictions affect major Georgian companies Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, Askaneli Brothers, Wineman and Georgian Beer Company, as well as Coca-Cola and Nabeglavi beverages produced in Georgia.

The list of banned products includes wine, brandy, beer, soft drinks and mineral water.

It is important to note that Russia has not imposed a blanket ban on Georgian wine or other beverages. The restrictions apply only to products from specific manufacturers.

The Russian document describes the decision as a sanitary measure. However, it does not specify which violations the authorities allegedly found in the companies’ products or explain why they selected these particular manufacturers.

On 12 October, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government was working on the issue and hoped Russia would reverse the decision.

Parliamentary Speaker Shalva Papuashvili called the decision unexpected and said the Georgian authorities did not understand it. However, he stressed that the ban targeted specific companies rather than Georgian products as a whole.

Why now? Experts on Moscow’s possible motives

Georgian politicians and experts have linked Moscow’s decision to political pressure.

Giorgi Rukhadze, founder of the Centre for Strategic Analysis, believes Russia is reminding the Georgian government that it can use economic leverage against the country. In his assessment, Moscow has already secured significant foreign policy concessions and may now be seeking further steps.

“I think events are unfolding as one would expect. You know the saying: ‘Appetite comes with eating.’ Russia has secured all the concessions that Georgian Dream was willing to make on the Western front,” Rukhadze said.

The expert believes that Moscow benefits from Georgia’s deteriorating relations with the EU and its Western partners. At the same time, Georgia has become increasingly dependent on Russia economically and in the energy sector.

Rukhadze believes the new restrictions are a way of demonstrating this dependence:

“I am convinced that Georgian Dream already understands what the Kremlin wants from it. In my view, this is Russian blackmail — a way of showing that Moscow can completely destabilise Georgia’s economy. Clearly, this move did not come out of nowhere: there are issues on which the two sides cannot agree. It appears that Georgian Dream is dragging its feet on something and failing to meet certain commitments.”

Rukhadze identifies two possible issues: restoring rail links between Russia and Armenia through occupied Abkhazia, and providing guarantees of non-use of force to Sukhumi and Tskhinvali.

However, he stresses that more information is needed to establish the specific reason behind Moscow’s decision.

Abkhazia, non-use of force and the Russian embargo: what is the connection?

On 9 October, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin met with the co-chairs of the Geneva International Discussions. They discussed preparations for the next round of talks, scheduled for November.

According to an official statement from Russia’s Foreign Ministry, Moscow continues to demand that Georgia provide guarantees of non-use of force against Sukhumi and Tskhinvali. It also wants Tbilisi to begin delimiting the so-called state borders and subsequently demarcate them.

These demands have two distinct aspects.

The first concerns the non-use of force. The Geneva International Discussions were established after the August 2008 war, and security and non-use of force have remained permanent items on the agenda.

However, Tbilisi and Moscow fundamentally disagree over who should make the relevant commitments. Russia demands guarantees regarding Sukhumi and Tskhinvali, thereby placing responsibility on Tbilisi. Georgia, by contrast, insists that the main security problem is Russia’s military presence and occupation.

The second issue is even more serious. By demanding the delimitation of so-called state borders, Moscow treats Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as states independent of Georgia.

This contradicts the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity, which the overwhelming majority of the international community recognises.

Expert Teona Akubardia sees these two demands as part of Russia’s broader political strategy.

In her assessment, Moscow is trying to formalise its influence over Georgia in legal and political terms. “Its ultimate goal is to formalise its strategic control over Georgia — control that Russia already exercises in practice, even though it has not been legally formalised,” she said.

Akubardia believes that Russia’s economic restrictions, the issue of the occupied regions and Georgia’s deteriorating relations with the West should not be viewed as isolated developments.

In her view, opening a transit corridor through Abkhazia may also be linked to Moscow’s demands.

Giorgi Rukhadze has also pointed to this possibility.

Georgia’s parliamentary speaker, Shalva Papuashvili, offers a different interpretation. He notes that Russia’s demands are not new and that Moscow has raised them at the Geneva talks for many years.

“There is nothing new in this statement. At every meeting within the Geneva format, Russian representatives raise exactly the same issue. We, in turn, raise the questions of the return of displaced people, the withdrawal of Russian occupation forces and other matters,” he said.

Nevertheless, experts believe this does not rule out the possibility that Moscow is using new economic levers to pursue its long-standing objectives.

Gia Khukhashvili: ‘Dependence on the Russian market carries the risk of constant pressure’

Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili describes Russia’s decision as a familiar form of economic coercion.

“This is Russia’s brazen ‘sledgehammer’ approach,” he said.

Khukhashvili believes Moscow’s actions could have two consequences: increased pressure on Georgia’s government and business sector, and conditions that encourage informal deals and corruption.

He argues that companies may try to cultivate ties with influential figures in Russia to circumvent the restrictions. However, he has provided no specific evidence of corrupt deals.

Khukhashvili is particularly critical of business models that rely heavily on the Russian market.

“The problem is that our businesses — constantly chasing short-term gains and worrying about how to please the authorities — have still failed to understand that they cannot tie themselves to the market of an enemy country. They should have done everything possible to diversify these risks,” he said.

In his view, short-term profits from operating in Russia could ultimately lead to much greater losses.

“I would tell winemakers this: you cannot ‘reach an agreement’ with Russia. Today, you may make a few pennies, but tomorrow you could lose ten times as much. Leave the Russian market alone. Find people who speak English and target other markets. Forget Russia and explore new opportunities — otherwise, you will remain trapped in this situation forever,” he said.

Khukhashvili’s recommendation draws directly on economic data showing just how heavily Georgia’s wine industry depends on the Russian market.

Russia accounts for almost two-thirds of Georgian wine exports

Between January and August 2026, Georgia exported $102.2 million worth of wine to Russia. Total Georgian wine exports over the same period amounted to approximately $163.6 million.

Russia therefore accounted for around 62.5% of the total value of Georgian wine exports. By volume, its share stood at approximately 66.6%.

Russia remains the largest export market for Georgian wine, despite a decline in sales compared with the previous year.

Poland ranks second, with Georgian wine exports worth around $10.7 million. Ukraine, China, Kazakhstan and Germany follow, but export volumes to these countries remain far below those to Russia.

Losing the Russian market would affect producers differently. Tbilvino offers a clear example.

According to the company’s chief executive, Zurab Margvelashvili, who spoke to BM.ge, Tbilvino exports wine to around 30 countries and has relatively little dependence on the Russian market. A potential ban would therefore cause some financial losses, but the company does not expect serious damage.

Margvelashvili also notes that the company exports to markets with strict quality standards, while the Russian side has provided no detailed information about any specific violations.

Energy dependence: a more powerful lever than wine

Roman Gotsiridze, an opposition politician and former head of Georgia’s National Bank, has highlighted natural gas imports in the context of the current developments.

According to figures he cited, Russia accounted for 1.7% of Georgia’s natural gas consumption in 2018. That share rose to 20% in 2023 and 25% in 2024. Estimates put it at around 28% in 2025.

Gotsiridze believes this growing dependence gives Russia an additional lever for economic pressure.

Unlike wine exports, natural gas supplies directly affect energy security, industrial operations and people’s everyday needs.

Gotsiridze has therefore warned the government about possible scenarios involving more severe pressure from Russia.

Could Russia expand the embargo?

Mamuka Pipia, leader of the openly pro-Russian party Solidarity for Peace, says the ban on Georgian beverages represents only the first wave of restrictions.

In his view, further measures will target other companies and product categories.

His prediction deserves particular attention because Pipia represents a political force that takes a favourable view of Russia.

Teona Akubardia also points to an earlier statement by Pipia. She notes that he mentioned a list of Georgian companies accused of supporting anti-Russian activity as early as June.

If such a list did exist, it would be important to establish whether the companies named on it overlap with those now facing restrictions.

Georgian experts also consider it possible that Russia will expand its measures.

Gia Khukhashvili believes Moscow could use new restrictions to pressure Georgian businesses into exercising political caution. Giorgi Rukhadze suggests that the initial decision may be intended to demonstrate Russia’s capacity to exert economic pressure.

These assessments point to several possible scenarios. The restrictions could remain limited to the seven companies and be lifted following negotiations. They could spread to other producers. Alternatively, Russia could make the use of trade restrictions a permanent instrument of pressure.

How is Georgian Dream responding, and has its strategy worked?

The Georgian government insists that maintaining economic ties with Russia serves the country’s interests and that businesses should not give up profitable markets for political reasons.

Georgian Dream also argues that other countries have economic leverage over Georgia.

Commenting on Russia’s latest restrictions, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili also raised the risks associated with trade relations with the European Union. He pointed to issues involving sanctions, tariffs and the port of Kulevi.

The Georgian Dream government justified its decision not to join international sanctions against Russia by arguing that it needed to protect the Georgian economy. Kobakhidze described the decision as correct and pragmatic.

However, Georgian Dream’s opponents ask what additional security Georgia has gained by maintaining economic ties with Russia.

The restrictions introduced on 9 October have shown that economic relations with Russia do not guarantee Georgian companies unrestricted access to the Russian market. Moscow continues to demand the establishment of so-called state borders with the occupied regions. At the same time, Russia’s sanitary watchdog has restricted imports of products from Georgian companies.

Opposition politician Shalva Kereselidze, a member of the For Georgia party founded by Giorgi Gakharia, links the situation to Georgian Dream’s foreign policy. He argues that the government has damaged relations with the European Union while failing to protect Georgia’s economic and political interests in its dealings with Russia.

“Do not think that the more you concede to Russia, the more favourably it will view you or the sooner it will take your interests into account. No — the outcome will be even worse,” he said.

Russian embargo on Georgian goods

World.title: Azerbaijan, China discuss economic ties, security, Middle Corridor (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Azerbaijan and China have discussed expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and logistics, as well as the Middle Corridor’s role in strengthening regional and interregional connectivity.

This was reflected in the statement of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan published on its X account.

The issues were discussed at a meeting between Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who is on a working visit to Azerbaijan. The meeting took place as part of Wang Yi’s visit to Azerbaijan to attend the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), held under Azerbaijan’s chairmanship.

The ministers emphasized that the high-level dialogue, mutual trust, and friendship between our nations serve as the main driving force for our relations.

"The sides highly commended the rapid development of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership established in 2025. It was emphasized that the landmark agreements reached during the State Visit of the President of Azerbaijan to China provide a robust foundation for expanding ties as the two nations approach the 35th anniversary of their diplomatic relations in 2027," the post reads.

Ministers discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation in trade and economic relations, investment, energy, transport, logistics, and connectivity, highlighting Azerbaijan’s role as a key link between Asia and Europe and the growing importance of the Middle Corridor in strengthening regional and interregional connectivity.

The sides reaffirmed their commitment to mutual support within the UN, CICA, and other international platforms.

The ministers also exchanged views on the broader regional security situation and recent developments, emphasizing the importance of sustained dialogue, diplomatic engagement, and multilateral cooperation in addressing existing challenges.

In addition, Jeyhun Bayramov informed his counterpart about the peace process with Armenia and Azerbaijan’s post-conflict and rehabilitation efforts in the liberated territories.

World.title: Azeri Light falls 2.92% to $124.14 per barrel at Italy’s Augusta
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The price of Azerbaijani “Azeri Light” crude oil on CIF terms at the Italian port of Augusta fell by $3.73, or 2.92%, compared to the previous figure, reaching $124.14 per barrel, a source in the oil market told Trend.

According to the information, the price of a barrel of “Azeri Light” crude on FOB terms at the Turkish port of Ceyhan fell by $3.72, or 3.19%, to $112.79.

The price of Urals crude fell by $2.33, or 2.72%, compared to the previous figure, reaching $83.45 per barrel.

The price per barrel of Dated Brent crude, produced in the North Sea, fell by $2.97, or 2.28%, compared to the previous figure, reaching $127.55.

Azerbaijan’s 2026 state budget assumes an average oil price of $65 per barrel.

According to Trading Economics, oil prices approached the $94-per-barrel mark on Thursday, likely due to a technical correction and profit-taking by investors following five consecutive sessions of price gains.

"Investors also reacted to reports that the United States is considering easing sanctions on ships carrying oil and petroleum products from countries such as Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, which are part of the so-called ‘shadow fleet’, in an effort to lower record-high global freight rates.

However, the sinking of a container ship in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday after it was struck by unidentified missiles heightened concerns about supplies. At the same time, Iran-backed Houthis continue to launch missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Russia also accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries on Wednesday, including the Ryazan refinery with a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day. Moscow claims that the attacks violated the “energy truce” announced by U.S. President Donald Trump," the report states.

World.title: Kazakhstan targets 100M tons of transit cargo annually by 2035
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Kazakhstan plans to increase its seaport capacity fourfold, expand its fleet capacity fivefold, and raise annual transit cargo volumes to 100 million tons by 2035, the Kazakh government reported.

Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov announced the plans at the eighth New Silk Way Business Forum, held in Astana on October 15-16 as part of Kazakhstan Transport Week 2026.

"President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has identified the development of the country's transport and logistics potential as one of its strategic priorities. Modern transport infrastructure helps expand international trade, attract investment, establish new production facilities, and strengthen economic ties between countries," Bektenov said.

He noted that Kazakhstan is implementing a large-scale program to develop its transport infrastructure.

Over the past seven years, Kazakhstan has built and repaired 36,300 kilometers of roads. Over the past five years, it has also built and modernized 5,000 kilometers of railways.

The country is also developing its border, maritime, and airport infrastructure. Its aviation safety level has reached 95.7%, according to the government.

In 2025, transit cargo volumes through Kazakhstan increased by 18% year-on-year to 39.1 million tons.

Bektenov also highlighted opportunities to improve international logistics and strengthen connectivity along the East-West and North-South transport corridors, the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, and the prospective Trans-Afghan corridor.

He identified infrastructure development, logistics digitalization, and seamless transit as key areas for international cooperation.

Priorities include removing infrastructure bottlenecks and administrative barriers, as well as introducing "green corridors" and a "single window" principle to facilitate cross-border transportation and reduce cargo delivery times and costs.

Bektenov also emphasized the importance of joint investment and infrastructure projects.

World.title: Uzbekistan signs MoU with China’s CRRC Dalian on rail, metro cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Transport, state-owned railway company Uzbekistan Railways, and China’s CRRC Dalian have signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation in railway transportation and metro development in Tashkent on October 14.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Transport.

According to the Ministry, the agreement aims to support the modernization of Uzbekistan’s railway and metro systems through the procurement of modern rolling stock, the introduction of advanced technologies, and the development of cooperation in manufacturing and technical maintenance.

Additionally, the memorandum provides for the exchange of expertise and the implementation of prospective joint projects, according to the Uzbek side.

The parties intend to explore opportunities to strengthen cooperation in the production and servicing of railway and metro equipment, as well as introduce modern solutions to improve transport infrastructure.

The memorandum establishes a basis for further cooperation between the parties. Details on specific procurement volumes, project timelines, investment amounts, and the types of rolling stock to be supplied were not provided in the announcement.

Founded in 1899, CRRC Dalian Locomotive & Rolling Stock Co. is a Chinese state-owned manufacturer specializing in diesel and electric locomotives, diesel engines, and urban rail transit vehicles. The company develops and manufactures railway equipment for domestic and international markets and also provides locomotive repair and maintenance services.

World.title: Middle Corridor key to transport connectivity in Caucasus, Central Asia - IMF
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Middle Corridor is one of the key routes for transport connectivity in the Caucasus and Central Asia, Subir Lall, Deputy Director of the Middle East and Central Asia Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), told Trend during a briefing.

“However, there are a number of economic corridors linking the East and the West that will play an important role in the region’s integration with Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and other markets. Two aspects must be taken into account here. The first is ‘hard’ infrastructure, that is, roads and transportation links. The second, equally important aspect is ‘soft’ infrastructure,” he said.

Subir Lall noted that while excellent roads can be built, if cargo is delayed at borders for several days due to customs regulations and clearance procedures, this will slow the development of transport connectivity both within the region and beyond.

“Therefore, it is extremely important to promote the development of economic corridors passing through the region in such a way that all countries can participate in this process and reap its benefits.

At the same time, policymakers must pay special attention to regulatory frameworks, the compatibility of relevant rules, and their harmonization,” he added.

World.title: Trade diversification vital for Caucasus and Central Asia growth - IMF
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Trade diversification will play an important role for the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia, the Director of the Middle East and Central Asia Department at the International Monetary Fund, Jihad Azour told Trend.

“Trade diversification will play an important role amid the fragmentation of the global economy, helping countries in the region sustain and accelerate economic growth. This applies to both the countries of the Caucasus and Central Asia and to the states of the Middle East,” he said.

According to Azour, the second important area is transport connectivity.

“Amid the fragmentation of the global economy, the development of transport links is becoming one of the key priorities for these countries. It is necessary not only to overcome shortages resulting from external shocks but also to expand economic opportunities,” he said.

Azour noted that the third area is regional integration.

“It is becoming a new tool for expanding markets, developing infrastructure, and increasing the resilience of economies to external shocks. All of these areas are of great importance for shaping regional economic policy. The IMF is working with countries and regions to accelerate the implementation of relevant reforms,” he noted.

World.title: Middle Corridor investment could deepen region’s global integration - IMF
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Potential investments in the Middle Corridor offer countries in the region the prospect of deeper integration into the global economy, the Director of the Middle East and Central Asia Department at the International Monetary Fund, Jihad Azour said, Trend's correspondent reports.

“Over the past few years, most countries in Central Asia and the Caucasus have demonstrated higher rates of economic growth compared to the previous cycle, that is, the period before 2022, as well as compared to many other countries around the world,” he said.

Azour stated that these countries have reaped certain benefits thanks to the redirection of investment and migration flows, increased investment, and the reorientation of trade routes.

“As a result, in recent years, economic growth rates in these countries have been higher than in most other countries in the region. Although, according to our forecasts, growth rates will gradually converge in 2026–2027, at the same time we are observing certain differences in the economic dynamics of individual countries.

This is due to a combination of external factors and domestic conditions, including a solid institutional framework, the ability to effectively implement monetary and fiscal policies, as well as deeper coordination and cooperation among countries in the region," he added.

At the same time, as Azour noted, the acceleration of economic growth in recent years has also revealed risks of rising inflation.

“Therefore, we recommend that countries continue to pay special attention to containing inflation, using monetary policy as the primary tool for response.

Undoubtedly, various shocks and the increasing fragmentation of the global economy have heightened the appeal of regional cooperation, as well as the strengthening of these countries’ ties with the rest of the world.

Potential investments in the Middle Corridor and opportunities to expand trade with China, Europe, and even the Middle East open up prospects for the countries of the region to integrate more deeply into the global economy," he said.

Azour added that countries are already investing in the infrastructure needed to realize these opportunities.

“However, this process may take time. In addition to infrastructure investments, it will be necessary to improve the institutional environment, expand the role of the private sector, reform state-owned enterprises, and reduce the scope of the state’s presence in the economy,” he stated.

World.title: Ex-police officer found guilty of sexually touching colleagues without consent
World.content:
A former NSW Police officer has been found guilty of sexually touching three of his colleagues without their consent before resigning from the force.

A District Court jury found Matthew Stephen Cameron, 33, guilty on Thursday of five counts of sexual touching without consent, and not guilty of another count of sexual touching without consent.

The jury failed to reach a verdict on three other counts of sexual touching without consent and one count of sexual assault.

Each count of sexual touching carries a maximum penalty of five years in jail.

Cameron was initially charged with nine counts of sexual touching without consent and one count of sexual assault against three male colleagues.

The trial, which lasted three weeks, previously heard Cameron touched his younger colleagues' genitals without their consent during or after social gatherings between December 2021 and April 2023.

An official investigation into the allegations began in mid-2023.

Cameron has since resigned from the NSW Police Force.

Former police gay liaison officer

The court heard Cameron was a constable at Northern Beaches Police Area Command (PAC) at the time, where he worked with the three alleged victims.

The court heard all three complainants were probationary constables at the time of the alleged offences, and the Crown argued Cameron's position, being a more experienced officer of a higher rank, was an aggravating factor.

But the jury found Cameron not guilty of the aggravated sexual touching charges, instead finding him guilty of the five alternate charges of sexual touching without consent.

The court previously heard Cameron was an openly gay man, who was acting as the gay liaison officer at the Northern Beaches PAC, while the alleged victims were heterosexual men.

Do you know more? If you have any information about a story, contact Lia Harris.

Defence barrister Margaret Cunneen SC previously told the court her client "has a very different version of events" and maintained the sexual touching acts were "completely and quite enthusiastically consensual".

"There was no criminality in anything that took place at all," Ms Cunneen told the court.

"Mr Cameron is a person of utterly unblemished character."

Cameron previously took the stand during his trial and denied the sexual assault, telling the court the allegation that he gave one of the victim's oral sex without his consent was false and the sexual act never happened.

He will remain free on bail until his sentencing hearing in December, while the prosecution decides whether to pursue another trial on the remaining charges.

World.title: Manosphere experts warn if we lecture boys 'we lose them'
World.content:
If you're worried about the pull of the manosphere, but don't know how to help someone in your life who has been drawn in, you're not alone.

We asked a panel of experts to answer your common questions about the manosphere, masculinity and how to approach conversations about it.

Read what developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey, psychologist Dr Zac Seidler from Movember and Genevieve Sheppard from Our Watch had to say below.

If you or someone you know needs help, you can click here to find a full list of resources at the end of this article.

What is the manosphere?

According to experts, manosphere content often opposes feminism and includes "toxic attitudes" toward women. (ABC News: Magie Khameneh)

There's no single definition of the manosphere, but generally, it's the term used to describe online communities that promote narrow definitions of masculinity that oppose feminism and the gains of the gender-equality movement.

As UN Women describes, "these communities promote the idea that emotional control, material wealth, physical appearance and dominance, especially over women, are markers of male worth".

G Genevieve Sheppard The ideas in the manosphere are nothing new. Misogyny has been prevalent for a very long time. What’s different today is the reach and business model. Online platforms connect these groups, algorithms amplify their messages, and influencers can profit from attention and outrage. A recurring tactic of those who promote messages on the manosphere is to take real difficulties — loneliness, financial insecurity or uncertainty about relationships — and blame women and feminism. That offers a simple, yet inaccurate explanation, which also reinforces male entitlement and resentment. This is a harmful message for all young people to believe and absorb. To counter this, we need to address the challenges boys and men face while challenging the idea that women owe them sex, attention or obedience. That means well-resourced respectful relationships education in every school across Australia, supportive communities and opportunities to build belonging and connection without dominance.

What are the signs someone is in the manosphere and how can I help?

D Dr Zac Seidler Watching out for this stuff early and discussing it in an open and curious way is the best solution to staying connected with someone skirting around the edges of this content, as it pulls you in very quickly if you are in a certain headspace. Some things to look out for: New language: Terms like "alpha", "high value", "red pill", "simp" or "the matrix", or talking about women in transactional or contemptuous ways. One-source thinking: Constantly quoting the same few influencers, and treating them as the only people telling "the truth". Rising grievance: A growing sense that the world is rigged against men, or that women, feminism or "the system" are to blame for how they feel. Pulling back: Withdrawing from friends or family who disagree, or becoming dismissive and defensive when challenged (this can also be a sign of broader mental health challenges or a change in character). Rigid self-improvement: Gym, money and discipline aren't bad things. It's a flag when they come with shame, contempt for "weak" men, or the idea that your worth depends on dominance. Some recommendations for what to do: Stay close! Your relationship is the best antidote, but it's key to avoid shocking or shaming them. Get curious, not combative. What does he like about this guy? What does that video tell him about what it means to be successful and what it is giving him? Usually there's a real need underneath: loneliness, rejection, feeling lost or unseen. Don't try to win in one conversation. You won't argue your way to victory. Be consistent and caring. Offer an alternative. Take him out, show him the world, and help him interact with other people.

How can we challenge misogynistic views without alienating boys?

D Dr Billy Garvey This can be tough, and I fail at it too. Start with curiosity because correction often leads to conflict. "What makes you feel like that, mate?" If we lecture them, we lose them. Separate the belief from who they are. "You've got such a big heart mate, you're better than saying those things about girls and women". We hold the line while also keeping our belief in them as good people. Look for the underlying need. Many boys are lost and unhealthy messages hook them with the promise of confidence, power and success. Once we understand that, we can offer better pathways for them to meet these needs, and help them see those voices are chasing their own money, status and control. We can also share our own story, the traps we've fallen into, the hurt we've experienced and caused, and most importantly how we repaired and found a better way ourselves.

How can I approach this with my younger kids?

D Dr Billy Garvey These conversations can be scary but they are already happening for our kids without us there to guide them. Our best chance is to start with low pressure, when our kids feel safe, like during a walk around the block with just us or while playing together with no-one else around. We know body language, tone of voice and lack of judgement are just as important as what we actually say, if not more. Getting down to their eye level, sitting side by side facing the same direction, and keeping the conversation slow and casual helps. We also want to explore their experiences. "What do you think boys are like? What about girls?" is a gentle way to understand their beliefs without pressure or shame. We can also go first as a way for them to be safe too. "When I'm scared, sometimes I get angry. It doesn't help much so I try to work on asking others for help instead." It's also important this never feels like a single conversation we need to deliver perfectly. The most important part is that over time our children feel more safe to come to us for support in understanding their world.

Is the manosphere a 'passing wave' or something bigger?

According to experts, manosphere content often opposes feminism and includes "toxic attitudes" toward women. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

D Dr Zac Seidler Honestly, I don't think it's either/or yet. It's going to take time to understand how the moment we are in potentially differs from the gender reckonings that have come before, but it would be remiss of me not to say that this is in no way a 'passing wave', given the volume and ferocity of online misogyny fuelled by tech platforms. The underpinning themes have not changed, their reach has. What I see clinically is that the content itself is a symptom. Our research at Movember has told us that young men aren't drawn in by misogyny. They're drawn in by someone finally speaking to their loneliness, their sense of purpose and their worries about the future. The misogyny comes bundled with that, and therefore can probably be purposefully decoupled.

What are young men searching for in these spaces?

D Dr Zac Seidler Many young men are lonely, often more than they'd admit, and these spaces offer an instant sense of brotherhood. You're part of something, you share a language and someone's on your side. Then there's direction. Plenty of boys feel lost about who they're meant to be and where their life is heading. The manosphere gives them a clear script: Here's what a man is, here are the rules, here's the plan. When everything feels uncertain, that clarity is very attractive. Respect and status matter too. Young men want to feel they count and that people see them as capable. When that isn't happening at school, at work or in relationships, someone promising to make them "high value" is hard to ignore. Underneath many of these is a need to make sense of pain. Rejection, failure, anxiety and feeling invisible all hurt, and most boys haven't been given the words or the space to talk about that. These spaces give them an explanation and often someone to blame. That can feel better than sitting with the hurt. None of these needs are the problem. They're completely normal, healthy human needs. The problem is that the manosphere offers a distorted way of meeting them. If we want boys to walk away, we have to offer them real belonging, purpose and respect in their everyday lives.

World.title: Bird flu detected in seal, bird samples taken from remote southern island
World.content:
Bird flu has been detected in a seal and a gull on Macquarie Island, a remote outpost halfway between Tasmania and Antarctica.

Samples collected from a southern elephant seal and a kelp gull were returned with island personnel and subsequently tested, returning a positive result for H5 bird flu.

Tasmania's Minister for Environment and Climate Change Guy Barnett said in a statement on Thursday it was the "first recorded detection in a marine mammal in Tasmania".

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins told parliament three other species had returned negative tests, including skuas, giant petrels and penguins.

She also said there had been no signs of any mass mortality events among the island's wildlife at this stage.

Ms Collins said the samples from the southern elephant seal and kelp gull would undergo further testing at a CSIRO laboratory.

The subantarctic island, 1,500 kilometres south-east of Hobart, is a World Heritage-listed wildlife sanctuary with up to 4 million seabirds and 100,000 seals.

In August, the ABC reported the Australian Antarctic Division planned to extract personnel from Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean due to the psychological risk posed by a potential outbreak of bird flu.

It is feared up to 90 per cent of baby elephant seals could perish, as happened on Heard Island over summer, where more than 13,000 pups are believed to have died from bird flu.

Macquarie Island expeditioners to be evacuated over bird flu fears The Australian Antarctic Division will launch a mission to extract personnel from Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean due to the psychological risk posed by a potential outbreak of bird flu at the remote wildlife sanctuary.

As bird flu continues to be detected in Tasmania, members of the public are being encouraged to continue reporting sick or dead birds.

"Reports play an important role in helping authorities detect and respond to potential cases," Mr Barnett said.

Avoid contact with sick or dead birds and report sightings through the government's website or by calling the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania provides regular public updates through media releases.

The latest testing and surveillance figures are updated on the department's website.

World.title: Breaking: Grandmother wins fight for inquest into murders of children by their mother
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the deaths of three children killed by their mother in Port Hedland has been requested by WA's Attorney General, after a sustained campaign led by their grandmother for answers and ongoing political pressure.

Margaret Hawke was sentenced to life in prison for the 2022 murders of the children aged 10, 7, and four months.

Tributes at the burial site of the three children in WA's north. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

It emerged during court proceedings that Hawke had sought help from a women's refuge the night before the murders, but was told by staff they did not have the capacity to assist.

The children's grandmother Dorothy Papertalk had called for an inquest into their deaths, a request denied by then coroner Phil Urquhart last year.

WA Attorney General Tony Buti had repeatedly said he was unable to order an inquest into the killings without new evidence, even releasing private legal advice on the matter.

That advice had been challenged by some of the state's top legal minds, including former Governor Malcolm McCusker KC and former president of the WA Children's Court Denis Reynolds, who said they believed Mr Buti did have the power to order the inquest.

Today Mr Buti said he had reviewed files related to the children's death, which he described as "heartbreaking".

"I'm now satisfied there is new evidence and circumstances that were not considered by the former coroner Philip Urquhart in his decision not to conduct an inquest," he said.

He said he had written to the current coroner requesting an inquest.

World.title: Man charged with 16yo girl's murder in remote NT community
World.content:
A 26-year-old man has faced Darwin Local Court over the alleged murder of a 16-year-old girl in a remote Northern Territory community.

Ashton Chungaloo has been in police custody since the alleged incident at Alpurrurulam on Monday.

This morning he was charged over the death of the teenage girl, who police say he was believed to be in a domestic relationship with.

Mr Chungaloo did not appear in court and did not seek bail.

His defence lawyer proposed that the matter should be shifted to Alice Springs, which Justice Stephen Ledek agreed to.

The remote NT community of Alpurrurulam is located near the Queensland-Northern Territory border. (ABC News: Victoria Pengilley)

Northern Territory Police, assisted by officers from Queensland, responded to the incident. Crime Command and Forensics also travelled to the community to investigate the death.

There has not been a permanent police station in the dry community since 2018, with the closest officers stationed 170 kilometres away at remote Avon Downs.

NT Police said a local clinic made a report at about 5:30am on Monday that a girl had died there.

Alpurrurulam is about 1,500 kilometres south-east of Darwin, and less than 20km from the Queensland border.

Mr Chungaloo will return to court on December 10 in Alice Springs.

World.title: Breaking: Person of interest identified after recording device found on navy ship
World.content:
An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest, after a recording device was found in the women's bathroom of a navy ship.

The device was discovered on October 11, on HMAS Leeuwin while it was docked in Cairns.

In a statement, Defence said the person was now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries.

"Navy's focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident," it said.

Chief of Navy Vice Admiral Matt Buckley labelled the incident a "despicable betrayal of trust".

"To provide assurance to all personnel Fleet Commander is undertaking a 100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet," Vice Admiral Buckley said in a statement.

" You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. "

The device was discovered on October 11, on HMAS Leeuwin while it was docked in Cairns. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

The alleged incident has prompted a cascade of political reaction from Canberra today.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the incident was "unacceptable".

"I can't speak to how widespread that is. What I can say is that those instances are utterly unacceptable," he said.

Recording device found in cabin of navy ship The recording device was discovered in female "shower facilities" on board the HMAS Leeuwin while it was stationed near Cairns.

Tasmanian senator Jacqui Lambie said Defence should "clean up" its culture, and called for an independent body to be established outside of the ADF to deal with the matter.

"The only way we're going to be able to stop this is by taking it out of Defence's hands and having an independent body that actually deals with this," Ms Lambie said.

Communications minister Anika Wells told ABC's New Breakfast it was "horrible".

"I really feel for all of the people on that ship who are learning this and the people that may have been victims of this act," she said.

"I would say [to the victims] you deserve to feel safe in your workplace and the rise of tech facilitated abuse … is horrific."

World.title: Child support worker guilty of 'snap' assault on autistic son
World.content:
A children's domestic violence support worker has been found guilty of punching her autistic teenage son in the face in a "snap" assault.

The 39-year-old woman, who cannot be named to protect the identity of her son, pleaded guilty to assault occasioning bodily harm in Hervey Bay District Court today.

At the time of the offence in January last year, the woman had worked for seven years at a support service for children who had experienced or who were at risk of harm, the court heard.

The woman's barrister, Lara Soldi, told the court that, at the time, her client had accepted a job with another organisation as a specialist domestic violence practitioner, and was "troubled" by the prospect of leaving her long-time employer.

The woman sat in the dock weeping as Crown prosecutor Joshua Francis read the facts of the case.

On the day of the incident, she had returned to her Hervey Bay home after spending the day managing a client who had been arguing with their child, the court heard.

She had been "pacing and crying" at home when she got into an argument with her son.

The court heard the boy had been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, and the woman "felt intimidated by him" because he weighed about 89 kilograms.

Ms Soldi said the woman began hyperventilating during the argument "and then effectively snapped".

The court heard the woman threw her phone at her son, rushed towards him and punched him in the nose and cheek.

Mr Francis told the court the boy sustained a deviated septum, nosebleeds and bruising to his eye sockets.

Following the assault, the boy packed his belongings and went to his father's home, where he had stayed since the incident.

Mr Francis said the boy had not spoken with his mother again during that time.

Ms Soldi told the court her client was a victim of domestic violence herself, perpetrated by her father and a former partner, and that was the reason she had chosen to work in the domestic violence support field.

The woman was remorseful for her actions and her blue card was cancelled because of the incident, Ms Soldi said.

"She knows how serious this is … given her education and her work history, this is not lost on her," she said.

Judge Nathan Jarro said it was "very ironic" that someone who had worked for a children's domestic violence support service had offended against her own son.

"'Surprising' and 'disappointing' are also adjectives that arise," Ms Soldi said.

Judge Jarro sentenced the woman to 18 months' probation and ordered her to pay $3,000 in compensation to her son by June next year.

No conviction was recorded.

World.title: Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days
World.content:
An Australian citizen is among 30 people unlawfully held in immigration detention in the last financial year, according to a Commonwealth Ombudsman report.

The person, named as Mx B, was wrongfully detained by Home Affairs for 945 days — two and a half years — due to incorrect reading of Australia's citizenship laws.

Mx B was born in Australia in 1989 to New Zealand parents, briefly left, then returned in 1992, and should have been granted automatic citizenship on their 10th birthday in accordance with the Citizenship Act. But this did not occur due to "poor record keeping".

The ombudsman report sets out a litany of departmental errors, incorrect assumptions and failed checks spanning four decades.

Three incorrect citizenship assessments

After growing up in Australia, Mx B was convicted of criminal offences and sentenced to prison in 2010 at the age of 21.

In 2018, while in jail, Home Affairs carried out a citizenship status assessment and incorrectly found Mx B was not an Australian citizen, due to their brief departure from the country as a baby.

"They [Mx B] were assessed as not having been ordinarily resident [in Australia] for the first 10 years of their life," the ombudsman report said.

"Officers failed to consider relevant case law about absences from Australia."

Fears migration changes may fuel coervice control A crackdown on overstayers is part of both federal government and opposition migration plans. But advocates against domestic and family violence warn it may worsen the situation for many.

In 2019, the department, acting on the mistaken understanding that Mx B was a New Zealand citizen in Australia on a special category visa, considered whether to cancel Mx B's visa on character grounds, but found their visa had ended in the 1990s.

A second citizenship assessment again determined Mx B was not a citizen, which the ombudsman described as another "failure to consider all available information and relevant case law".

Upon Mx B's release from jail in 2022, the department placed them into immigration detention.

"Mx B claimed to be an Australian citizen on multiple occasions throughout their detention," the ombudsman report stated.

In 2024, Mx B's legal representative sent the department correspondence regarding Mx B's claimed Australian citizenship.

"The Department completed a further citizenship status assessment for Mx B based on existing information in its systems," the report states.

For the third time, the department determined Mx B was not an Australian citizen, "failing to take into account the new information indicated by Mx B's legal representative".

Eventual release after High Court NZYQ ruling

In November 2023, the High Court's NZYQ ruling found the indefinite detention of non-citizens where there was no reasonable prospect of removal was illegal.

That triggered the release of more than 300 people from immigration detention.

Mx B was not one of them, remaining in detention until April 2025, when the New Zealand government told the Home Affairs department that Mx B was not a New Zealand citizen.

High Court decision could lead to large immigration claims There are warnings a High Court ruling allowing a man to sue for false imprisonment over his indefinite immigration detention will lead to more claims running into the tens of millions of dollars.

"The Department subsequently found Mx B to be affected by the outcome in NZYQ because their removal from Australia was not reasonably practicable in the foreseeable future," the ombudsman report said.

"On the same day, the Department granted Mx B a Removal Pending bridging visa on strict conditions and released them from held detention."

A fourth and final citizenship assessment found that Mx B was an Australian citizen.

'Mx A' wrongfully detained for 304 days

Mx B is not alone. The ombudsman report found 30 out of the 4,247 people placed into immigration detention between July 2024 and June 2025 were unlawfully detained.

Of those, 60 per cent of cases were due to a delay in communicating a ministerial visa approval to the department, leaving 18 people in unlawful detention for one day.

One individual, known as Mx A, was wrongfully detained for 304 days due to a decision maker's "incorrect understanding of the law".

Of those affected, none have filed compensation claims against the government.

The report has made three recommendations, including that the department work with the Home Affairs minister to "formalise policies and procedures relating to the communication of Ministerial intervention decision".

It also recommended Home Affairs apologise to those impacted.

The Home Affairs department has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Greens senator takes leave after letter raises allegations of inappropriate comments to women
World.content:

Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Greens’ disability spokesman Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the Greens party room as new party leader David Shoebridge has ordered an independent investigation into allegations from party members that the WA senator made multiple inappropriate comments to women. In a letter sent to Shoebridge on Tuesday night and seen by this masthead, seven current Greens members write that the group are aware of “multiple allegations” against Steele-John between 2017 and 2025. Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Jordon Steele-John in the Senate on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen “We have been made aware of multiple allegations ... being made against WA Federal Senator, Jordon Steele-John spanning almost a decade (2017-2025). These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to … be alone with him,” the authors state. “These warnings have come from inside and outside the party, demonstrating that knowledge of his alleged reputation extends beyond party membership and out into the community.”



The signatories include five current and former staffers and two active branch members. This masthead is aware of the identity of the authors of the letter sent to Greens party leaders this week but has chosen not to name them to protect their privacy, and in some cases to protect their current employment. In response to inquiries from this masthead about the range of allegations in the letter, Shoebridge announced that Steele-John was taking leave from the Greens party room. It was not clear if that included taking leave from parliament. Senator Jordon Steele-John talking with party leader David Shoebridge. Alex Ellinghausen Steele-John said that “I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not. I have referred this matter to the WA Greens, so that a fair, independent process can be commissioned that upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved. “These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it. The letter says that victims of sexual and family violence should be at the centre of any investigation. I agree. In the one complaint of which I have been made aware, I am the person who experienced family violence.”



Steele-John stated that he believed one of the allegations related to a former partner. “I believe an allegation arises from a former relationship in which I was the victim of extensive, prolonged and deeply distressing domestic abuse ... I have been working with WA Police to address the abuse I have experienced.” Deputy Greens leader Senator Steph Hodgins-May and Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge, who said it was not up to him to determine if findings of the inquiry would be made public. Alex Ellinghausen Shoebridge, said the Greens took allegations of this nature extremely seriously. “This matter needs to be resolved via a fair and independent review that ensures all parties are entitled to natural justice and procedural fairness,” he said.



“The Australian Greens take complaints seriously, and as leader I want to make it clear that the integrity of the complaints process is essential. In the circumstances Senator Steele-John has requested leave from the Party Room and I have accepted it.” A spokesman for Shoebridge said the investigation into Steele-John would be funded by the Western Australian branch of the Greens but it would be conducted by an independent third party. Steele-John is one of the best-known Greens senators in parliament and, as spokesman for disability and mental health, he has led the party’s campaign against Labor’s cuts to the NDIS. He entered parliament in November 2017 aged 23, the youngest senator ever at the time, through a casual vacancy created when Scott Ludlam resigned from the Senate after discovering he was ineligible as a dual citizen.



In the letter seen by this masthead, the authors state “many of us joined the Greens because of their strong public position to believe women. This should be the premise upon which an investigation is commenced. “Any allegation ... levelled against anyone in the party must be investigated thoroughly and with the victim at the centre. It must also be investigated from our public position of believing the courageous women who make these reports.” The authors ask Shoebridge to take three steps: commission an independent investigation into every allegation against Steele-John; require the party to update protocols so the threshold for acting on allegations does not rely on police charges; and notify all signatories to the letter of the outcome of the investigation. The letter notes that “all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the Party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations.” The authors go on to claim that “for every person brave enough to sign this letter, there are multiple others who were too fearful of backlash by Senator Steele-John and others in the party to sign on. This is power in action, silencing those who want to be heard, but who feel too unsafe to speak.”



And it concludes by reminding Shoebridge that he had recently posted to his Instagram account that “men need to speak up. In the clubrooms, at the pub, on our streets. Demand better from our mates, our team, our colleagues.” The authors then state: “This is us demanding better from our party.” Senator Jordon Steele-John at the start of his parliamentary career with then-leader Richard Di Natale. Andrew Meares The allegations about Steele-John’s conduct present a challenge to Shoebridge, who has promised to be more consultative with Greens party members and has outlined plans for his party to take the fight to Labor, rather than simply support government legislation. At a press conference in Canberra on Thursday afternoon, Shoebridge said he was not previously aware of the allegations reported by this masthead against Steele-John.



“No, I received the correspondence in my capacity as leader of the Australian Greens, and I’ve dealt with it with … urgency,” he said. Shoebridge said would be “inappropriate” for him to determine if the findings of the inquiry into the allegations would be made public. “This will be an independent inquiry, and it would be totally inappropriate for me to determine how that inquiry is undertaken,” Shoebridge said. “But I stress, the key parameters for this inquiry are fair, and independent, and timely.” Shoebridge said that he had confidence the inquiry would be independent, which was “necessary for all parties to be involved”. “It is not my role, and it would be inappropriate for me, as the leader of the Australian Greens in the federal parliament, to be imposing controls on that.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Golden Dragon Mining has unearthed a substantial 2.2-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly from recent auger drilling at its Stella Range project outside Laverton in Western Australia.

The untested discovery sits in a well-endowed gold neighbourhood, 120km southeast of the prolific Laverton goldfield and just 12km along strike from Brightstar Resources’ Lord Byron deposit, which hosts 5.39 million tonnes grading 1.5 grams per tonne (g/t) for 267,000 ounces of gold.

Golden Dragon Mining’s auger drilling has defined a 2.2km-long gold anomaly at its Stella Range project outside Laverton in Western Australia.

The company says the coherent, northwest-trending anomaly is also supported by key pathfinder elements, particularly copper and tellurium. The geology adds further weight to the discovery, with Stella Range’s main gold anomaly sitting within a magnetic low that mirrors the setting at Lord Byron. The anomaly is also interpreted to lie on the same northwest-trending magnetic corridor as the deposit, raising the prospect of a similar gold-bearing system lurking beneath the surface.

The ground was previously explored by the likes of BHP for large komatiite-style nickel sulphide deposits, with Golden Dragon taking a different tack after reviewing the historical work through a gold-tinted lens.

World.title: The Renshaw influence behind breakout star’s shock push for World Cup berth
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket The Renshaw influence behind breakout star’s shock push for World Cup berth Nick Wright October 15, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Matthew Renshaw’s influence on Australian cricket is stretching beyond his first Test heroics in South Africa, with breakout one-day gun Hugh Weibgen shedding light on how the reborn batsman has shaped his own international ambitions. As Renshaw spearheaded the nation to a 214-run victory, Weibgen was pushing his credentials for a shock 2027 World Cup berth – striking back-to-back centuries for Queensland in the unfamiliar position of opener, as he seeks to turn his hyped talent into a dominant career. The 21-year-old’s first ton of the summer came against a New South Wales attack boasting Australian limited overs stars Sean Abbott and Ben Dwarshuis, while his second against Western Australia anchored the Bulls’ innings of 261 to inspire a 15-run win. Hugh Weibgen, pictured in action for Australia at the 2024 Under-19s World Cup, has begun to capitalise on his potential with back-to-bakc centuries for Queensland. Gallo Images Australia currently sits fourth in the ODI rankings, however their form in the 50-over game has been patchy at best, winning just four of 12 series since their 2023 World Cup triumph in India.



Only one Australian – Travis Head – is within the world’s top-20 ranked batsmen (17), as the nation hunts for its winning formula following the retirements of Steve Smith, David Warner and Glenn Maxwell from the XI who claimed the trophy. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Pick and stick’: Waugh urges Aussie selectors to stop ‘messing about’ Weibgen, who led the nation to Under-19s World Cup glory in 2024, told this masthead he would not look too far ahead, despite selectors showing a willingness to throw younger men into the fray – headlined by Ollie Peake, who has played more one-day cricket for Australia than his state Victoria (eight of 15 total games). “Obviously, you dream to play for Australia one day, so you think about that, but I haven’t really given it too much thought. I’m just trying to win games for Queensland, and if I can do that, I’m sure that will take care of itself,” he said. But Weibgen revealed it was Renshaw’s recommendation to link him with the same psychologist who has helped inspire his own ascent to an Australian three-format player which has laid the foundations for the rookie to propel himself towards being in the conversation for higher honours.



Renshaw has previously stressed the key to his resurgence across the short and long cricket codes stemmed from a more relaxed outlook to his game, with life off the pitch more stable than when he was younger and in a mental bubble pushing for greater success. That new outlook has coincided with T20 international selection and ODI success (including a maiden century against Zimbabwe last month), before culminating in his match-winning 190 and 82 in the first South Africa Test. Loading It was a lesson his fellow Brisbane Grammar School alumnus was eager to take on board, who has since consulted Stuart Smith “a couple of times a week” for the past year-and-a-half. “I put lots of time into batting, bowling and fielding, and those things like recovery, but I probably didn’t have that consistent mental training. I was already thinking of going down that route, and then simply asked Rens if he saw someone, and he flicked me through the details,” Weibgen said.



“It’s helping me unlock the most positive version of myself whilst I’m batting. I guess having other stuff go on in my life, it’s always good for me to find that balance. I’m always on the side of cricket is everything, but having that balance has been a lot better and probably healthier. “But the big focus is how can I improve in that batting side of things and deal with the highs and lows and try stay nice and level.” A self-confessed cricket tragic who actively seeks out his childhood idol Mike Hussey whenever he is nearby, Weigben’s determination to cement himself as a future linchpin of Australian cricket meant he barely had an off season. A winter spent playing club cricket in England was followed by his inclusion in a development tour to India as he sought to hone his craft. Those experiences supported two development areas. In the UK, he took a more positive, attacking approach to his batting, while in India, he broadened his stroke play – including “a couple of sweep shots” – to improve his prospects against spin bowling.



While the World Cup is still 12 months away, and the right-hander is still very much in the fledgling stages of his career, Weigben sensed the conditions he had been exposed to would pave the way to become a more consistent contributor in Bulls – and ideally, Australian – colours. “Being put in different positions, batting in different spots in the order and different conditions all helps add to your craft, learning your own game plan and what you need to do in different situations,” he said. “All those experiences have definitely helped me.” Queensland faces South Australia in the One-Day Cup from 10am AEST on Thursday. World.title: Broken Hill lines up drill bit on huge copper-gold target in SA
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill lines up drill bit on huge copper-gold target in SA Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd October 15, 2026 — 4:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Broken Hill Gold has launched a 3000-metre drilling campaign at its White Dam project in South Australia to test a major geophysical target lurking beneath recent high-grade copper-gold hits, raising the tantalising prospect of linking several deposits into one large system. The company’s latest induced polarisation (IP) and ground magnetic surveys have outlined a robust 1.5-square-kilometre chargeability anomaly coinciding with a one-square-kilometre magnetic anomaly beneath its Icebreaker discovery, suggesting the once gold-focused project could be emerging as a massive copper-gold system at depth. Broken Hill Gold’s geophysical surveys have outlined a large, deep target at its White Dam project in South Australia. With drilling set to kick off this weekend, Broken Hill is poised to put its compelling new target to the test in a rapidly emerging iron ore copper gold (IOCG) province, where the potential for major discoveries has major players circling. The discovery of a high-grade sulphide system at Icebreaker came about almost entirely by accident, after the company punched through its shallow, 20,400-ounce oxide gold resource into a richer gold-copper sulphide zone below.



‘We now have coincident IP and magnetic anomalies over a large area, in a zone we already know is well mineralised’ Broken Hill Gold chief executive officer Matthew Boyes Now, the geophysics suggests Icebreaker could be just the tip of the iceberg. The IP survey defined two key features, including a shallower northwestern anomaly sitting directly beneath high-grade sulphide mineralisation already struck at Icebreaker, pointing to potential extensions of the known copper-gold system both at depth and along strike. However, a deeper and much stronger eastern anomaly is shaping up as the main prize. It shows a chargeability reading six times the background level and trends north from the edge of another historic Hannaford deposit. A ground magnetic survey has also defined a hefty one-square-kilometre high-intensity feature coinciding with the IP chargeability anomalies, which the company says points to iron oxide alteration, consistent with the magnetite-pyrite alteration observed at Icebreaker and a hallmark of large IOCG deposits. Broken Hill Gold chief executive officer Matthew Boyes said: “This is an excellent result, delivered in a very short turnaround time, and the geophysics crews have performed exceptionally. We now have coincident IP and magnetic anomalies over a large area, in a zone we already know is well mineralised – that is an extremely compelling set of drill targets. The strength and consistency of the IP anomaly makes it an outstanding target in its own right.” The project sits within South Australia’s Curnamona Province, a region renowned for its major IOCG deposits. Havilah Resources’ Kalkaroo project, just 40km north of White Dam, hosts a massive 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold, alongside 23,200 tonnes of cobalt. That project has now attracted heavyweight interest, with Sandfire Resources securing the right to acquire an 80 per cent stake for consideration of up to A$222.6 million, while committing a further A$30 million to regional exploration.



Importantly, the existing Hannaford deposit, which hosts a resource of 43,300 ounces of gold, along with the Icebreaker and Rolling prospects, all sit around the margins of the combined geophysical anomalies. Their positioning suggests they could form part of a single, much bigger alteration system that remains largely untested at depth, with most historical drilling averaging just 50m. The company is now preparing to put the theory to the test with an initial reverse circulation (RC) and diamond drilling campaign designed to probe the system at depth for the first time. Deeper diamond holes will reach depths of up to 400m, providing the first serious test of both the northwestern and main eastern induced polarisation (IP) anomalies. With White Dam continuing to produce gold doré and offering a potential pathway to self-funded exploration, Broken Hill has an enviable platform from which to chase a much bigger prize. If the drill bit backs up the geophysics, the company could be on the cusp of transforming White Dam from a modest gold producer into a much bigger copper-gold story, with Icebreaker potentially opening the door to a district-scale discovery.
