World.title: Kmart sold fingernail glue that burnt without safety warnings, watchdog says
World.content:
Breaking BusinessConsumer affairsConsumer safety Kmart sold fingernail glue that burnt without safety warnings, watchdog says Elias Visontay and Jessica Yun Updated October 15, 2026 — 4:23pm ,first published 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The consumer watchdog has taken Kmart to court alleging the retailer sold millions of bottles of glue used for fake fingernails without adequately warning customers about burn risks. Customers, including children, claimed they suffered third-degree burns and required hospitalisation and in some cases skin grafts to treat injuries caused by Kmart’s home brand OXX nail glue, according to Federal Court legal documents filed by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on Thursday. The ACCC has taken legal action against Kmart. iStock In addition to burning skin, consumers complained the glue caused steaming, smoking, burning or melting when it came into contact with fabric. The ACCC is alleging Kmart breached consumer law in selling seven varieties of its OXX nail glue. Even through it received more than 50 customer complaints between August 2017 and December 2024, Kmart continued selling the products without disclosing burn risk warnings, the ACCC said. It updated its packaging in December 2024, but continued selling pre-existing products without the warning until February 2025, court documents said.



“It’s a chemical reaction, in essence, where the glue comes into contact with fabric,” ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe told this masthead. Related Article Consumer rights ‘Left with no choice’: Amazon accused of ripping off Prime customers with ads “Let’s say, for example, you were applying the product onto your hands, and you were wearing a pair of trousers. If the product dripped onto the trouser, that’s where the reaction would occur … if the fabric is on your skin, it burns, and in some instances, can stick.” The product is still for sale on Kmart’s website. Kmart has been contacted for comment. There was no information about the risk of burns on either the packaging or the bottle, despite containing instructions and other safety warnings about avoiding contact with skin and eyes; using the product with irritated or infected nails or skin; and when to seek medical advice if the glue came into contact with eyes or was swallowed, the ACCC alleged.



“Not all consumers can afford to go regularly to the nail salon to have these products applied professionally. However, we expect that consumers will be warned about material risks that they are engaging with, so they can make a choice at the time of purchase about whether or not they are comfortable to take on that risk,” said Lowe. “That opportunity, we say, was not provided to consumers in this instance.” Lowe said it was an “incredibly serious matter” that Kmart failed to warn customers of burn risks, despite receiving numerous reports of burn injuries. “The intention is the warning is immediately visible to consumers as they’re scanning the range of products on shelves,” she said. “We expect all businesses, especially large businesses like Kmart, to have consumer safety front of mind, and withholding safety information can amount to false or misleading representations in breach of the Australian consumer law.” The ACCC’s legal action also alleges additional breaches of consumer law related to Kmart selling button batteries in kids digital watches and GPS smart tags for tracking.



Button batteries are small flat discs that have a history of causing death and serious injury in children who unwittingly swallow them. They can burn through the oesophagus within hours of being ingested. Related Video Video icon 1:46 Urgent warning over potentially deadly button batteries While products containing button batteries are legal to sell, there are strict information standards requiring labelling to warn parents of the potential danger. The ACCC has alleged Kmart failed in its requirement to conduct safety feature testing for two models of Anko kids digital watches and seven models of analogue watches prior to selling them to customers. It sold about 64,000 of the button battery-powered watches between June 2022 and November 2024.



“These watches contained button batteries, but Kmart did not test them prior to supply to show that young children could not open the battery compartments. This is despite many of the watches being specifically designed for children,” Lowe said. The ACCC claims Kmart sold 800 Anko-branded GPS tracking tags that did not comply with safety standards because they carried some but not all warnings required by the law. A Kmart spokeswoman said the company was “disappointed at [the ACCC’s] decision to take action on historical matters” given the retailer had cooperated with the watchdog’s investigation and had addressed the issues. In relation to the fingernail glue products, the spokeswoman said:“We regret any injury associated with these products and apologise to anyone affected.” “Kmart remains of the view the labelling and warnings were appropriate to prevent misuse. We take our reporting obligations seriously and submitted mandatory injury reports about these products to the ACCC,” the spokeswoman said.



Under consumer law, selling products without mandatory safety information carries a maximum penalty of $100 million for a company. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Augustus circles giant PNG gold prize in Porgera backyard
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Augustus circles giant PNG gold prize in Porgera backyard Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 15, 2026 — 4:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Augustus Minerals has its sights firmly set on elephant country, updating the market on its strategic push into Papua New Guinea (PNG), where it’s angling to secure the highly prospective 2.5-million-ounces gold equivalent Mt Kare gold-silver project, a stone’s throw from one of the world’s most significant gold mines. The company’s subsidiary, ACM PNG, holds a “second-in-time” exploration licence application over the Mt Kare project, positioned a mere 15 kilometres from Barrick Gold’s colossal 32-million-ounce Porgera gold mine. Brian Rodan, executive chairman of Augustus Minerals, holding drill core from the 2.5-million-ounce Mt Kare gold-silver project in PNG. The geological credentials of Mt Kare are particularly compelling. The project is classed as a rare alkalic-epithermal gold deposit, a geological clan that hosts some of the planet’s most lucrative members such as PNG’s own Lihir mine, with a hefty 47 million gold ounces and the Cadia-Ridgeway system in New South Wales, featuring more than 50 million ounces. In the past, Mt Kare has thrown up some monster drill hits including 111m at 9.8 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 4m and 17.7m at 100g/t gold from 59m, along with a coffee-spitting 20m at 443g/t gold - the sorts of numbers that would get the West Perth mining fraternity leaping out of bed each morning.



‘Augustus holds an opportunity to potentially secure future access to the world-class Mt Kare gold project.’ Augustus Minerals executive chairman Brian Rodan Augustus says Mt Kare and Porgera are geological cousins, both sitting within the 2300km-long New Guinea Metallogenic Belt. The company’s modelling suggests Mt Kare may represent a higher-level, less-eroded expression of a much larger, deep-seated gold system, with the world-class Porgera mine representing the deeper root of a similar system. Notably, the Mt Kare deposit is about 500 metres higher in elevation than Porgera, while historical drilling has only tested to about 350m below the surface, leaving its deeper gold potential largely untested. First discovered in 1987, the project boasts a rich exploration history and an extraordinary early gold rush. Between 1988 and 1991, an estimated one million ounces of alluvial gold were reportedly recovered from the area by some 3000 artisanal miners, highlighting the sheer richness of the system. Previous owners have reportedly sunk $60 million into exploration, including 350 diamond holes. Augustus is now leveraging this wealth of information after purchasing all available open-file data from PNG’s Mineral Resources Authority. It has since compiled a full technical memorandum on the project’s history, geology and mineralisation.



While the prize is immense, the path to securing it is complex. The Mt Kare application is contested, with Augustus currently second in line. Crucially, it’s not necessarily first in best dressed, with the government having the final say on who secures the coveted exploration licence. Its assessment considers a raft of criteria, including technical expertise, financial capacity, proposed work programs, landowner support and consent and compliance with environmental and statutory requirements. So the company isn’t sitting idly by, waiting for a decision from bureaucrats. Notably, Augustus’ executive chairman Brian Rodan, a mining veteran with half a century of industry experience, has some previous form at Mt Kare. He was the managing director of mining contractor ACM PNG when it was awarded a contract in 2012 to do the stage-one underground drilling and all important mine development at the project, ticking several big boxes on the government’s wish list. Ticking a further but equally important box, the company has also been actively building relationships on the ground, a critical component for success in PNG. The company’s management has held numerous meetings with landowner groups and key executives from the Enga and Hela provinces. In a significant show of its commitment to the region, company executives recently attended a People’s Party Foundation Dinner at the invitation of the Enga Provincial Governor, Grand Chief Sir Peter Ipatas, with PNG Prime Minister James Marape as the keynote speaker. Augustus Minerals executive chairman Brian Rodan said: “The Mt Kare Gold deposit is located 15km from the Porgera gold mine and shares many geological analogies, including roscoelite mineralisation and bonanza gold zones. Augustus has positioned itself as an applicant for Mt Kare through the purchase of ACM PNG, which holds a valid second in time exploration licence application, and thus holds an opportunity to potentially secure future access to the world class Mt Kare gold project.” The company’s PNG strategy is not a one-trick pony. It also holds an application over the 1900-square-kilometre Vanapa River gold project, sitting just 35km north of Port Moresby and 40km along strike from the 1.5-million-ounce Tolukuma gold mine.



In what could be a savvy bet, multi-billion-dollar gold producer Gold Fields emerged as a 5.33 per cent holder in Augustus in June this year, giving it a seat at the table should Mt Kare be awarded to the company. Its substantial stake also gives the mega miner a foothold in Augustus’ Music Well project, which covers a 1345-square-kilometre groundholding in Western Australia. Music Well sits at the heart of the storied Leonora-Laverton gold belt with a total endowment of more than 28 million ounces. Augustus’ ground abuts tenements held by regional giants Northern Star Resources and Genesis Minerals, alongside other major gold projects in the neighbourhood such as Darlot, King of the Hills and Thunderbox. The game in PNG is often won long before a drill rig ever turns a rod by demonstrating mining expertise and patient, respectful engagement with the people who own the land. While the geological prize at Mt Kare is tantalisingly big, it is Augustus’ groundwork in building political and social capital that may ultimately prove to be its most valuable asset. For the company, this elephant hunt appears to be a carefully choreographed campaign, not just a random shot at the stumps. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.content:
Breaking BusinessThe economyJobs The three factors driving NSW unemployment to a five-year high Matt Wade and Shane Wright October 15, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The number of people without a job in NSW has jumped by 34,000 in three months and the unemployment rate has reached a five-year high as rising interest rates, elevated petrol prices and falling house prices sap demand for employment across the state. The NSW unemployment rate hit 4.7 per cent last month, the highest since November 2021 when the state economy was recovering from the disruptions of the pandemic lockdowns. The number of people looking for work in NSW reached 223,000, also the highest since the COVID-19 crisis, figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show. Unemployment in NSW has reached a five-year high. Louie Douvis. If not for a fall in the labour force participation rate – the share of people in work or looking for work – last month’s jobless rate in NSW would have been higher.



The Reserve Bank raised interest rates in February, March and May and the latest figures show demand for employment in NSW has deteriorated sharply following those hikes: since June, the state’s unemployment rate has climbed from 4 per cent to 4.7 per cent. The total number of employed people in NSW last month was the lowest since January, meaning most of the jobs added this year have since been lost. KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said the rise in unemployment reflected the economic headwinds buffeting NSW. “We’ve had interest rate increases, we’ve got the fuel price shock working through the system, which is feeding into cost of living pressures, so all these factors have taken a bit of steam out of the NSW labour market,” he said. “Unfortunately, that does mean many people are not finding the hours they’re looking for, or not finding the jobs they’re looking for.”



Full-time male employment in NSW has been hit especially hard by the weakening jobs market – since June the number of men in the state with a full-time job has fallen by more than 31,000. Related Article Jobs RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits five-year high The figures pre-date the Reserve Bank’s most recent interest rate increase at the end of last month when it lifted the official cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. That move threatens to further sap demand for workers in NSW. Analysis by state Treasury, published in the June budget, showed the NSW economy is more sensitive to interest rate increases than other states. “The sensitivity arises from the higher level of house prices and the resulting larger mortgage payment burden relative to income for NSW households, which amplifies the effects of higher interest rates on disposable incomes, consumption, and housing market conditions,” the budget papers said.



In the March quarter of 2026, the average new housing loan for owner occupiers in NSW was $860,000, 28 per cent more than in Victoria. The September jobs figures show the state’s unemployment rate is now higher than forecast in the June budget which predicted the jobless rate would be 4.5 per cent in 2026-27. The NSW unemployment rate was consistently better than the national figure during the first half of this year, but the persistent economic headwinds have changed that. The lowest unemployment rate among the states in September was in South Australia and Western Australia, at 4.2 per cent, followed by Queensland with 4.5 per cent. The weaker employment conditions in NSW helped lift the national unemployment rate to a near five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September. Employment in Australia fell by 39,000 in the month. Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said the figures confirmed the overall softening in the nation’s jobs market which had become evident over recent months.



“The rise in the unemployment rate to 4.7 per cent gives the RBA more room to be patient and assess incoming inflation data before raising rates again. This is consistent with our view that a further rate hike will come in the first quarter of next year,” he said. World.title: Greens senator takes leave after letter raises allegations of inappropriate comments to women
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalWorkplace culture Greens senator takes leave after letter raises allegations of inappropriate comments to women James Massola Updated October 15, 2026 — 5:01pm ,first published 1:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Greens’ disability spokesman Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the Greens party room as new party leader David Shoebridge has ordered an independent investigation into allegations from party members that the WA senator made multiple inappropriate comments to women. In a letter sent to Shoebridge on Tuesday night and seen by this masthead, seven current Greens members write that the group are aware of “multiple allegations” against Steele-John between 2017 and 2025. Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Jordon Steele-John in the Senate on Thursday. Alex Ellinghausen “We have been made aware of multiple allegations ... being made against WA Federal Senator, Jordon Steele-John spanning almost a decade (2017-2025). These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to … be alone with him,” the authors state. “These warnings have come from inside and outside the party, demonstrating that knowledge of his alleged reputation extends beyond party membership and out into the community.”



The signatories include five current and former staffers and two active branch members. This masthead is aware of the identity of the authors of the letter sent to Greens party leaders this week but has chosen not to name them to protect their privacy, and in some cases to protect their current employment. In response to inquiries from this masthead about the range of allegations in the letter, Shoebridge announced that Steele-John was taking leave from the Greens party room. It was not clear if that included taking leave from parliament. Senator Jordon Steele-John talking with party leader David Shoebridge. Alex Ellinghausen Steele-John said that “I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not. I have referred this matter to the WA Greens, so that a fair, independent process can be commissioned that upholds the principles of natural justice and ensures procedural fairness for everyone involved. “These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it. The letter says that victims of sexual and family violence should be at the centre of any investigation. I agree. In the one complaint of which I have been made aware, I am the person who experienced family violence.”



Steele-John stated that he believed one of the allegations related to a former partner. “I believe an allegation arises from a former relationship in which I was the victim of extensive, prolonged and deeply distressing domestic abuse ... I have been working with WA Police to address the abuse I have experienced.” Deputy Greens leader Senator Steph Hodgins-May and Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge, who said it was not up to him to determine if findings of the inquiry would be made public. Alex Ellinghausen Shoebridge, said the Greens took allegations of this nature extremely seriously. “This matter needs to be resolved via a fair and independent review that ensures all parties are entitled to natural justice and procedural fairness,” he said.



“The Australian Greens take complaints seriously, and as leader I want to make it clear that the integrity of the complaints process is essential. In the circumstances Senator Steele-John has requested leave from the Party Room and I have accepted it.” A spokesman for Shoebridge said the investigation into Steele-John would be funded by the Western Australian branch of the Greens but it would be conducted by an independent third party. Steele-John is one of the best-known Greens senators in parliament and, as spokesman for disability and mental health, he has led the party’s campaign against Labor’s cuts to the NDIS. He entered parliament in November 2017 aged 23, the youngest senator ever at the time, through a casual vacancy created when Scott Ludlam resigned from the Senate after discovering he was ineligible as a dual citizen.



In the letter seen by this masthead, the authors state “many of us joined the Greens because of their strong public position to believe women. This should be the premise upon which an investigation is commenced. “Any allegation ... levelled against anyone in the party must be investigated thoroughly and with the victim at the centre. It must also be investigated from our public position of believing the courageous women who make these reports.” The authors ask Shoebridge to take three steps: commission an independent investigation into every allegation against Steele-John; require the party to update protocols so the threshold for acting on allegations does not rely on police charges; and notify all signatories to the letter of the outcome of the investigation. The letter notes that “all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the Party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations.” The authors go on to claim that “for every person brave enough to sign this letter, there are multiple others who were too fearful of backlash by Senator Steele-John and others in the party to sign on. This is power in action, silencing those who want to be heard, but who feel too unsafe to speak.”



And it concludes by reminding Shoebridge that he had recently posted to his Instagram account that “men need to speak up. In the clubrooms, at the pub, on our streets. Demand better from our mates, our team, our colleagues.” The authors then state: “This is us demanding better from our party.” Senator Jordon Steele-John at the start of his parliamentary career with then-leader Richard Di Natale. Andrew Meares The allegations about Steele-John’s conduct present a challenge to Shoebridge, who has promised to be more consultative with Greens party members and has outlined plans for his party to take the fight to Labor, rather than simply support government legislation. At a press conference in Canberra on Thursday afternoon, Shoebridge said he was not previously aware of the allegations reported by this masthead against Steele-John.



“No, I received the correspondence in my capacity as leader of the Australian Greens, and I’ve dealt with it with … urgency,” he said. Shoebridge said would be “inappropriate” for him to determine if the findings of the inquiry into the allegations would be made public. “This will be an independent inquiry, and it would be totally inappropriate for me to determine how that inquiry is undertaken,” Shoebridge said. “But I stress, the key parameters for this inquiry are fair, and independent, and timely.” Shoebridge said that he had confidence the inquiry would be independent, which was “necessary for all parties to be involved”. “It is not my role, and it would be inappropriate for me, as the leader of the Australian Greens in the federal parliament, to be imposing controls on that.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Golden Dragon Mining has unearthed a substantial 2.2-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly from recent auger drilling at its Stella Range project outside Laverton in Western Australia.

The untested discovery sits in a well-endowed gold neighbourhood, 120km southeast of the prolific Laverton goldfield and just 12km along strike from Brightstar Resources’ Lord Byron deposit, which hosts 5.39 million tonnes grading 1.5 grams per tonne (g/t) for 267,000 ounces of gold.

Golden Dragon Mining’s auger drilling has defined a 2.2km-long gold anomaly at its Stella Range project outside Laverton in Western Australia.

The company says the coherent, northwest-trending anomaly is also supported by key pathfinder elements, particularly copper and tellurium. The geology adds further weight to the discovery, with Stella Range’s main gold anomaly sitting within a magnetic low that mirrors the setting at Lord Byron. The anomaly is also interpreted to lie on the same northwest-trending magnetic corridor as the deposit, raising the prospect of a similar gold-bearing system lurking beneath the surface.

The ground was previously explored by the likes of BHP for large komatiite-style nickel sulphide deposits, with Golden Dragon taking a different tack after reviewing the historical work through a gold-tinted lens.

World.title: The Renshaw influence behind breakout star’s shock push for World Cup berth
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket The Renshaw influence behind breakout star’s shock push for World Cup berth Nick Wright October 15, 2026 — 4:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Matthew Renshaw’s influence on Australian cricket is stretching beyond his first Test heroics in South Africa, with breakout one-day gun Hugh Weibgen shedding light on how the reborn batsman has shaped his own international ambitions. As Renshaw spearheaded the nation to a 214-run victory, Weibgen was pushing his credentials for a shock 2027 World Cup berth – striking back-to-back centuries for Queensland in the unfamiliar position of opener, as he seeks to turn his hyped talent into a dominant career. The 21-year-old’s first ton of the summer came against a New South Wales attack boasting Australian limited overs stars Sean Abbott and Ben Dwarshuis, while his second against Western Australia anchored the Bulls’ innings of 261 to inspire a 15-run win. Hugh Weibgen, pictured in action for Australia at the 2024 Under-19s World Cup, has begun to capitalise on his potential with back-to-bakc centuries for Queensland. Gallo Images Australia currently sits fourth in the ODI rankings, however their form in the 50-over game has been patchy at best, winning just four of 12 series since their 2023 World Cup triumph in India.



Only one Australian – Travis Head – is within the world’s top-20 ranked batsmen (17), as the nation hunts for its winning formula following the retirements of Steve Smith, David Warner and Glenn Maxwell from the XI who claimed the trophy. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Pick and stick’: Waugh urges Aussie selectors to stop ‘messing about’ Weibgen, who led the nation to Under-19s World Cup glory in 2024, told this masthead he would not look too far ahead, despite selectors showing a willingness to throw younger men into the fray – headlined by Ollie Peake, who has played more one-day cricket for Australia than his state Victoria (eight of 15 total games). “Obviously, you dream to play for Australia one day, so you think about that, but I haven’t really given it too much thought. I’m just trying to win games for Queensland, and if I can do that, I’m sure that will take care of itself,” he said. But Weibgen revealed it was Renshaw’s recommendation to link him with the same psychologist who has helped inspire his own ascent to an Australian three-format player which has laid the foundations for the rookie to propel himself towards being in the conversation for higher honours.



Renshaw has previously stressed the key to his resurgence across the short and long cricket codes stemmed from a more relaxed outlook to his game, with life off the pitch more stable than when he was younger and in a mental bubble pushing for greater success. That new outlook has coincided with T20 international selection and ODI success (including a maiden century against Zimbabwe last month), before culminating in his match-winning 190 and 82 in the first South Africa Test. Loading It was a lesson his fellow Brisbane Grammar School alumnus was eager to take on board, who has since consulted Stuart Smith “a couple of times a week” for the past year-and-a-half. “I put lots of time into batting, bowling and fielding, and those things like recovery, but I probably didn’t have that consistent mental training. I was already thinking of going down that route, and then simply asked Rens if he saw someone, and he flicked me through the details,” Weibgen said.



“It’s helping me unlock the most positive version of myself whilst I’m batting. I guess having other stuff go on in my life, it’s always good for me to find that balance. I’m always on the side of cricket is everything, but having that balance has been a lot better and probably healthier. “But the big focus is how can I improve in that batting side of things and deal with the highs and lows and try stay nice and level.” A self-confessed cricket tragic who actively seeks out his childhood idol Mike Hussey whenever he is nearby, Weigben’s determination to cement himself as a future linchpin of Australian cricket meant he barely had an off season. A winter spent playing club cricket in England was followed by his inclusion in a development tour to India as he sought to hone his craft. Those experiences supported two development areas. In the UK, he took a more positive, attacking approach to his batting, while in India, he broadened his stroke play – including “a couple of sweep shots” – to improve his prospects against spin bowling.



While the World Cup is still 12 months away, and the right-hander is still very much in the fledgling stages of his career, Weigben sensed the conditions he had been exposed to would pave the way to become a more consistent contributor in Bulls – and ideally, Australian – colours. “Being put in different positions, batting in different spots in the order and different conditions all helps add to your craft, learning your own game plan and what you need to do in different situations,” he said. “All those experiences have definitely helped me.” Queensland faces South Australia in the One-Day Cup from 10am AEST on Thursday. World.title: Broken Hill lines up drill bit on huge copper-gold target in SA
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill lines up drill bit on huge copper-gold target in SA Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd October 15, 2026 — 4:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Broken Hill Gold has launched a 3000-metre drilling campaign at its White Dam project in South Australia to test a major geophysical target lurking beneath recent high-grade copper-gold hits, raising the tantalising prospect of linking several deposits into one large system. The company’s latest induced polarisation (IP) and ground magnetic surveys have outlined a robust 1.5-square-kilometre chargeability anomaly coinciding with a one-square-kilometre magnetic anomaly beneath its Icebreaker discovery, suggesting the once gold-focused project could be emerging as a massive copper-gold system at depth. Broken Hill Gold’s geophysical surveys have outlined a large, deep target at its White Dam project in South Australia. With drilling set to kick off this weekend, Broken Hill is poised to put its compelling new target to the test in a rapidly emerging iron ore copper gold (IOCG) province, where the potential for major discoveries has major players circling. The discovery of a high-grade sulphide system at Icebreaker came about almost entirely by accident, after the company punched through its shallow, 20,400-ounce oxide gold resource into a richer gold-copper sulphide zone below.



‘We now have coincident IP and magnetic anomalies over a large area, in a zone we already know is well mineralised’ Broken Hill Gold chief executive officer Matthew Boyes Now, the geophysics suggests Icebreaker could be just the tip of the iceberg. The IP survey defined two key features, including a shallower northwestern anomaly sitting directly beneath high-grade sulphide mineralisation already struck at Icebreaker, pointing to potential extensions of the known copper-gold system both at depth and along strike. However, a deeper and much stronger eastern anomaly is shaping up as the main prize. It shows a chargeability reading six times the background level and trends north from the edge of another historic Hannaford deposit. A ground magnetic survey has also defined a hefty one-square-kilometre high-intensity feature coinciding with the IP chargeability anomalies, which the company says points to iron oxide alteration, consistent with the magnetite-pyrite alteration observed at Icebreaker and a hallmark of large IOCG deposits. Broken Hill Gold chief executive officer Matthew Boyes said: “This is an excellent result, delivered in a very short turnaround time, and the geophysics crews have performed exceptionally. We now have coincident IP and magnetic anomalies over a large area, in a zone we already know is well mineralised – that is an extremely compelling set of drill targets. The strength and consistency of the IP anomaly makes it an outstanding target in its own right.” The project sits within South Australia’s Curnamona Province, a region renowned for its major IOCG deposits. Havilah Resources’ Kalkaroo project, just 40km north of White Dam, hosts a massive 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold, alongside 23,200 tonnes of cobalt. That project has now attracted heavyweight interest, with Sandfire Resources securing the right to acquire an 80 per cent stake for consideration of up to A$222.6 million, while committing a further A$30 million to regional exploration.



Importantly, the existing Hannaford deposit, which hosts a resource of 43,300 ounces of gold, along with the Icebreaker and Rolling prospects, all sit around the margins of the combined geophysical anomalies. Their positioning suggests they could form part of a single, much bigger alteration system that remains largely untested at depth, with most historical drilling averaging just 50m. The company is now preparing to put the theory to the test with an initial reverse circulation (RC) and diamond drilling campaign designed to probe the system at depth for the first time. Deeper diamond holes will reach depths of up to 400m, providing the first serious test of both the northwestern and main eastern induced polarisation (IP) anomalies. With White Dam continuing to produce gold doré and offering a potential pathway to self-funded exploration, Broken Hill has an enviable platform from which to chase a much bigger prize. If the drill bit backs up the geophysics, the company could be on the cusp of transforming White Dam from a modest gold producer into a much bigger copper-gold story, with Icebreaker potentially opening the door to a district-scale discovery. World.title: Kmart sold fingernail glue that burnt without safety warnings, watchdog says
World.content:
Breaking BusinessConsumer affairsConsumer safety Kmart sold fingernail glue that burnt without safety warnings, watchdog says Elias Visontay and Jessica Yun Updated October 15, 2026 — 4:23pm ,first published 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The consumer watchdog has taken Kmart to court alleging the retailer sold millions of bottles of glue used for fake fingernails without adequately warning customers about burn risks. Customers, including children, claimed they suffered third-degree burns and required hospitalisation and in some cases skin grafts to treat injuries caused by Kmart’s home brand OXX nail glue, according to Federal Court legal documents filed by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) on Thursday. The ACCC has taken legal action against Kmart. iStock In addition to burning skin, consumers complained the glue caused steaming, smoking, burning or melting when it came into contact with fabric. The ACCC is alleging Kmart breached consumer law in selling seven varieties of its OXX nail glue. Even through it received more than 50 customer complaints between August 2017 and December 2024, Kmart continued selling the products without disclosing burn risk warnings, the ACCC said. It updated its packaging in December 2024, but continued selling pre-existing products without the warning until February 2025, court documents said.



“It’s a chemical reaction, in essence, where the glue comes into contact with fabric,” ACCC deputy chair Catriona Lowe told this masthead. Related Article Consumer rights ‘Left with no choice’: Amazon accused of ripping off Prime customers with ads “Let’s say, for example, you were applying the product onto your hands, and you were wearing a pair of trousers. If the product dripped onto the trouser, that’s where the reaction would occur … if the fabric is on your skin, it burns, and in some instances, can stick.” The product is still for sale on Kmart’s website. Kmart has been contacted for comment. There was no information about the risk of burns on either the packaging or the bottle, despite containing instructions and other safety warnings about avoiding contact with skin and eyes; using the product with irritated or infected nails or skin; and when to seek medical advice if the glue came into contact with eyes or was swallowed, the ACCC alleged.



“Not all consumers can afford to go regularly to the nail salon to have these products applied professionally. However, we expect that consumers will be warned about material risks that they are engaging with, so they can make a choice at the time of purchase about whether or not they are comfortable to take on that risk,” said Lowe. “That opportunity, we say, was not provided to consumers in this instance.” Lowe said it was an “incredibly serious matter” that Kmart failed to warn customers of burn risks, despite receiving numerous reports of burn injuries. “The intention is the warning is immediately visible to consumers as they’re scanning the range of products on shelves,” she said. “We expect all businesses, especially large businesses like Kmart, to have consumer safety front of mind, and withholding safety information can amount to false or misleading representations in breach of the Australian consumer law.” The ACCC’s legal action also alleges additional breaches of consumer law related to Kmart selling button batteries in kids digital watches and GPS smart tags for tracking.



Button batteries are small flat discs that have a history of causing death and serious injury in children who unwittingly swallow them. They can burn through the oesophagus within hours of being ingested. Related Video Video icon 1:46 Urgent warning over potentially deadly button batteries While products containing button batteries are legal to sell, there are strict information standards requiring labelling to warn parents of the potential danger. The ACCC has alleged Kmart failed in its requirement to conduct safety feature testing for two models of Anko kids digital watches and seven models of analogue watches prior to selling them to customers. It sold about 64,000 of the button battery-powered watches between June 2022 and November 2024.



“These watches contained button batteries, but Kmart did not test them prior to supply to show that young children could not open the battery compartments. This is despite many of the watches being specifically designed for children,” Lowe said. The ACCC claims Kmart sold 800 Anko-branded GPS tracking tags that did not comply with safety standards because they carried some but not all warnings required by the law. A Kmart spokeswoman said the company was “disappointed at [the ACCC’s] decision to take action on historical matters” given the retailer had cooperated with the watchdog’s investigation and had addressed the issues. In relation to the fingernail glue products, the spokeswoman said:“We regret any injury associated with these products and apologise to anyone affected.” “Kmart remains of the view the labelling and warnings were appropriate to prevent misuse. We take our reporting obligations seriously and submitted mandatory injury reports about these products to the ACCC,” the spokeswoman said.



Under consumer law, selling products without mandatory safety information carries a maximum penalty of $100 million for a company. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Augustus circles giant PNG gold prize in Porgera backyard
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Augustus circles giant PNG gold prize in Porgera backyard Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 15, 2026 — 4:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Augustus Minerals has its sights firmly set on elephant country, updating the market on its strategic push into Papua New Guinea (PNG), where it’s angling to secure the highly prospective 2.5-million-ounces gold equivalent Mt Kare gold-silver project, a stone’s throw from one of the world’s most significant gold mines. The company’s subsidiary, ACM PNG, holds a “second-in-time” exploration licence application over the Mt Kare project, positioned a mere 15 kilometres from Barrick Gold’s colossal 32-million-ounce Porgera gold mine. Brian Rodan, executive chairman of Augustus Minerals, holding drill core from the 2.5-million-ounce Mt Kare gold-silver project in PNG. The geological credentials of Mt Kare are particularly compelling. The project is classed as a rare alkalic-epithermal gold deposit, a geological clan that hosts some of the planet’s most lucrative members such as PNG’s own Lihir mine, with a hefty 47 million gold ounces and the Cadia-Ridgeway system in New South Wales, featuring more than 50 million ounces. In the past, Mt Kare has thrown up some monster drill hits including 111m at 9.8 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 4m and 17.7m at 100g/t gold from 59m, along with a coffee-spitting 20m at 443g/t gold - the sorts of numbers that would get the West Perth mining fraternity leaping out of bed each morning.



‘Augustus holds an opportunity to potentially secure future access to the world-class Mt Kare gold project.’ Augustus Minerals executive chairman Brian Rodan Augustus says Mt Kare and Porgera are geological cousins, both sitting within the 2300km-long New Guinea Metallogenic Belt. The company’s modelling suggests Mt Kare may represent a higher-level, less-eroded expression of a much larger, deep-seated gold system, with the world-class Porgera mine representing the deeper root of a similar system. Notably, the Mt Kare deposit is about 500 metres higher in elevation than Porgera, while historical drilling has only tested to about 350m below the surface, leaving its deeper gold potential largely untested. First discovered in 1987, the project boasts a rich exploration history and an extraordinary early gold rush. Between 1988 and 1991, an estimated one million ounces of alluvial gold were reportedly recovered from the area by some 3000 artisanal miners, highlighting the sheer richness of the system. Previous owners have reportedly sunk $60 million into exploration, including 350 diamond holes. Augustus is now leveraging this wealth of information after purchasing all available open-file data from PNG’s Mineral Resources Authority. It has since compiled a full technical memorandum on the project’s history, geology and mineralisation.



While the prize is immense, the path to securing it is complex. The Mt Kare application is contested, with Augustus currently second in line. Crucially, it’s not necessarily first in best dressed, with the government having the final say on who secures the coveted exploration licence. Its assessment considers a raft of criteria, including technical expertise, financial capacity, proposed work programs, landowner support and consent and compliance with environmental and statutory requirements. So the company isn’t sitting idly by, waiting for a decision from bureaucrats. Notably, Augustus’ executive chairman Brian Rodan, a mining veteran with half a century of industry experience, has some previous form at Mt Kare. He was the managing director of mining contractor ACM PNG when it was awarded a contract in 2012 to do the stage-one underground drilling and all important mine development at the project, ticking several big boxes on the government’s wish list. Ticking a further but equally important box, the company has also been actively building relationships on the ground, a critical component for success in PNG. The company’s management has held numerous meetings with landowner groups and key executives from the Enga and Hela provinces. In a significant show of its commitment to the region, company executives recently attended a People’s Party Foundation Dinner at the invitation of the Enga Provincial Governor, Grand Chief Sir Peter Ipatas, with PNG Prime Minister James Marape as the keynote speaker. Augustus Minerals executive chairman Brian Rodan said: “The Mt Kare Gold deposit is located 15km from the Porgera gold mine and shares many geological analogies, including roscoelite mineralisation and bonanza gold zones. Augustus has positioned itself as an applicant for Mt Kare through the purchase of ACM PNG, which holds a valid second in time exploration licence application, and thus holds an opportunity to potentially secure future access to the world class Mt Kare gold project.” The company’s PNG strategy is not a one-trick pony. It also holds an application over the 1900-square-kilometre Vanapa River gold project, sitting just 35km north of Port Moresby and 40km along strike from the 1.5-million-ounce Tolukuma gold mine.



In what could be a savvy bet, multi-billion-dollar gold producer Gold Fields emerged as a 5.33 per cent holder in Augustus in June this year, giving it a seat at the table should Mt Kare be awarded to the company. Its substantial stake also gives the mega miner a foothold in Augustus’ Music Well project, which covers a 1345-square-kilometre groundholding in Western Australia. Music Well sits at the heart of the storied Leonora-Laverton gold belt with a total endowment of more than 28 million ounces. Augustus’ ground abuts tenements held by regional giants Northern Star Resources and Genesis Minerals, alongside other major gold projects in the neighbourhood such as Darlot, King of the Hills and Thunderbox. The game in PNG is often won long before a drill rig ever turns a rod by demonstrating mining expertise and patient, respectful engagement with the people who own the land. While the geological prize at Mt Kare is tantalisingly big, it is Augustus’ groundwork in building political and social capital that may ultimately prove to be its most valuable asset. For the company, this elephant hunt appears to be a carefully choreographed campaign, not just a random shot at the stumps. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.content:
Breaking BusinessThe economyJobs The three factors driving NSW unemployment to a five-year high Matt Wade and Shane Wright October 15, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The number of people without a job in NSW has jumped by 34,000 in three months and the unemployment rate has reached a five-year high as rising interest rates, elevated petrol prices and falling house prices sap demand for employment across the state. The NSW unemployment rate hit 4.7 per cent last month, the highest since November 2021 when the state economy was recovering from the disruptions of the pandemic lockdowns. The number of people looking for work in NSW reached 223,000, also the highest since the COVID-19 crisis, figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show. Unemployment in NSW has reached a five-year high. Louie Douvis. If not for a fall in the labour force participation rate – the share of people in work or looking for work – last month’s jobless rate in NSW would have been higher.



The Reserve Bank raised interest rates in February, March and May and the latest figures show demand for employment in NSW has deteriorated sharply following those hikes: since June, the state’s unemployment rate has climbed from 4 per cent to 4.7 per cent. The total number of employed people in NSW last month was the lowest since January, meaning most of the jobs added this year have since been lost. KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said the rise in unemployment reflected the economic headwinds buffeting NSW. “We’ve had interest rate increases, we’ve got the fuel price shock working through the system, which is feeding into cost of living pressures, so all these factors have taken a bit of steam out of the NSW labour market,” he said. “Unfortunately, that does mean many people are not finding the hours they’re looking for, or not finding the jobs they’re looking for.”



Full-time male employment in NSW has been hit especially hard by the weakening jobs market – since June the number of men in the state with a full-time job has fallen by more than 31,000. Related Article Jobs RBA on notice to hold off on rate rises as jobless rate hits five-year high The figures pre-date the Reserve Bank’s most recent interest rate increase at the end of last month when it lifted the official cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. That move threatens to further sap demand for workers in NSW. Analysis by state Treasury, published in the June budget, showed the NSW economy is more sensitive to interest rate increases than other states. “The sensitivity arises from the higher level of house prices and the resulting larger mortgage payment burden relative to income for NSW households, which amplifies the effects of higher interest rates on disposable incomes, consumption, and housing market conditions,” the budget papers said.



In the March quarter of 2026, the average new housing loan for owner occupiers in NSW was $860,000, 28 per cent more than in Victoria. The September jobs figures show the state’s unemployment rate is now higher than forecast in the June budget which predicted the jobless rate would be 4.5 per cent in 2026-27. The NSW unemployment rate was consistently better than the national figure during the first half of this year, but the persistent economic headwinds have changed that. The lowest unemployment rate among the states in September was in South Australia and Western Australia, at 4.2 per cent, followed by Queensland with 4.5 per cent. The weaker employment conditions in NSW helped lift the national unemployment rate to a near five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September. Employment in Australia fell by 39,000 in the month. Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said the figures confirmed the overall softening in the nation’s jobs market which had become evident over recent months.



“The rise in the unemployment rate to 4.7 per cent gives the RBA more room to be patient and assess incoming inflation data before raising rates again. This is consistent with our view that a further rate hike will come in the first quarter of next year,” he said. World.title: Auckland's Carmel College principal slams 'unacceptable' behaviour after students' cars egged
World.content:
The Principal of an Auckland girls school is raising concerns after students' cars were egged, calling the behaviour unacceptable.

Carmel College principal Sarah Kemble has sent a message to the school community, saying while throwing eggs at cars may be intended as a joke, she's concerned it could escalate to property damage or harm to students.

"We have been in contact with our neighbouring secondary schools, Westlake Boys and Girls High Schools and Rosmini College, as this behaviour is unacceptable and is a concern for our wider school communities," she said.

They did not want senior students sitting their practical exams to be distracted or stressed by the pranks, she said.

"I also ask that students do not retaliate or take matters into their own hands, as this could further escalate the situation," Kemble said

She was urging caregivers to have conversations at home about the pranks and impact actions can have on others.

"If you (your daughter) drives to school, you may also wish to discuss whether using public transport is an option while this behaviour is occurring."

World.title: Holding the centre: Future voters might thank National and Labour for unsexy politics
World.content:
Audio player for " Winding up Winston, the rule of ruling things out, Peter Dunne's heir, and the boring work of saving democracy " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/1927783%2Fholding-the-centre-future-voters-might-thank-national-and-labour-for-unsexy-politics

Winding up Winston, the rule of ruling things out, Peter Dunne's heir, and the boring work of saving democracy Caucus Download MP3 52m

Analysis: The Election 2026 campaign so far has failed to catch fire. It's been a series of promises failing to capture the moment. A flurry of hand grenades that have failed to detonate. An October with no surprise. A trail with no destination. But maybe there's a reason to celebrate all the same.

On this week's Caucus podcast, RNZ's deputy political editor Craig McCulloch said he was relieved he wasn't in the studio for the NZ Herald Leaders' Debate because he "might have lost the will to live". The rehearsed attacks, recycled arguments, and lack of vision arguably sums up the "rinse and repeat" campaign we've seen so far.

"Primarily it's the curse of the economic and global climate. But it's also a curse of leadership."

Watching Chris Hipkins and Christopher Luxon debate the State of the Nation, it's hard not to see two men who lack the political imagination to move the dial. The commentary on their two debates thus far has been pretty scathing.

But, as the Caucus team discuss in this week's episode, there's another way to look at these two major party leaders, stuck on 20 percent approval ratings and leading parties with a combined vote of 56-58 percent, the lowest in the MMP era. Uninspiring, sure. Losing ground to the other parties, undoubtedly. But how about - responsible?

Take a step back and view this election from, say, 2050, and you might have a very different take on these supposedly boring, stale parties sitting in the centre of our political spectrum. Maybe the 2050 voter might be grateful to those who took on the thankless task of holding the centre during this turbulent time in politics.

NZME / Dean Purcell

This is by no means an endorsement of them or a dismissal of the minor parties as radical or extreme. But there's no doubt we are living in polarising times when democratic norms are fracturing. There are some good reasons for that, including the failure of mainstream parties like National and Labour failing to deliver on their promises. And there are some nutty and conspiratorial reasons.

But more and more people are undoubtedly looking to the edges of our politics and outsiders for solutions. It was notable that Luxon, in Wednesday's debate, referred to himself several times as someone who was not a career politician and who had only been in parliament six years. When Keith Holyoake or Robert Muldoon was running his party, that would have been seen as a liability. Today, he's selling it as a badge of honour.

Yet strip away the hyperbole, fearmongering, and strongly worded attack lines, and both Labour and National have relatively similar, centrist approaches to large chunks of government. They're not twins. What they prioritise and how they operate vary. Their differences on, say, pay equity and education standards have real world impacts and mean your vote matters. But the self-imposed boundaries they operate within in - the fiscal plans, norms of political behaviour, and rules of social cohesion - are relatively similar and centrist.

So there's a case to be made that Labour and National are doing the unsexy work of a tight forward, propping up our stable government and strong democracy like a forward would a scrum. They're being damned as stale and boring, but perhaps they are stopping the scrum screwing in a way that reins in the extreme left-right swings we are seeing in some parts of the world. So, whoever we support, perhaps we should give them some flowers for being the kings of continuity and the sultans of stability. As unpopular as it is right now, maybe our future selves will be grateful of parties who held to some orthodoxy in these unorthodox times.

Two examples: If you're a left-wing voter despairing at the agenda of the current right-wing coalition, perhaps consider the importance of National in refusing to ditch the Climate Change Commission and withdraw from the Paris Agreement. Or if you're a right-wing voter anxious about the promises of a high-spending left-wing coalition, think how important it is to New Zealand's continuity that Labour is ruling out rapid tax reform and such a minimal capital gains tax.

For the first time in a long time, nearly half of voters have no patience for this orthodoxy and, for now at least, are determined to resist the pull of the centre. Only time will tell whether that's for the good of New Zealand or not. But in a world where political norms are collapsing and elections have become times of immense volatility, maybe, just maybe, a couple of boring Chrises holding to either side of the centre deserve a little more credit than they're getting.

World.title: Starship Hospital's cancer ward three months away from full staff after chemotherapy delays
World.content:
Audio player for " Some Starship child cancer treatments delayed amid staff shortages " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/1927376%2Fstarship-hospital-s-cancer-ward-three-months-away-from-full-staff-after-chemotherapy-delays

Some Starship child cancer treatments delayed amid staff shortages Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

Health NZ says it will be three months before Starship Hospital's cancer ward is fully staffed.

It said 20 cycles of chemotherapy had been delayed over the past four months due to a lack of staff, but noted that delays never exceeded a week.

"For context, we deliver over that period around 500 to 600 cycles of chemotherapy," Health NZ's director of operations for Auckland Dr Mike Shepherd told Checkpoint.

Two bone marrow transplants had been delayed, and two patients from outside Auckland had been transferred to Christchurch.

The Nurses Organisation said nurses had long been concerned about the lack of staff in Starship's cancer ward.

"This has been signalled by nurses for a long time, there should have been a lot more energy put into workforce recruitment, retention and supporting and training nurses into this specialised area," NZNO Kaiwhakahaere Kerri Nuku said.

"There is no excuse for this under-resourcing of a really vulnerable service."

She said staffing data it obtained under the Official Information Act showed that in August, 86 percent of the shifts in Starship's oncology ward were below target staffing levels.

Shepherd confirmed the figure, but noted that this had decreased to 73 percent in September and to 33 percent in the first two weeks of October.

Health NZ

"We are really pleased to say we have been recruiting well. We have four new staff started and a further seven arriving over the next three months or so and I think that'll get us up to full complement and that'll be great for our team," Shepherd said.

"We will continue to use nursing staff across the rest of the organisation to complement the nurses we have in that ward."

The Nurses Organisation said it was only given data up to the end of August.

The number of "shifts below target" had steadily risen since January, when 18 percent of shifts were understaffed, up to 53 percent in July, before spiking in August.

Nuku said the short staffing was "deliberate."

"This is equivalent to 6 full-time nurses short in the haematology and oncology inpatient ward for August."

Tertiary providers were recently told to limit nursing enrolments to 2025 levels, because there are not enough student placement spots available in hospitals.

Nurse educators told RNZ on Wednesday the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) directive makes no sense as pressure on the workforce builds.

Tertiary Education Commission chief executive Tim Fowler said told Morning Report on Thursday the limit would mean around 700 less enrolments.

World.title: Auckland's Starship Hospital delays some cancer treatments due to nurse shortage
World.content:
The health minister has confirmed some cancer treatments have been delayed by up to seven days at Auckland's Starship Children's Hospital.

Earlier on Thursday morning, Health New Zealand's Starship Hospital director, Dr Greg Williams said the paediatric haematology/oncology service has had to reschedule some treatments due to a shortage of nurses.

"These decisions are not made lightly and are based on clinical need. Starship is recruiting experienced and new graduate nurses as quickly as possible," Dr Williams said.

Do you know more? Get in touch at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

A spokesperson for Health Minister Simeon Brown told RNZ he had asked Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley for an explanation.

The spokesperson says all children at Starship Hospital are still being treated, though a handful of chemotherapy sessions have been delayed for a few days - but no more than seven.

Two bone marrow transplants were moved "slightly", but both were still going ahead.

The spokesperson said vacancies at Health NZ are the result of natural attrition such as parental leave and retirement and there is no hiring freeze.

Dr Williams said the oncology departments are being supported by staff in other parts of Starship and Auckland City Hospital.

Though the spokesperson for Brown's office stressed no treatments were suspended, only rescheduled, Nurses Organisation Kaiwhakahaere Kerri Nuku was unconvinced.

"Health Minister Simeon Brown can argue oncology services are being postponed and not suspended but such semantics are unlikely to be important to whānau with children with cancer," she said in a statement.

"The haematology/oncology ward 27B at Starship has been under-staffed all year and Te Whatu Ora should have hired more nurses before they were forced to suspend vital cancer treatments for sick children."

Health NZ data showed 86 percent of shifts at Starship's Haemotology/Oncology Ward were understaffed during August.

Health NZ

The number of "shifts below target" had steadily risen since January, when 18 percent of shifts were understaffed, up to 53 percent in July, before spiking in August.

Nuku said the short staffing was "deliberate."

"This is equivalent to 6 full-time nurses short in the haematology and oncology inpatient ward for August."

A nurse had anonymously told the New Zealand Herald she and other staff were "horrified and appalled" by the news, which had the potential to adversely affect patient outcomes.

She believed parents would be shocked by the development.

"You're increasing the risk of complications and death from cancers," the nurse told the Herald.

RNZ has asked how many patients have been affected by the delays and how many staff the hospital is short of. Health New Zealand is yet to answer those questions.

The nurse also told the Herald that the severe staffing shortage was not only related to the winter flu spike but had been critical "all of this year".

"Over the last year with budget constraints, they've not hired new nurses. Anytime a nurse left, they weren't replaced."

The Herald also reported the nurse said the hospital had lost a lot of senior nurses.

Tertiary providers were recently told to limit nursing enrolments to 2025 levels, because there are not enough student placement spots available in hospitals.

Nurse educators told RNZ on Wednesday the Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) directive makes no sense as pressure on the workforce builds.

Audio player for " TEC defends limits on nursing student enrolments " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/1918105%2Fauckland-s-starship-hospital-delays-some-cancer-treatments-due-to-nurse-shortage

TEC defends limits on nursing student enrolments Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Tertiary Education Commission Chief executive Tim Fowler said told Morning Report on Thursday the limit would mean around 700 less enrolments.

He said enrolments in nursing have gone up by 30 percent in the last six years - from about 8000 to just over 11,000.

A Nelson councillor whose child was treated for neuroblastoma at Starship said upon hearing the news she felt "primal rage."

"I felt everything I've eaten today come up in my throat, I wanted to be sick," Labour-endorsed councillor Sarah Kerby said.

"So much of your life is uncertain when you're going through that treatment, and I thought of the siblings at home who don't know when mum or dad is going to be with them next.

"I think of those people who've travelled from across the Pacific to access those supports at Starship and the impact this is having."

She said delays and staffing issues would damage New Zealanders' faith in the health system.

"The right to free, quality public healthcare is something that New Zealanders would consider part of our national identity.
